en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*, Volume One.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was in the realm of space, the differentiation of the dharma-realm.

The dwelling place—universally adorned and pure, stainless and immaculate, manifested by the merit, wisdom, and sovereign power of all Tathāgatas; transcending the conditioned activities of the triple world, surpassing all analogies, inconceivable, and born of the karmic fruition of all Tathāgatas—stood upon a most excellent pavilion with a sublime jewel terrace. There, he was accompanied by a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats, endowed with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and possessed of both types of liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*).

Together with a multitude of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were utterly pure, who had attained the meditative realm of the samādhi of permanence and impermanence, who contemplated the sphere of activity of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), who had reached the further shore of the dharma-realm that is neither middle nor extreme, who had fulfilled all the vows of Bodhisattvas, who were endowed with all the masteries of Bodhisattvas, who adorned themselves with ten inexhaustible and immeasurable merits, and who were possessed of all Bodhisattva dhāraṇīs, samādhis, and the four types of unimpeded wisdom;

together also with hundreds of thousands of millions of devas of great majesty and power—nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra-devendra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings—along with their retinues, also numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions.
At that time, the sūtra spoken by the Bhagavān was titled "The Dharma Gate of Entering the Successive Stages of All Practices. It is as follows:
those who see the various noble ones (āryas) are able to give rise to faith; those who attain faith accomplish the mind of aspiration;
those who attain the mind of aspiration for wholesome dharmas accomplish the uninterrupted mind; and those who attain the uninterrupted mind accomplish...

The mind of meaning; one who attains the mind of meaning accomplishes the higher mind (*adhi-citta*). This is because one who practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) accomplishes great wealth;
one who practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) accomplishes the fruits of rebirth among humans and devas;

and one who practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) accomplishes all forms of adornment. One who practices the perfection of... [vigour]... [accomplishes... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated.]
The *dāna-pāramitā* is for the sake of accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas;
the practitioner of the *dhyāna-pāramitā* accomplishes a pliant and supple mind; the practitioner of the *prajñā-pāramitā* accomplishes wisdom that transcends all worlds;
and the practitioner of the *upāya-pāramitā* accomplishes all things without obstruction.
Because of its unimpeded nature; because one who practices the perfection of aspiration spontaneously accomplishes all tasks;
because one who practices the perfection of power achieves that which is indestructible;
because one who practices the perfection of wisdom achieves the state of being a refuge for all the world; and because the renunciant acts for the sake of accomplishing the Noble Path.
Wearing dyed robes is for the sake of distancing oneself from all worldly affairs; begging for alms is for the sake of destroying all prideful minds;
dwelling in forest hermitages (āraṇya) is for the sake of accomplishing fearlessness;

sitting in meditative seclusion is for the sake of accomplishing the immeasurable supernormal powers (abhijñā) and so forth; and hearing and upholding the Dharma is for the sake of accomplishing the four [reliances].
Because they are unimpeded; because those who cultivate the skillful means of mindfulness achieve dhāraṇīs;

because those who cultivate the skillful means of intention achieve the wisdom that discerns the distinctions between phenomena; because those who cultivate firm practice achieve fearlessness in large assemblies;
because those who cultivate the skillful means of eloquence achieve unerringness in their prophetic explanations; [and] because they cultivate the aggregates...

The skillful means of the bases (*āyatana*) are for the sake of accomplishing the distinctions of *prajñā*; the skillful means of the elements (*dhātu*) are for the sake of accomplishing the distinctions of subtle *prajñā*;
the skillful means of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) are for the sake of accomplishing the mind’s detachment from internal and external delusion;
the skillful means of the truths (*satya*) are for the sake of accomplishing non-deception of all sentient beings; and the skillful means of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
One who practices in accordance with the intentions of all Buddhas achieves success;
one who cultivates the skillful means of śamatha achieves a tranquil mind; one who cultivates the skillful means of vipaśyanā achieves a disciplined mind;
one who cultivates a mind free from pride achieves the fulfillment of the knowledge of all-knowledge; and one who cultivates freedom from arrogance [achieves the same].
Because of accomplishing reverent faith, one achieves the practice of not deceiving any sentient being, even to the extent of enabling a single person to have faith;
because of practicing steadfast prajñā, one achieves the conduct of all gods and humans;
because of practicing according to what has been taught, one achieves the fulfillment of the qualities of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); [and] because of practicing...
Because one who practices internal reflection achieves spontaneous awakening; because one who practices the subduing of the mind achieves the state of a Dharma King;
because one who practices non-attachment to the body achieves the Buddha-body;

because one who practices reverence for the Triple Gem with an indestructible mind achieves the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*); and because one practices skillfulness...

One who accomplishes what is to be done does so by virtue of the power of knowledge regarding the ripening of karma; one who practices without disparaging others does so by virtue of the power of knowledge regarding the sharpness or dullness of the faculties;
one who practices to enter into the accumulation of subtle causes and conditions does so by virtue of the power of knowledge regarding the various natures of beings;
and one who practices to teach and transform sentient beings within the Three Jewels does so by virtue of the power of knowledge regarding faith.

Because he desires the power of knowledge (*jñānabala*), he practices the non-destruction of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) in all places and preaches the Dharma equally for the sake of all sentient beings,
thereby accomplishing the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminīpratipad-jñānabala*);
because he practices the teachings of dhyāna to transform sentient beings, he accomplishes the power of knowledge regarding the defilement, purity, and arising of dhyāna, samādhi, and samāpatti.
One practices the True Path to become a guide who shows the True Path to sentient beings who have lost it, thereby accomplishing the power of knowledge regarding the divine eye;
one practices bestowing right mindfulness upon all sentient beings, thereby accomplishing the power of knowledge regarding past lives;
and one practices bestowing pure and wholesome dharmas upon all sentient beings, thereby accomplishing the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows.
Those who practice extensive learning and teach and transform sentient beings achieve the majesty and virtue of not fearing great assemblies.
Thus, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma-gate called "The Sequential Entry into All Practices," there were two bodhisattvas within that great assembly:
one named Asamudācāra (Non-Arising) and the other named Pradīptamati (Vigorous Wisdom), both seated upon a precious hall in a separate pavilion together with their retinues.
As these two bodhisattvas sat there, they gave rise to this thought:
"We should proclaim the Great Dharma Collection of the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vikramamati addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpādita to say: "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the birth of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas?"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the true body of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
How does he know that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are established for the sake of others as conditions and causes?
How does one know that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are truly and eternally abiding?
How does a bodhisattva know the great parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
How does a bodhisattva know the conduct of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
How does a bodhisattva know the correspondence with similes?
How does a bodhisattva know how many kinds of Buddhas there are?
How does a bodhisattva know that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach the Dharma solely by relying on words and expressions?
How does a bodhisattva know the meaning of emptiness?
How does a bodhisattva know the phenomena that are the counterparts of emptiness?
How does a bodhisattva know those who speak of emptiness?
How does a bodhisattva know the meaning of the Dharma teacher?
How does a bodhisattva know the analogies corresponding to the Dharma teacher?
How do the bodhisattvas know the dharmas of non-cohabitation?
How do bodhisattvas know the matters of transformation?
How do bodhisattvas know the supreme and wondrous fruits of all roots of goodness?
Son of good family!
“How does a bodhisattva know that all untainted roots of goodness obtain supreme and wondrous fruits of retribution?
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anutpāda addressed the Bodhisattva Vikramamati, saying: “Good son!
You have asked well concerning this profound collection of the Dharma.
Son of good family!
This is the Dharma gate of the sublime and vast collection of the Dharma.
"Good son! Listen attentively now;
relying upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the empowering force of the Tathāgata, I shall explain for you which is the Dharma-gate of the Great Collection of Dharmas."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva enters ten kinds of dharma-practices, they are able to know the birth of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. What are these ten?
It is said that because one is far removed from all conceptualizing minds of activity, one is born;

because one has turned away from and transcended the body of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), one acts with tranquility; because of all arising and ceasing, one manifests the conduct of arising and ceasing;
because one arises based on past conduct, one performs all actions of karmic fruition; and thus one attains non-obstruction.
Because it is the gathering of all that is produced within the *dharmadhātu*, it gathers all karmic activities;
because it fulfills hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* vows by taking the ten great vows as its head, it serves as an adornment;

because it receives the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) bestowed by all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, it is called "the empowerment of the Buddhas"; and because it accords with the skillful means for teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
Because of the activity of the faculties, all karmic actions arise and assemble; because of great loving-kindness and great compassion, they skillfully transform and teach sentient beings;
because they dwell at all times to sustain the roots of goodness in sentient beings and blow upon their minds, they attain the profound mind;
and because they accord with the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, they manifest various births.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which he is able to know the birth of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, good son!"
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter ten kinds of dharma-practices, they are able to know the true body of the Tathāgata.
What are these ten? They are:
having reality as their essence, because it is pure and stainless;
It has the dharma-realm as its essence, because it is without differentiation;
it has the limit of reality as its essence, because it reaches everywhere;
it has emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as its essence, because it is truly quiescent.

It has as its essence illusion, transformation, a mirage, an echo, the moon in water, a city of Gandharvas, and a whirling firebrand, because it exists through the causes and conditions of transformation;
it has as its essence non-arising and non-ceasing, because it is without substance;
it has as its essence the self-nature of all phenomena, because that self-nature is pristine and pure.
The past does not come, because it is without interval;
the future does not go, because it is without form;
the present does not abide, because the past and future do not exist.
"Good son! These are called the ten kinds of dharma-practices by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters and is able to know the true body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the ten kinds of dharma-practices, he knows that the Tathāgata is accomplished for the sake of being a causal condition for others. What are these ten?
That is to say: because heedfulness (*apramāda*) serves as the seed, the fruits of wholesome dharmas are brought to fruition;

because wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*) arise, there is no transgression; because the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) serves as the feet, one is able to proceed well;
because the bodhicitta serves as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), one does not perish; and because of *śamatha*...
With *vipaśyanā* as their hand, they are able to perform skillful deeds;
with faith in the retribution of karma as their eye, they manifest direct vision through wisdom; by accomplishing the practice of all the *pāramitās*, they dwell securely in the unsurpassed state;
and by relying on the conduct of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they cultivate firm resolve. Cultivation...
Because they take the wisdom of emptiness as their primary guide, they are free from conceptual discrimination;
and because they practice without weariness, without alarm, without terror, and without fear, they do not abandon the work undertaken for the sake of all sentient beings.

"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s entry into the ten types of dharma-practice, by which one is able to know that the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas are accomplished for the sake of others as their causes and conditions."
“Good son! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter the ten kinds of dharma-practices, they know that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas truly abide eternally.”
What are these ten? They are:
being free from all faults of malice and resentment, thus not grasping at the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self";
and constantly acting as a basis for the wholesome Dharma for all sentient beings, just like a skilled physician.
Because past virtuous vows have been fulfilled, what is attained is non-regressive;
because great compassion is aroused toward all sentient beings, one skillfully performs all deeds;
and because the mind is directed solely toward the affairs of others, one is able to benefit all sentient beings.
Because they relinquish their own benefit, they undergo suffering on behalf of others;
because they are far removed from the conceptual mind that seeks nirvana, they regard the mundane world and nirvana as having the single characteristic of one flavor;
and because their practice is free from weariness, all that they do is spontaneously accomplished.
Because he is far removed from all things sought after, he has no skeletal or fleshy body;
because he is free from the marks of obstruction, he manifests nirvana in all places. Good son!
This is called the bodhisattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which one can know that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are truly and eternally abiding. “Good son!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the ten kinds of dharma-knowledge, they realize the great parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. What are these ten?
This is because they have ultimately transcended all afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions;
because they have thoroughly realized the emptiness of self, the emptiness of phenomena, and non-self;
and because they have attained the complete transformation of the mental faculty to give rise to the Dharma-body.
They perform the Buddha-work for all sentient beings spontaneously and without ceasing because they have attained complete wisdom;
because they have attained the undifferentiated Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
and because they are far removed from the dualistic mind of samsara and nirvana.
Because it is the root of the purification of all phenomena;
because one attains the wisdom that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing through practice;
and because one attains the wisdom of the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because they have attained the wisdom of the equality of the intrinsic nature of all dharmas and the nature of nirvāṇa.
Good son, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which he is able to know the great parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
By entering ten kinds of dharma-practices, a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained Great Parinirvāṇa."
What are these ten? They are as follows:
all afflictions have seeking as their root, arising because of seeking;
the Buddhas have no such seeking and are thus free from afflictions; being free from afflictions, they attain Great Nirvana.
"Because he does not seek, he is called the Tathāgata who does not grasp at a single dharma;
because he does not grasp, he neither acts nor abides;
because he does not grasp, he is said to have attained nirvāṇa."
"How is it that the Tathāgata neither goes nor abides?
Being free from those two dharmas, the Dharma-body is neither extinguished; being neither extinguished nor born, the Tathāgata is therefore said to have attained nirvāṇa."
"How is it that the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished?
That Buddha, the Tathāgata, cannot be spoken of by anyone, because he is ineffable; this is called the Tathāgata’s attainment of Great Nirvāṇa."
"There is no self and no sentient beings; there are only phenomena subject to arising and ceasing. Being free from those dependent phenomena, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa.
All afflictions and secondary afflictions are merely adventitious;
the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is quiescent, neither coming nor going. Therefore, the nature of phenomena is neither guest nor host."
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal; therefore, the Tathāgata attains Great Nirvāṇa.
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the substantial reality, while phenomena that are not True Suchness are illusory.
The substantial reality is True Suchness, and True Suchness is the Tathāgata; for this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained Nirvāṇa.
"The ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) is free from conceptual proliferation (aprapañca), whereas other phenomena are characterized by conceptual proliferation;
the Tathāgatas have reached the ultimate limit of the ultimate reality, and for this reason, the Tathāgatas are said to have attained nirvāṇa."
“Non-arising is reality; all other phenomena subject to arising and ceasing are inverted, deceptive, and false speech.
The Buddha does not speak falsely; he is free from falsehood, having truth as his essence. For this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa.”
"Unreal phenomena can be produced, while real phenomena cannot be produced;
the Tathāgata is precisely the real phenomenon, and his body is unconditioned. For this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa."

“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which he is able to know the great parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!
By entering ten kinds of dharma-practices, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva realizes the great parinirvāṇa of all buddhas, tathāgatas, arhats, and samyaksaṃbuddhas."
What are these ten? They are as follows:

giving and the fact that the fruit of giving is without self and without what belongs to a self; the Tathāgata’s thorough knowledge of giving and the fruit of giving, being free from conceptual discrimination and devoid of inversion. For this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa.

“Morality and the karmic fruit of morality are without self and without what belongs to a self. The Tathāgata thoroughly knows morality and the karmic fruit of morality, remaining free from conceptual discrimination and devoid of inversion; therefore, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa.”

“Patience and the karmic fruit of patience are without self and without what belongs to a self. The Tathāgata thoroughly knows patience and the karmic fruit of patience, remaining far removed from conceptual discrimination and free from inversion; therefore, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa.”

“Vigor and the karmic fruit of vigor are without self and without what belongs to a self. The Tathāgata thoroughly knows vigor and the karmic fruit of vigor, remaining free from conceptual discrimination and devoid of inversion; for this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa.”

“Dhyāna and the fruit of dhyāna are without self and without what belongs to a self; the Tathāgata thoroughly knows dhyāna and the fruit of dhyāna, being far removed from conceptual discrimination and free from inversion. For this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa.”

“Prajñā and the fruit of prajñā are without self and without what belongs to a self. The Tathāgata thoroughly knows prajñā and the fruit of prajñā, remaining far removed from conceptual discrimination and free from inversion; for this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa.”

"All sentient beings are not sentient beings; all dharmas are without self. The Tathāgata is far removed from all inverted characteristics and far removed from all inverted dharma-characteristics; for this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa."
"Those who possess the mark of self-grasping have something to seek; because they have seeking, they are defiled by afflictions.
Those who are free from the mark of self-grasping have no seeking at all; because they have no seeking, they are free from the defilement of afflictions."
Because he is free from the defilement of afflictions, the Tathāgata is said to have attained *nirvāṇa*.
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are measurable, whereas unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are immeasurable.

Since the Tathāgata has transcended both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, he possesses only the unconditioned *dharmakāya*, which is beyond measure; therefore, the Tathāgata is said to have attained *nirvāṇa*.

"If the Tathāgata were apart from emptiness, he would neither perceive sentient beings nor perceive dharmas—emptiness is itself dharma, dharma is itself the Dharma-body, and the Dharma-body is itself the Tathāgata—for this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have attained nirvāṇa."
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which he can know the great parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the ten kinds of dharma-knowledge, they know the knowledge of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
What are these ten? They are:
the upholding of the Dharma as an upholding, because the Dharma is perfectly pure;
the upholding of sentient beings as an upholding, because one’s own vows are fulfilled.
Self-benefit and benefiting others are without dual characteristics because they are practiced through common purpose;
they are like a pure mani-jewel, free from discrimination because the dharma-realm is pure and non-discriminatory;
and they attain a state of peace and security because all thorns of suffering for sentient beings have been extinguished.
They attain the state of fearlessness because they have forever severed all enemies that are the afflictions;
they attain freedom from the dread of being intimidated by great assemblies because they have distanced themselves from all doubts regarding the Dharma;
and they subdue all Māras and hostile adversaries because they have attained a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
They are able to manifest immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of transformation bodies because they have attained the power of thoroughly purified supernormal faculties;
they skillfully manifest all forms and images without obstruction because they have attained a thorough purity like that of space.

"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s entry into the ten kinds of dharma-practices by which one is able to know the knowledge of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the ten kinds of knowledge of phenomena, he knows the conduct of all buddhas, tathāgatas, arhats, and samyaksaṃbuddhas.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
the Tathāgata does not give rise to this thought:
"The dharmas of the world abound in faults, whereas nirvāṇa is tranquil and possesses immeasurable merits."
The Tathāgata attains a mind of equanimity toward both the world and nirvāṇa; he dwells neither in the world nor in nirvāṇa, yet he does not abandon the benefit of all sentient beings.
"Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to this thought:
'These sentient beings possess inverted wisdom and are defiled by various afflictions and secondary afflictions; I am able to deliver such sentient beings.'"

For all Tathāgatas, based on their past vows and practices, act spontaneously within each respective practice without making any distinctions, in accordance with the faculties, natures, and inclinations of sentient beings.
“Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to this thought:
‘I shall speak such a Sūtra, such a Geya, such a Vyākaraṇa, such a Gāthā, such an Udāna, such a Nidāna, such an Itivṛttaka, such a Jātaka, and such a Vaipulya.’”
"Good son! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not give rise to this thought:
'I am preaching the *abuddhadharma*.'"
Yet the Tathāgatas have no such discrimination, for those various sentient beings naturally achieve realization according to the Dharma they hear.
"Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to this thought:"

"For the sake of alms, I enter various kingdoms, large and small cities, and all villages; I go to the dwellings of such kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, kings, princes, ministers, commoners, and all sentient beings."
Furthermore, for all Tathāgatas, wisdom is paramount, as their physical, verbal, and mental actions are spontaneously perfected.

"Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have no hunger or thirst, nor do they have the need for excrement or urine; their bodies are free from emaciation, fatigue, or the suffering of illness. Yet, for the sake of sentient beings, they manifest the practice of begging for food."
Nevertheless, although sentient beings say that the Tathāgata eats, the Tathāgatas do not actually eat.

This is because they manifest the act of eating for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings; yet regarding all such matters, they remain without discrimination, as these things are spontaneously accomplished.
“Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to this thought:

‘These sentient beings possess inferior, middling, or superior faculties; for these classes of sentient beings with inferior, middling, or superior faculties, I shall accordingly proclaim the inferior, middling, or superior teachings.’”
Yet, the Tathāgatas possess no discriminating mind; the Dharma they teach is spontaneously accomplished, neither increasing nor decreasing, as it is received according to the capacity of the vessel.
“Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to such a thought:
‘If sentient beings do not make offerings to me, do not revere me, or revile and abuse me, I shall not teach and transform such sentient beings.’”
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who make offerings to me, revere, respect, praise, and attend upon me; such sentient beings I should transform and guide.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgatas, through their tranquil samādhi and universal compassion, cover those sentient beings, naturally abiding in the dharma of equality. Good son!"

The Tathāgata has no high-mindedness, no low-mindedness, no conceited mind, no mind of attachment, no greedy mind, no angry mind, no mind that follows greed, no clinging mind, no obstructed mind, no hindered mind, no mixed-up mind, no mind of affliction, no mind that follows affliction, no hateful mind, no deluded mind, no mind that follows hatred, and no mind that follows delusion, O son of good family!
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas are naturally quiescent and abide in the realm of quiescence because they praise the realm of quiescence. "Good son!

There is not a single dharma that the Tathāgata does not know, does not understand, or does not awaken to; he is ultimately fulfilled regarding all realms and knows them all directly before him. Moreover, when the Tathāgatas perceive various things and the various karmas performed by various sentient beings, these are spontaneously accomplished."

“Good son! When the Tathāgata sees sentient beings accomplishing their practice, he does not feel joy; when he sees sentient beings who do not practice, he does not give rise to sorrow. Rather, for all Tathāgatas, unobstructed great loving-kindness is constantly present toward sentient beings who are practicing correctly, and unobstructed great compassion is constantly present toward sentient beings who engage in deviant practices.”
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which they are able to know the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Good son! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the ten kinds of dharma-knowledge, they understand that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are characterized by analogies.
What are these ten? Good son!

It is like the rising of the sun, which appears equally and shines universally upon all sentient beings—superior, middling, and inferior—whether they have faith or lack faith, whether they show reverence or do not show reverence.

Good son! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: toward all sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior; whether they have faith or lack faith; whether they show respect or do not show respect—he appears with equanimity, and his light of equal wisdom shines everywhere.
“Good son! For example, space has no obstruction toward any sentient beings, yet that space is obscured by various things such as smoke, clouds, dust, and mist.

Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise in this regard; they encounter no obstruction with respect to all sentient beings. Yet, because [sentient beings] are obstructed by smoke, clouds, dust, mist, the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-mala*), they do not see the Tathāgata and do not receive the merit and benefits of the Tathāgata.
“Good son! For example, although a tree possesses the nature of fire, it does not manifest its function because of the absence of causal conditions. Good son!”

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise: although they possess immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers, because sentient beings lack the causal conditions of diligence, faith, and so forth, [the Buddhas] do not appear in the world nor perform buddha-works.

“Good son! It is like placing various perfumes in one vessel to scent various garments, and then placing various dyeing colors in another vessel to color those scented garments; according to what they were scented with, the garments receive different colors, yet those various colors do not give rise to thoughts of discrimination or distinction.”

"Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this. Adorned with various roots of goodness and merits, they appear to sentient beings according to the differences in their respective perfumings of faith and other qualities; thus, the merits received from the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, differ and are not the same. Yet, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to thoughts of discrimination or distinction."
“Good son! It is like the flowing waters of various rivers which, being full to the brim, will all flow downstream regardless of whether people praise or revile them;
it is impossible for them to flow upstream.”
Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this: whether people praise or revile them, they always act in accordance with wisdom;
it is impossible for them to ever follow pride.
“Good son! It is like sugarcane: whether it is cut or not cut, its sweet flavor is not lost. Good son!”

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise in this regard: whether people draw near, make offerings to, and revere them, or do not draw near, make offerings to, and revere them, they never abandon the sweet flavor of liberation.
“Good son! It is like the great earth, whose nature is stable and firm, making no distinctions among sentient beings.

If there is someone who desires to obtain its fruits and seeds, and who can plow and sow at the proper times, and weed out the grasses and weeds as they arise, that person will harvest the fruits when the time comes.
If one does not plow, sow, or weed away the weeds and impurities, that person will ultimately never obtain its fruit.
Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this: they are like the great earth, which remains tranquil and eternally abiding, making no distinctions among sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings who seek the merits of the Buddha and are able to give rise to faith, make offerings, and show reverence, those people will achieve the fruit of merit;
if they do not give rise to faith, make offerings, or show reverence, they will not obtain the fruit of merit.

“Good son! It is like a person who, having first reviled, slandered, or abused sandalwood, camphor, or other such fragrances, later applies them to his body; yet that sandalwood, camphor, and other fragrances do not fail to emit their scent because of this.”

"Good son! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are also like this: even if someone should harbor anger toward them, slander them, or revile them, yet subsequently draws near to them, makes offerings, shows reverence, and practices according to their teachings, the Tathāgatas will always bestow upon that sentient being a fullness of merit."

“Good son! It is like a bridge or a level royal highway, which remains impartial toward all sentient beings—whether of superior, middling, or inferior nature—who travel upon it, providing them with the joy of unimpeded passage.”

Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise in this regard: toward all sentient beings—whether of superior, middling, or inferior nature—they abide with equanimity toward those who practice, without distinction of high or low, bestowing upon them the joy of unimpeded cultivation.

“Good son! For example, in the Snowy Mountains there is a king of medicinal trees named Sudarśana; whoever beholds that king of medicinal trees immediately becomes free from all suffering of illness.”
“Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this: those sentient beings who behold them are freed from all the sicknesses and sufferings of affliction. Good son!”

This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which they are able to know the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas through their corresponding analogies.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters ten kinds of dharma-practices, they are able to know all buddhas. What are these ten?

These are what are called the Buddha of Habitual Tendencies, the Buddha of Retributive Fruit, the Buddha of Samādhi, the Buddha of Vows, the Buddha of Mind, the Buddha of Reality, the Buddha of Identity, the Buddha of Transformation, the Buddha of Offerings, and the Buddha of Physical Images.
“Good son! What is the Buddha of Habit-Energy?
The Buddha of Habit-Energy refers to the fruits and rewards obtained through the various pāramitās; it is the various pāramitās that are able to accomplish those dharmas.”
That which arises based on the various pāramitās is called the Buddha of Habitual Tendencies (*vāsanā-buddha*).
"Good son! What is the Buddha of Retribution (*vipāka-buddha*)?"
As for the *vipākaphala-buddha* (fruition-retribution Buddha), it is produced based on that fruition-retribution of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Because that fruition establishes the *rūpakāya-rūpa-buddha* (retribution-form Buddha), which abides through the sustaining power of sentient beings and the sustaining power of the Dharma, it is called the fruition-retribution Buddha.
“Good son! What is the Buddha of Samādhi?

As for the Buddha of Samādhi, whenever the Tathāgata enters a particular samādhi, by the power of that entered samādhi, he spontaneously and without further mental effort can manifest hundreds of thousands of myriads of Buddhas.”
Because they are able to manifest through the sustaining power of that samādhi, they are called Samādhi Buddhas. "Good son,
what is a Prāṇidhāna Buddha?"
Regarding the vow of the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas make this aspiration:
"In accordance with whatever sentient beings there may be, by whatever causes and through whatever dharmas, we shall manifest various form-bodies to deliver those sentient beings."
In such and such ways, he manifests various forms, appearances, postures, and modes of coming and going for those various sentient beings.
According to what body those sentient beings should be delivered through, he manifests that Buddha-body to transform them.
This is called the Buddha of Vows. "Good son,
what is the Buddha of Mind?

Regarding the "Mind-Buddha": the various bodhisattvas have attained mastery over the mind; by virtue of this mastery over the mind, these bodhisattvas bring about the accomplishment of all diverse phenomena in accordance with their will.

These bodhisattvas, according to those sentient beings who are to be transformed by perceiving the body of a Buddha, immediately manifest the body of a Buddha through their sovereign mind; this is called the "mind-Buddha."
Furthermore, good son!
There is another meaning:
when all sentient beings, through the purity of their own minds, are able to see the Buddha, know the Buddha, and believe in the Buddha, this is called the "Buddha of the mind."
“Good son! What is the Real Buddha?

The Real Buddha is far removed from all defilements of affliction; he is inconceivable, stainless, and pure. He has ultimately perfected various forms and colors—the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and the marks of a Great Man—and his subtle and wondrous form can be perceived by sight; this is called the Real Buddha.”
“Good son! How is it that one is the same as the Buddha?

To be the same as the Buddha means to share with all sentient beings their resources, occupations, and enjoyments; their food and drink; their walking, standing, going, and coming; and their dignified deportment and movements. This is called being the same as the Buddha.”
“Good son! What is a transformation Buddha?
A transformation Buddha refers to the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas who have attained the samādhi for manifesting all forms of physical bodies.”

Those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have achieved mastery; through their great kindness and great compassion, they are all able to manifest emanations, using the physical bodies of transformation-Buddhas to deliver all sentient beings—this is called a transformation-Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha).
“Good son! How does one make offerings to the Buddha?
As for making offerings to the Buddha, if there is a person who is a teacher or a preceptor (upādhyāya) who is like the Buddha, the World-Honored One, one should regard them in such a manner.”

That person should regard their teacher and preceptor as the Buddha, the World-Honored One; they should see them in this way, making offerings to and supporting them. By relying on them, they receive the Dharma, fulfill the Buddha-Dharma, and accomplish the Buddha-Dharma; this is called making offerings to the Buddha.
“Good son! What is the Buddha of images?

As for the Buddha of images, there may be someone who, whether others have made a Buddha image or they have made one themselves, offers it worship, respect, reverence, praise, attendance, and service through all manner of offerings and honors.
When such a person, by relying on that image, fulfills the Buddha-dharma and accomplishes the Buddha-dharma, this is called the "image-Buddha.
"Good son! This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices and being able to know ten kinds of Buddhas."

“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the ten kinds of dharma-knowledge, he understands that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Dharma solely by relying on words and expressions.”
What are these ten? They are:

speaking of the aggregates as mere words; speaking of the elements, speaking of the sense-bases, speaking of sentient beings, speaking of karma, speaking of birth, speaking of aging, speaking of death, speaking of being born again after death, and speaking of nirvana as also being mere words in order to bring about detachment from those things.
“Good son! How is it said that the aggregates (skandhas) are merely words? Good son!”
In the ultimate sense, that aggregate of form does not exist.

If the aggregate of form were to exist in the ultimate sense, then the relinquishing of that aggregate of form would constitute annihilation, and the relinquishing of those phenomena would constitute liberation.
If it were so, then within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) there would be both form (*rūpa*) and a place for liberation to go or stay;
yet such is not the case. Therefore, it is said that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is merely conventional terminology.
“Good son! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Good son!”
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) does not exist.

If the aggregate of consciousness were to exist in the ultimate sense, then the relinquishing of that conscious dharma would constitute annihilation; and the relinquishing of that dharma would itself be liberation.
If it were so, then within the ultimate truth (paramārtha) there would exist consciousness as well as a place for liberation, going, or staying;
yet such is not the case. Therefore, it is said that consciousness is merely a matter of conventional expression.
“Good son! The meaning of the elements (dhātu) and sense-bases (āyatana) is likewise so. Good son!”
Why is it said that sentient beings are merely words?
Good son, there are only conditioned phenomena; there are no sentient beings.
If sentient beings truly existed as substantial entities, they should not perish together with the aggregates.
If they were to perish together with the aggregates, they would be like empty space;
if this were not the case, they would be identical to the five aggregates, both being conditioned phenomena.
Yet the meaning is not so; therefore, it is said that sentient beings are merely words.
"Good son, why is it said that karma is merely words?"
Good son! That which performs action is neither existent nor non-existent.
If the performing of action were existent, then the agent of that action would be non-existent, and that agent would be like empty space.
Furthermore, just as the aggregates (skandhas) are conditioned, so too is the agent.
For this reason, there is neither that agent nor any action performed, being just like space.
How could there be an agent? Therefore, there is no such thing as an action.
Apart from that agent, how could there be an action?
Therefore, it is said that karma is merely a matter of words. "Good son,
how is it said that birth is merely a matter of words?"
Good son! In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no arising.
If there were arising in the ultimate sense, then arising would be permanent.
If this is so, then birth is not truly birth.
Furthermore, as for that which gives rise to birth and that which causes affliction through birth—what exactly is it?
Therefore, it is said that birth is merely a conventional expression.
“Good son! Why do you say that old age is merely a matter of words? Good son!
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no aging.
If there were aging within the ultimate sense, then there would be no one who is not subject to aging.
Furthermore, if there were such a thing as aging, it would mean that one ages at the very moment of youth.
If aging does not exist at the time of youth, then it exists at the time other than youth; since there is no aging in that which is young, there is therefore no aging at the time of youth.
If one is separated from aging, how can it be called "aging"?
In this way, old age cannot truly age.
If one were to say that old age can age, then it would be the youth itself that is aging; therefore, it is said that "old age" is merely a conventional expression. "Good son!
To speak of "death" is merely a matter of conventional expression. Noble son,
in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no death.
If there were death in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), then the phenomenon of death would be obtainable.
If it were obtainable, only a single person could experience it, and others should not die;
yet there are further deaths. Therefore, in the ultimate sense, the phenomenon of death does not exist.

Furthermore, that which dies comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; the nature of this phenomenon of death is empty and quiescent. Therefore, it is said that "death" is merely a conventional expression.
“Good son! Why do you say that death followed by rebirth is merely a matter of words? Good son!
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), death does not give rise to rebirth.
If, in the ultimate sense, death were to give rise to rebirth, then death would be identical to birth and birth would be identical to death.
If this were so, then death and birth would be one and the same phenomenon.
Furthermore, there should be two bodies:
first, that which is capable of taking birth; second, that which has already taken birth.
If there is one who takes birth, there must necessarily be the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that take birth.
Why is this? Because apart from the five aggregates, that consciousness does not arise.
It is by depending on the dharmas of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and so forth, that the mind of consciousness is able to arise.
Because consciousness abides by depending upon the aggregates, it remains supported by them.
If separated from its support, that conscious mind does not abide for even a single moment.
Just as those phenomena abide, so too is rebirth like a seed producing a sprout; therefore, to say that after death one is born again is merely a conventional expression.
"Good son! How is it that, being free from those things, parinirvāṇa is said to be merely words? Good son!"
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that nirvāṇa does not exist.
As for nirvāṇa, it is known as nirvāṇa because of the cessation of the world; yet it is not the case that the world itself is called nirvāṇa, nor is there a nirvāṇa that exists apart from the world.
The world is like a dream and like an illusion; it is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent.
Yet this existing phenomenon is likewise neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent—this is called arising.
It is likewise neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent—this is called ceasing.
The quiescent cessation of all worldly characteristics is called nirvāṇa.
Thus, perception is like a mirage and feeling is like a bubble.
Just as those mirages and bubbles arise and perish without reality, so too are the world and nirvāṇa; therefore, it is said that the world and nirvāṇa are merely words.

“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which he is able to know that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Dharma solely by means of verbal expressions.”
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva enters ten kinds of dharma-practices and is well able to understand the meaning of emptiness. What are these ten?
That is to say, knowing that there is no self, no sentient being, no life-principle, no person, no creator, no arising, no ceasing, no agent, no instructor, and no sovereign.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the emptiness of non-self? Good son!”
Emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent.
Good son! If emptiness were existent, emptiness would be conditioned; if it were truly existent, it would necessarily be permanent.
Good son! If emptiness were not non-existent, then emptiness would not be empty.
Therefore, that emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent; this is what is called knowing the emptiness of non-self.
"Good son! How does one know the emptiness of non-existent sentient beings? Good son!"
Sentient beings are neither empty nor non-empty.
If sentient beings were empty, then the karma of killing them would be without fault;
if sentient beings were not empty, they would necessarily be eternal.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that sentient beings are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither conditioned nor unconditioned; this is called knowing the emptiness of sentient beings.
“Good son! How does one know that there is no life-principle and that it is empty? Good son!
Emptiness is neither born nor does it die. Why is this?
O son of good family!
The eye is empty, being free from "I" and "mine.
Why is the eye empty, being free from "I" and "mine"?
Because those phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished.
In this way, the ear, nose, tongue, and body are empty and devoid of "I" and "mine.
How is it that the ear, nose, and so forth are empty and devoid of "I" and "mine"?
Because those dharmas are neither born nor extinguished.
This is called knowing the emptiness of the absence of a life-principle (*jīva*). "Good son!..."
How is it known that there is no life-principle (jīva) and that all is empty? Good son!
That which is empty is not reckoned among the categories of a life-principle.
Those aggregates, elements, and sense bases are all entirely empty; based upon those aggregates, elements, and sense bases, there exists the conventional designation "living being.
Because it is a mere designation, its existence or non-existence cannot be described as having any characteristic.
This is called knowing the emptiness of the absence of a life-principle (*jīva*). "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva know the emptiness of the absence of a creator?"
Good son! Apart from emptiness, there is not a single dharma that can be called a creator.
Furthermore, it is impossible for emptiness itself to be a creator.
This is called knowing the emptiness of the absence of a creator.
"Good son, how does one know the emptiness of non-arising?
Good son! The dharma of emptiness is unarisen; if emptiness could arise, it would not be emptiness, and such emptiness would not be empty.
If there were originally no emptiness, then there would be no dharma of emptiness.
Furthermore, that which first arises as empty is itself not empty.
This is called knowing the emptiness of non-arising. "Good son!
How does one know the emptiness of non-extinction?
If a phenomenon arises, it must have its extinction; since empty phenomena do not arise, how could they have extinction?
This is called knowing the emptiness of non-extinction.
“Good son! How does one know the emptiness of non-action? Good son!

Emptiness is neither created by another nor created by itself; the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are all entirely empty. It is in dependence upon the aggregates, elements, and sense bases that the dharma of emptiness exists; this is called knowing the emptiness of non-action.
“Good son! How does one know that the unmanifest (avijñapti) is empty? Good son!...”
There is not a single person who teaches emptiness to create such various things as these; this is what is meant by "knowing emptiness through the absence of a teacher. "Good son!
How does one know the emptiness of that which lacks a sovereign? Good son!
Emptiness has no objective realm and is free from objective realms; it is far removed from mind, thought, and consciousness. This is called knowing the emptiness of that which lacks a sovereign.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s entry into the ten kinds of dharma-practices by which one is well able to know the meaning of emptiness. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter ten kinds of dharma-practices, they are able to know the dharmas that are the counterparts to emptiness.
What are these ten? They are:

the dharma of ignorance, the dharma of craving, the dharma of karma, the dharma of consciousness, the dharma of grasping, the dharma of views, the dharma of doubt, the dharma of wrong adherence, the dharma of pride, and the dharma of restlessness.
"Good son! These are called the ten dharmas that correspond to emptiness. Good son!"
Ignorance has two kinds of capacities and four kinds of causes.
What are the two capacities?
First, the obscuration of afflictions; second, the obscuration of knowledge.
What are these four causes? They are:
the cause for craving the realm of desire, the cause for craving the realm of form, the cause for craving the formless realm, and the cause for craving non-existence. "Good son!
Craving has two kinds of causes and four kinds of seeking.
What are the two kinds of causes?
First, the root of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*); second, the root of the means of subsistence.
What are the four kinds of seeking?
First, craving for sensual desire; second, craving for form; third, craving for the formless; and fourth, craving for non-existence.
“Good son! Karma has one kind of cause, three kinds of characteristics, and three kinds of retributions. Good son!”
What is the single cause of origination?
It is what is called the mind.
What are the three characteristics?
These are the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Good son! What are the three kinds of retributive fruits?
That which is called the black-and-black retribution, the white-and-white retribution, and the black-and-white/black-and-white retribution.
"Good son! What is consciousness?
What are called the six types are the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are named the six types of consciousness.
These consciousnesses further comprise three kinds.
What are these three?
First, inverted mindfulness; second, non-inverted mindfulness; and third, non-mindfulness. Good son!
What is inverted mindfulness?
It is mindfulness of the desire realm, mindfulness of the form realm, and mindfulness of the formless realm.
What is non-inverted mindfulness?
This refers to mindfulness of the nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna. What is non-mindfulness?
It is called non-mindfulness when one is free from those two types of mindfulness.
How does one abandon those two thoughts?
It means to keep in mind the unsurpassed qualities of all Buddhas. "Good son!..."
There are four kinds of grasping:
namely, grasping at desire, grasping at views, grasping at precepts and rituals, and grasping at a self. "Good son!
What is the grasping at views?
There are two kinds of grasping at views:
namely, wrong knowledge and the knowledge of [erroneous] views.
"Wrong knowledge" refers to the knowledge of wrong views.
"Knowledge of views" refers to an arhat’s false perception of nirvana and their false pursuit of nirvana; this is called "knowledge of views"—such knowledge of views is censured by all Buddhas.
“Good son! What is doubt? There are two kinds of doubt:”
First, it obstructs the Mahāyāna; second, it obstructs the stage of true certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Good son!
What is meant by "doubt that obstructs the Mahāyāna"?
This refers to those such as the śrāvakas, whose minds are narrow and inferior, and who aspire to swiftly realize the enlightenment of the Hīnayāna. Why is this?
Because they think as follows:
"The path of the Buddha is long and distant; it is difficult to achieve success through the immeasurable practices required.
Therefore, I should seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka to quickly escape all suffering.
For this reason, one retreats from the Mahāyāna; this is called "doubt that obstructs the Mahāyāna."
What is doubt that obstructs the state of certainty?
Because of that doubt, one does not realize the state of certainty and fails to attain the bodhisattva’s stage of Mahāyāna wisdom; this is called doubt that obstructs the state of certainty.
“Good son! What is wrong grasping (*mithyā-parigraha*)?
Wrong grasping refers to seeking the karmic fruits of existence through various practices such as giving (*dāna*), and giving rise to such a thought:”
"I shall cultivate such practices as giving and observing the precepts in order to obtain the superior fruits of happiness among devas and humans.
All such forms of wrong seeking are called wrong grasping (*mithyā-adhyavasāna*).
“Good son! What is pride?
To give rise to a mind of superiority and inferiority is called pride.”
"To think, 'He is inferior to me' or 'I am superior to him,' and such thoughts of superiority and inferiority, victory and defeat, are called pride. Good son!
What is restlessness?"
Restlessness is of two kinds:
first, that which gives rise to afflictions; second, that which is agitated and disturbed by those who give rise to afflictions.

Through false conceptualization and discrimination, one perceives form as pure; for this reason, the actions of body, speech, and mind all become inverted, and thus it is censured by all the noble ones.
What is agitation? Agitation refers to the fact that one’s mind does not abide within the supramundane path;
this is called restlessness. "Good son!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices by which one can know the phenomena that are the counterparts to emptiness. "Good son!
By entering these ten kinds of dharma-practices, the bodhisattva mahāsattva knows how to speak of emptiness."

What are these ten? They are: being one who does not destroy; one who does not disturb; one who is neither greedy nor weary; one who neither practices nor does not practice; one who neither disputes nor competes; one who neither increases nor decreases; one who is able to endure with patience upon hearing that the self-nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inherently quiescent; one who is neither startled nor terrified upon hearing that ordinary beings do not give rise to a single dharma and that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not extinguish a single dharma; one who does not give rise to doubt upon hearing that the nature of the world and the nature of nirvāṇa are equal as a pair; and one who possesses correct faith and correctly enters into the eternal, blissful, wondrous body and inexhaustible Dharma-body of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
“Good son! What is meant by ‘one who can explain emptiness without causing disintegration’? Good son!”
One who is able to expound emptiness cannot be destroyed by worldly dharmas.
Why is this? Because the mind does not rely upon the eight worldly concerns.

What are these eight? They are: not relying on matters such as gain or loss; not giving rise to sorrow or joy at sounds of praise or blame; being free from the two states of elation and dejection, or defamation and fame; having no fluctuation of high or low in the mind; and neither craving nor loathing any form of suffering or pleasure.
Thus, worldly dharmas cannot destroy it; for this reason, one is called "the one who can explain emptiness without being destroyed.
Son of good family!
This is what is meant by a bodhisattva who can explain emptiness without being destroyed.
“Good son! How does one know that one who can speak of emptiness is undisturbed? Good son!
One who can speak of emptiness neither grasps at phenomena nor abandons phenomena.
Regarding what phenomena does one neither grasp nor abandon?
It is precisely by knowing that these phenomena are empty, and seeing that these phenomena are empty.
If one can thus neither grasp nor reject, this is called a mind that is undisturbed and capable of expounding emptiness.
"Good son, what is meant by being neither greedy nor weary, yet capable of expounding emptiness?"
"Good son! One who can speak of emptiness has no dharma to be craved and no dharma to be loathed.
Regarding what dharma would one neither crave nor loathe?"
One knows that these phenomena are empty and sees that these phenomena are empty.
If one gives rise to desire or aversion toward any phenomena, such a bodhisattva is not said to know emptiness nor see emptiness;
if one can have no desire or aversion toward phenomena in the mind, they are called one who is neither desirous nor averse and is able to explain emptiness.
“Good son! What is meant by ‘one who can speak of emptiness through neither practicing nor not practicing’? Good son!”
One who can speak of emptiness neither practices nor does not practice dharmas.
Regarding what dharmas does one who can speak of emptiness neither practice nor not practice?
One knows that these dharmas are empty and sees that these dharmas are empty, yet this is not a failure to practice the dharmas that assist awakening.
If one can thus know emptiness and see emptiness, this is called a bodhisattva who neither practices nor does not practice, and who is able to speak of emptiness.
“Good son! How is it that one who is without contention or rivalry can speak of emptiness? Good son!”
Regarding those who preach emptiness, if they engage in dispute or contention with sentient beings, they do not know emptiness and do not see emptiness.

Because these bodhisattvas know and see emptiness even toward those who dispute, they do not engage in dispute or contention; thus, they are called those who can preach emptiness without disputing or contending.
“Good son! How does one know that which neither increases nor decreases, and is able to explain emptiness? Good son!”

One who can speak of emptiness does not know that a single dharma increases, nor do they know that a single dharma decreases; they do not see a single dharma increasing, nor do they see a single dharma decreasing.
If one perceives increase or decrease regarding any dharmas, such a bodhisattva does not know emptiness and does not see emptiness.

If one can know emptiness and perceive emptiness, then one sees neither increase nor decrease in all phenomena; this is called the ability to teach emptiness through non-increase and non-decrease. "Good son!
"What is meant by one who, upon hearing it said that the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is quiescent, attains mental forbearance and is able to speak of emptiness?
Son of good family!

One who is able to speak of emptiness does not perceive the arising of a single dharma, nor does he perceive the cessation of a single dharma; this is called one who, upon hearing it said that the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena is quiescent, attains mental forbearance and is able to speak of emptiness."

“Good son! How is it that one who hears that ordinary beings do not produce a single dharma and the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not extinguish a single dharma, is neither startled nor terrified, and is able to speak of emptiness?”
Good son! One who is able to speak of emptiness does not give rise to the thought:
"This is an ordinary person; this is a Buddha."
"Knowing that the Tathāgata and all ordinary beings are equal in their essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*).
If one views ordinary phenomena as inferior and the Buddha-dharma as superior, such a bodhisattva does not know or see emptiness."

If one hears that ordinary beings do not produce a single dharma, this is the emptiness of ordinary beings; if one hears that the Buddhas do not extinguish a single dharma, this is the emptiness of the Buddhas. Thus, hearing it said that ordinary beings do not produce a single dharma and the Tathāgatas do not extinguish a single dharma, one is neither startled nor terrified. This is called one who does not see the production of a single dharma and does not see the extinction of a single dharma, and is thus able to expound emptiness.
“Good son! How does one know that the nature of the world and the nature of nirvāṇa are equal in these two respects, thereby giving rise to no doubt and knowing how to explain emptiness?”
"Good son! If one perceives that there is a nature of nirvāṇa apart from the nature of the world, such a bodhisattva does not know or see emptiness.

If one perceives the *tathatā*-nature of the world and the *tathatā*-nature of nirvāṇa as two distinct things, yet these two natures of phenomena are in fact but a single characteristic—namely, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nature."

If one perceives that the *tathatā* (suchness) of the world and the *tathatā* of nirvāṇa are equal in their characteristics, without distinction of high or low, and thus gives rise to no doubt, nor experiences alarm or fear, this is called knowing the equality of the two dharmas—the nature of the world and the nature of nirvāṇa—and being able to explain emptiness.

“Good son! How is it that one who hears the teaching on the eternal, blissful, and wondrous body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, the inexhaustible Dharma-body, can possess right faith, enter correctly, and be able to speak of emptiness?”
"Good son! If one gives rise to this thought:
'The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are bodies that have reached ultimate extinction.'"
"In this way, the bodhisattva does not know or see emptiness.
Why is this? The body of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is the body of true suchness (tathatā) and emptiness; it is not a body of adventitious afflictions (kleśa) or secondary afflictions (upakleśa)."
Thus, this is called hearing the teaching that the Tathāgata’s body of eternal bliss and wondrousness is the inexhaustible Dharma-body, which is able to expound emptiness.

Good son! This is called a bodhisattva who, having heard the teaching that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess the body of eternal bliss and wondrousness and the inexhaustible Dharma-body, enters with right faith and right understanding into that which is able to expound emptiness.
“Good son! These are called the ten kinds of dharma-practices through which a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters and is able to speak of emptiness.
The *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*, Scroll One.
The *Sūtra on the Collection of the Dharma* (Dharmasaṃgītisūtra), Fascicle Two, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters ten kinds of dharma-practices, he is able to know the Dharma-preacher.”
Meaning. What are the ten? They are:
achieving great learning;
They achieve the dhāraṇīs;
they achieve the ocean-like accumulation of the wisdom of hearing and the treasury of the wisdom of hearing, yet they do not give rise to arrogance regarding this wisdom of hearing;

they are fully endowed with the unimpededness of meaning, the unimpededness of phenomena, the unimpededness of expression, and the unimpededness of eloquence, and they seek diligent progress without ceasing.

Knowing the world, knowing the time, knowing the proper measure, knowing the Dharma, and knowing sentient beings, yet not abandoning the cultivation of practice; honoring the conduct practiced by those of long-standing virtue;
knowing the discourses, knowing their meaning, and knowing which sentient beings are ready for conversion, yet not abandoning the matter of inquiry;
accomplishing such practices as few desires and contentment, yet not abandoning the task of providing for the venerable ones.
They have achieved a mind that is wondrously serene, tranquil, supple, and free from cowardice, yet they do not abandon the practice of shame and remorse;
they have achieved profound and immeasurable merit, yet they are able to manifest worldly defiled conduct for which they are not liberated;

and for the sake of conforming to sentient beings, they have achieved a naturally upright mind, a gentle mind, and a peaceful mind, yet they are able to manifest the same conduct as those who break the precepts.

They accomplish generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, yet they give rise to no mind of attachment toward any object and do not discriminate among spheres of experience;
they remain far removed from all thorns of secondary afflictions such as greed, yet they do not abandon their diligent practice of severing the afflictions for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Noble son! These are called the ten kinds of dharma-practices through which a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters and is able to understand the meaning of the Dharma-preacher’s teachings.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter ten kinds of Dharma-practices, they are able to understand the meaning of the Dharma-master.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
namely, that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas remain far removed from all seeking, yet do not abandon the vigor of all the merits of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
He thoroughly understands that all phenomena are quiescent, yet he does not realize bodhi while failing to relinquish any act of generosity or diligence;
he realizes that all phenomena are ultimately inexhaustible, yet he does not abandon the practice of patience and peaceful bliss;
he constantly dwells in the profound realm of samādhi, yet he is able to never forsake the work of cultivating the roots of goodness for all sentient beings.
They are fully endowed with wondrous, sublime tranquility, yet they never abandon the practice of teaching and transforming sentient beings with distracted or inverted minds;
they achieve *dhāraṇī* and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, yet they never abandon the diligent pursuit of extensive learning and wisdom;

they achieve the secret treasury of all dharmas, yet they are able to never abandon the diligent pursuit of the Dharma by traveling even hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* for the sake of a single verse.
Knowing that all phenomena do not depend on others, yet never abandoning the diligent effort of attending upon and revering teachers;
knowing that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, yet never abandoning the diligent effort of protecting the Dharma;
seeing neither sentient beings nor the names of sentient beings, yet never abandoning the diligent effort of transforming all sentient beings to attain great Bodhi.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices to be able to know the meaning of the Dharma-master.
Furthermore, good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter ten kinds of Dharma-practices, they are able to understand the meaning of the Dharma-preacher’s teachings. What are these ten?
They are: by virtue of accomplishing and embracing speech, they are able to practice the deeds of giving, kind words, beneficial action, and cooperation;
Because they have accomplished gentle speech, they are able to give rise to great compassion;
because they have accomplished compliant speech, they are then able to accord with tranquility, accord with the departure from afflictions, and accord with liberation;
because they have accomplished compliant speech, they are then able to accord with śamatha, accord with vipaśyanā, and accord with the path of suchness.
Because they have accomplished skillful speech, they are able to possess speech that is clear and distinct, speech free from reproach, and speech that cannot be refuted;
because they have accomplished speech regarding the meaning of words, they are able to abandon evil speech and possess speech endowed with meaning;
because they have accomplished speech free from flattery and crookedness, they are able to shatter the ignorance and deception of sentient beings.
Because they have accomplished speech that is free from doubt, they are able to directly perceive the characteristics of all phenomena;
because they have accomplished speech that is far removed from all latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), they are able to extinguish the causes of all primary and secondary afflictions;
and because they have accomplished speech that does not give rise to roots [of action], being stainless and non-originary.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices to be able to know the meaning of the Dharma teacher.
Furthermore, good son!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter ten kinds of dharma-practices, they are able to understand the meaning of the Dharma-preacher. What are these ten?
They are as follows: the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva preaches all dharmas based on being sustained by the sublime Dharma, and does not preach based on being sustained by offerings or honor;
They preach in reliance upon that which is upheld by all Buddhas, not in reliance upon what is upheld by their own minds;
they preach in reliance upon the root of great loving-kindness and great compassion, not in reliance upon the roots of afflictions and secondary afflictions;

they preach in reliance upon severing the flow of the fetters that conform to ordinary beings, not in reliance upon severing the practice in accordance with the Dharma that conforms to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Jewels.
One preaches the Dharma for the benefit of others out of great compassion, not for the sake of enjoying pleasure or self-interest;
one who preaches the Dharma does so by relying on that profound Dharma, because it is ultimately characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one who preaches the Dharma does so by relying on those superior persons, because they are able to accord with and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
The teacher of the Dharma speaks while subduing all Māras and adversaries, for they are able to subdue the māra of the aggregates, the māra of death, the māra of afflictions, and the celestial māra;
the teacher of the Dharma speaks in accordance with the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), for they are worthy of being honored by the entire world;

the teacher of the Dharma speaks in accordance with the knowledge of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), for they ultimately attain the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices and being able to know the meaning of the Dharma-preacher’s teachings. Furthermore, good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter ten kinds of Dharma-practices, they are able to understand the meaning of the Dharma-preacher. What are these ten?
They are: delighting in the livelihood of pure conduct (brahmacarya) rather than delighting in worldly means of subsistence;
They delight in the Dharma practiced by the sages, yet are able not to abandon the teaching and transforming of sentient beings; they do not engage in the blameworthy actions of ordinary worldlings.
Bodhisattvas always delight in the food of the Dharma and do not crave worldly flavors;
they always delight in forest hermitages and do not cling to cities or villages.
They always delight in the Bodhi of the Buddhas and do not seek the Bodhi of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
they always delight in severing the cognitive hindrances and do not delight in severing the afflictive hindrances;
they always delight in the accomplishment of the physical body with its thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and do not delight merely in realizing the Dharma-body alone.

They always delight in accomplishing the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, rather than delighting solely in realizing the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;
they always delight in accomplishing roots of goodness that accord with all sentient beings, rather than delighting solely in accumulating roots of goodness for themselves;

they always delight in severing all afflictions as well as the habitual tendencies of those afflictions, rather than merely delighting in severing the dharmas that constitute the obstacle of affliction.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices to be able to know the meaning of the Dharma-master. Good son!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who enter ten kinds of dharma-practices are able to know the analogies corresponding to the Dharma-preacher. What are these ten?
"That is to say, noble son!..."
For example, the great earth is equal in nature; it is vast enough to bear the weight of all sentient beings, yet it does not seek any repayment of gratitude from them. Good son!
The Bodhisattva Dharma Master is like that great earth; his mind is impartial, universally able to bear the burden of all sentient beings, yet he seeks no recompense from them for his kindness.

“Good son! It is like a great body of water, whose nature is to provide universal moisture; it nourishes and benefits all things, causing them to flourish, yet it seeks no repayment of gratitude from those things.”
The Bodhisattva Dharma Master is also like this: by means of his own merit, he benefits and brings peace and security to all sentient beings, yet he does not seek any recompense from them.
“Good son! It is like the nature of fire, which has the power to ripen all fruits and yet harbors no expectation for those results.

The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher is also like this: through his own merit and wisdom, he brings to maturity the fruits of the roots of goodness in all sentient beings, yet he seeks no reward from them.”

“Good son! For example, the nature of wind has the power to cause all medicinal herbs and seeds to grow, yet it does not give rise to discrimination regarding those things, nor does it harbor any expectation.”
