The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher is also like this: his power is able to increase the birth-body and the dharma-body of all sentient beings, yet he seeks no repayment of gratitude from them.

“Good son! It is like the realm of space, which is immeasurable and boundless; its essence is without obstruction and it accommodates all things, yet it makes no distinctions regarding those objects and has no attachment to them.”

The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher is also like this: having accomplished immeasurable and boundless virtuous merits, his essence is free from obstruction as he benefits all sentient beings, yet he makes no discriminations regarding those beings and has no attachment to them.

“Good son! It is like the bright moon appearing in the void, pure and full; all sentient beings who see it love and delight in it, and its light illuminates all things in the world without being defiled by the obscurations of darkness.

The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher is likewise so: appearing in the world, fully endowed with merit, all who see him in whatever place find delight in him; he delivers the world yet remains unstained by worldly dharmas.

“Good son! It is like the rising sun, whose light shines everywhere, destroying all darkness and being free from any obscuration; the various activities and undertakings of all sentient beings are thereby fully accomplished. Yet, the nature of that sun makes no distinctions among sentient beings, nor does it harbor any thought of seeking a reward for its kindness.”

The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher is likewise: appearing in the world, he shatters the dark ignorance of all sentient beings and illuminates them universally with the light of wisdom, causing their various roots of goodness to flourish; yet that Bodhisattva makes no discrimination regarding those sentient beings and seeks no small measure of gratitude in return.

“Good son! It is like a ship that is sturdy, thick, and well-fastened; it does not leak nor is it broken, and it is able to ferry all sentient beings across the great ocean, yet it does not seek any payment from those beings.”

The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher is also like this: taking wisdom as the thick padding, the various pāramitās as the sturdy frame, and great compassion as the excellent binding, he is able to ferry all sentient beings across the great ocean of birth and death, yet he seeks no price or reward from those beings.
“Good son! It is like a violent river, flowing with rapid current, perilous and terrifying.
Within it there is a bridge that is impartial toward all sentient beings, providing them all with the joy of crossing over, yet without any conceptual thought of ‘crossing over.’”

The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher is likewise thus: amidst the torrential river of afflictions—difficult to cross due to its swift current, perilous, fearsome, and a treacherous path of rapid flow—he is able to act as a great bridge. He imparts the bliss of liberation equally to all sentient beings, yet he possesses no discriminating mind regarding their deliverance.

“Good son! It is like lighting a great lamp in a dark room; it illuminates all sentient beings—whether inferior, middling, or superior—with universal equality, yet that lamp-light has no notion of ‘self’ or ‘what belongs to self’ regarding its illumination.”

The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher is also like this: in the dark chamber of ignorance, he kindles the lamp of wisdom, which shines equally and universally upon all sentient beings—whether inferior, middling, or superior—yet that Bodhisattva possesses no mind of "self" or "mine" regarding that which is illuminated.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices to be able to know the corresponding analogies for the Dharma-preacher. Good son!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the ten kinds of dharma-knowledge, they know the dharmas of non-dwelling together.
What are these ten? They are:
not dwelling together with those of small minds, those who seek little, and those who are narrow-minded and inferior beings; [and so forth].
They do not dwell together with sentient beings who fail to give rise to a vast mind or great practice, nor with those who are indolent;
they do not dwell together with those who rely on conceit, overweening pride, and the pride of self, which stand like lofty banners;
they do not dwell together with sentient beings who are stingy, envious, immoral, resentful, indolent, distracted, or deluded.
The mind does not coexist with thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, or harmfulness;
it does not coexist with any conceptualization, differentiation, or manifold discrimination;
nor does it coexist with any hindrances, obscurations, secondary afflictions, or latent tendencies.
It does not coexist with any thoughts of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or worldly concerns;
it does not coexist with any thoughts of seeking honor, praise, or prostration;
and it does not coexist with any thoughts of "I" or "mine."
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva entering ten kinds of dharma-practices to be able to know the dharma of non-common dwelling.
Furthermore, good son!”
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell together with ten kinds of equanimity. What are these ten?

That is to say: one abandons the mind that embraces the sublime Dharma and does not dwell with it; one abandons the mind that listens to the sublime Dharma and does not dwell with it; one abandons the mind that teaches and transforms sentient beings and does not dwell with it; one abandons the mind that bestows the Dharma upon sentient beings and does not dwell with it; one abandons the mind of respect, reverence, and making offerings to all [the Buddhas] and does not dwell with it; one abandons the mind that subdues Māra and his like and does not dwell with it; one abandons the mind that crushes and destroys non-Buddhists and does not dwell with it; one abandons the mind that protects and upholds the sublime Dharma and does not dwell with it; one abandons the mind that practices the various pāramitās and does not dwell with it; and one abandons the mind that dedicates through the three accumulations and does not dwell with it.
“Good son! These are called the ten kinds of equanimity with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not cohabit. Good son!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter ten kinds of dharma-practices to understand the matters of transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*).
What are these ten? They are:

the manifestation as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), the manifestation as Śakra, the manifestation as Brahmā, the manifestation as a śrāvaka, the manifestation as a pratyekabuddha, the manifestation as a bodhisattva, the manifestation as a buddha, the manifestation of a buddha-field, the manifestation of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and the manifestation of the great assembly.
"Good son! These various manifestations of response by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all depend upon the faculties, dispositions, and desires of sentient beings.
Furthermore, good son!"

If there are sentient beings whose minds revere the Wheel-Turning Sage King, observing the precepts and practicing the ten wholesome paths of action with dignified deportment, at that time the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests the majestic array of a Wheel-Turning Sage King to benefit those beings.
"Furthermore, noble son!

As for the wheel-treasure that adorns a Wheel-Turning Sage King, it is complete with a thousand spokes, made entirely of Jambūnada gold, surpassing those of humans and devas, not the work of human hands, born from the merit of his own vows being fulfilled as he wished, such that those who behold it never tire of looking; these qualities are beyond the reach of any other ordinary wheel-turning kings."

"As for the Elephant Jewel, its body is magnificent and vast, pure white and immaculate, endowed with six tusks and perfect in all its characteristics; those who behold it never tire of the sight. It travels through the air with a speed as swift as that of the Airāvaṇa elephant or the Garuḍa bird. Born from the power of the merit of supreme roots of goodness, it is something that other ordinary wheel-turning kings cannot possess."

"As for the Horse Jewel, its color is deep blue; its nature is noble and gentle, like that of the horse-king Balāha. It travels through the air with a swiftness as rapid as the wind. Like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), it accords with whatever the King thinks of, never failing to satisfy his wishes—something no other ordinary wheel-turning kings can possess."

"The maṇi jewel is perfected with its eight facets; it is not a human artifact but exists spontaneously. It is endowed with radiance, and its brilliant color outshines the sun, the moon, the stars, and all other fires. It fulfills every need according to one's wishes—things that ordinary universal monarchs cannot possess."

"As for the Woman Jewel (*strī-ratna*), her complexion is radiant and pure, and her wondrous features are exceptionally prominent. Her proportions—whether black or white, long or short, plump or slender—are perfectly balanced. There is no aspect of her dignified demeanor or composure that one does not admire. She is thoroughly proficient in all worldly arts and the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*). Her speech is harmonious and elegant, soft and subtle; her phrasing is skillful, and she is endowed with eloquence."

Like a wish-fulfilling jewel that possesses all supreme and wondrous things, his mind is always at peace as he practices all wholesome dharmas—something no other ordinary wheel-turning kings can achieve.
"As for the Treasure of the Minister of the Treasury, his body is vast and his nature is firm and stable.

Like the Vajrapāṇi King Vaiśravaṇa, his appearance is dignified and majestic, and his speech is flowing and gracious; all who see or hear him find joy and delight. He has perfected the fleshly eye and is fully endowed with compassion."

Just as everything one thinks of is obtained through a wish-fulfilling gem, this treasure-minister is likewise born from the roots of virtue of that wheel-turning monarch; it is something that other ordinary wheel-turning monarchs cannot possess.
"The Treasure of the General of the Army is born from all merits and roots of goodness.
Because it functions like a mani-jewel mirror-image, whatever the king has not yet thought of is already accomplished beforehand."
By perceiving these signs, he knows all matters; his basis is preeminent and beyond reproach.

He travels through the air with sovereign ease and without obstruction, proceeding ahead according to the King’s thoughts. Wherever he goes, there is nothing that is not subdued—a feat no other ordinary wheel-turning monarch can achieve.

"Thus, all these miraculous manifestations adorned with the seven treasures of a universal monarch are brought about by the power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas' mastery over the mind, intended to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings."

This jewel of a human king and his activities are all preeminent and beyond reproach; with a sincere mind, a profound mind, a supple mind, and a mind that accords with the Dharma, he turns the Great Wheel of the Dharma, upholds the ten wholesome paths of action, is endowed with the thirty-two marks, and transforms sentient beings—this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s majestic transformation as a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin).

“Good son! If there are sentient beings whose minds revere the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Bodhisattva at that time transforms himself into the body of Śakra, possessing a hundred eyes and dwelling in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and says:
‘All dharmas are entirely impermanent; you should all distance yourselves from negligence.’”

"Good son! If there are sentient beings whose minds revere and honor the Great Brahma King, the Bodhisattva at that time transforms himself into a Brahma King, with exceptionally sublime deportment, and for the sake of the Brahma hosts, he preaches the four dhyānas and so forth."

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the body of a śrāvaka, and cannot be delivered by means of the body of a pratyekabuddha or the body of a buddha, the bodhisattva at that time manifests the body of a śrāvaka and teaches those sentient beings how to exhaust all suffering and attain the bliss of the unconditioned.”

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the body of a pratyekabuddha, and cannot be delivered by means of the body of a śrāvaka or the body of a Buddha, the bodhisattva at that time manifests the body of a pratyekabuddha and teaches them the path of a pratyekabuddha—explaining that all phenomena are entirely impermanent; delighting in secluded and tranquil places; teaching the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, samāpattis, and the four bases of psychic power; and declaring the pratyekabuddha to be a great field of merit—thereby preaching the subtle and wonderful Dharma to transform and teach sentient beings so that they may attain right faith.”

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of a bodhisattva’s body, the bodhisattva at that time, by means of his own subtle, wondrous, and pure form-body, teaches the six pāramitās, the four dharmas of tranquility, great loving-kindness and great compassion, as well as the various masteries, the various patiences, and the various stages to transform those sentient beings.”

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who possess superior faculties and should be delivered by means of a Buddha-body, the Bodhisattva at that time manifests as a Buddha-body, preaches for them the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and displays the supreme supernatural powers of all Buddhas to transform those sentient beings.”

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of a supremely wonderful, adorned, and pure Buddha-field, the Bodhisattva at that time transforms the trichiliocosm so that it is as level as the palm of a hand, without any elevations or depressions. Its ground is as soft as kācilinda grass; whoever touches it experiences nothing but bliss.”
Some have the color of lapis lazuli or crystal; some emit the fragrance of uraga-sandalwood; there are no evil realms there, nor are there the bodies of women or eunuchs.

Alternatively, they may manifest various mountains adorned with the seven treasures, as well as various extraordinary trees of flowers, fruits, and fragrances; being free from all black mountains, pits, ravines, mounds, gravel, thorns, and impure vegetation, they manifest these sublime things to transform those sentient beings.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who should be liberated by seeing a supremely wonderful and adorned site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Bodhisattva at that time manifests an adorned tree of the site of enlightenment. Its form is twelve *yojanas* in height and breadth; its roots are deep and firm, impossible to shake. It has a trunk made of Jāmbūnada gold, with branches and leaves composed of various jewels such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and agate. Furthermore, he manifests the bodies of immeasurable celestial maidens to transform those sentient beings.”

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who should attain liberation by seeing a superior assembly, at that time the Bodhisattva immediately manifests as a deity of great majesty and virtue, or as a nāga, yakṣa, gandharva, asura, garuḍa, kiṃnara, mahoraga, Śakra-devendra, Brahmā-rāja, or one of the four world-protectors; or he may manifest as a śrāvaka who has attained the four analytical knowledges and both types of liberation; or he may manifest as a bodhisattva dwelling in the tenth stage who has attained the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, in order to transform those sentient beings.”
“Good son! These are called the ten kinds of dharma-practices through which a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters and is able to know the matters of manifestation and transformation. Good son!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter ten kinds of dharma-practices to know the supreme and wondrous fruits of all roots of goodness.
What are these ten?
They are as follows, noble son:
For example, because of the form of the moon in the sky, one perceives various images of the moon in the water, yet the moon in the sky does not reach the water.
O son of good family!

In this way, through the causes and conditions of various roots of goodness and karmic actions, there arise diverse and sublime fruits of retribution; whatever the mind desires is entirely accomplished.

Just as the moon in the sky does not enter into the water, so too the causes and conditions of the various good deeds performed do not physically enter into the fruit. Although they do not enter the fruit, nevertheless, based upon those causes and conditions of the roots of goodness, there arise distinct and differing varieties of sublime fruits of retribution.
“Good son! For example, due to the causal conditions of karmic actions, various colors are seen within a single eye of a peacock feather;
in the same way, based on the causal conditions of the karmic actions of various roots of goodness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses immeasurable distinctions in their retributive fruits.”

Just as those karmic actions do not reach the hair-circle (keśoṇḍuka), yet although they do not reach it, by the power of the causal conditions of those karmas, various colors appear within that hair-circle.

In this way, the various roots of goodness and karmic actions performed do not directly reach their fruit; yet, although they do not directly reach the fruit, there arise distinct and differing superior fruits of retribution based upon those causes and conditions of the roots of goodness.

“Good son! For example, just as various kinds of flowers rain down from the sky based upon those sublime and excellent roots of goodness, and these flowers are endowed with exquisite color, fragrance, flavor, and texture, yet those roots of goodness do not enter into the flowers because the characteristics of the roots of goodness and the flowers in the sky are distinct; so it is here.”

In this way, the roots of goodness and karmic actions performed do not directly reach their fruit; yet, although they do not directly reach the fruit, there arise distinct and diverse superior fruits of retribution based upon those causes and conditions of wholesome karma.

“Good son! It is like when, based upon those supreme and wondrous virtuous deeds, various kinds of music, subtle sounds, and joyful festivities spontaneously arise in the void as an offering; yet those virtuous deeds do not enter into the music, sounds, and so forth, because these virtuous deeds and the various musical performances have distinct characteristics.”
Although their characteristics differ, various musical performances exist in the void space based upon those karmas.

In this same way, superior fruits of retribution arise based on the causal conditions of the practice of various roots of goodness; yet, those virtuous practices do not themselves reach the fruit. Although they do not reach the fruit, there are distinct differences in the superior fruits of retribution based upon the causal conditions of those roots of goodness.

“Good son! It is like a multicolored rainbow arising in space; although it arises based on the predominant conditions of the four great elements, those four great elements do not enter into the rainbow.”

Although it does not reach the rainbow itself, by the power of the causal conditions of those four great elements, various rainbow colors arise in their manifold differences: from the causal condition of the earth element, yellow arises; from the causal condition of the water element, blue arises; from the causal condition of the fire element, red and various variegated colors arise; and from the causal condition of the wind element, the circular form of the rainbow arises.
In this way, through the dominant causal conditions of various roots of goodness, there is the fulfillment of supreme and wondrous karmic rewards. "Good son!

It is like a wheel-turning king who, by virtue of upholding the causes and conditions of the ten paths of wholesome action, obtains the seven treasures in their entirety and naturally grown non-glutinous rice that does not require sowing. Yet, the causes and conditions of upholding the ten paths of wholesome action do not themselves reach the seven treasures, nor do they reach the naturally grown non-glutinous rice; rather, it is by depending on the causes and conditions of upholding the ten paths of wholesome action that the wheel-turning king’s supreme and wondrous karmic rewards come to be."

Thus, because one has well generated the superior mind, well initiated various practices, and well maintained the power of roots of goodness, there arises that sublime and wondrous karmic retribution of a wheel-turning monarch; yet, since that causal karma does not enter into the fruit itself, it is said that cause and effect are dissimilar.

“Good son! For example, through the superior and virtuous causes and conditions of the devas, there spontaneously arise *mandārava* flowers, various exquisite celestial palaces, and food of a hundred flavors; yet those roots of goodness do not themselves enter into the fruit. Nevertheless, it is not that these superior and wondrous fruits of retribution for the devas exist without depending upon the causes and conditions of those roots of goodness.”

“Good son! For example, by the power of the causal conditions of a supreme, wish-fulfilling supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), one encounters no obstruction when facing a stone wall; yet those causal conditions of the supernatural power do not themselves reach into the state of non-obstruction—it is simply that non-obstruction exists in dependence upon those causal conditions of the supernatural power.”
In this way, through the causes and conditions of the roots of goodness of heedfulness, there arises that supreme and wondrous retribution. "Good son!
It is like fire, which arises dependent on wind; apart from it, it does not arise."

Once the fire has arisen, its power is able to mature the color and provide luminous illumination; yet the nature of that fire does not come from the wind, because those qualities of luminous color and hot touch do not exist within the wind.
In this way, all fruits and rewards of the roots of goodness arise from causes and conditions.
You should know, son of good family!

For example, when a bhikṣu who practices according to the Dharma attains the merit of untainted roots of goodness, he achieves mastery such that by mere thought, he accomplishes the totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) of space—earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white—achieving them with mastery and without obstruction.

Furthermore, that unobstructed mind does not actually reach space; although the unobstructed state and so forth do not reach there, the mere thought of it can accomplish the task of being unobstructed. Therefore, without departing from that mind, one can accomplish the unobstructed state of the earth and other elements.
In this way, all untainted roots of goodness (anāsrava-kuśalamūla) possess the excellence of their resultant retribution through causes and conditions. "Good son!
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s entry into the ten kinds of dharma-practices by which one can know the superior and wondrous retribution of all roots of goodness."

“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters ten kinds of dharma-practices, they will be able to know how to attain the supreme and wondrous fruit-retribution of untainted (anāsrava) roots of goodness. What are these ten?

These are what are called the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā), the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭābhibhvāyatana), the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana), the ten masteries (daśavaśitā), the ten truths (daśasatya), the nine successive meditative attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), the samādhis (samāpatti), the ten powers (daśabala), and the ten knowledges (daśajñāna).
“Good son! What are the six supernormal powers?

They are the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the power of transformation, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows; these are called the six supernormal powers.”

“Good son! As for the divine eye of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, it is endowed with all roots of goodness and merit; it is unimpeded, unattached, immeasurable, unobstructed, non-abiding, non-active, without error, and without mistake. Being able to see in this manner, it is beyond reproach.”

It is not shared with any of the world’s śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it is far removed from all afflictions and all habitual tendencies of affliction; it is without erroneous vision and without erroneous prediction.

With the divine eye, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees all sentient beings—whether being born or dying, whether beautiful or ugly, whether coarse or sublime—and knows them as they truly are, according to the karmic actions performed by those beings and in accordance with their causes and effects.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s divine eye ultimately enables the attainment of buddha-knowledge and ultimately achieves buddha-knowledge; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s divine eye.

“Good son! The divine ear of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is without obstruction; it is fully endowed with all roots of goodness and merit, surpassing those of all ordinary beings, Śakra Devānām-Indra, the Four Heavenly Kings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.”

By means of this supreme, wondrous, unobstructed, and pure divine ear, one hears all sounds—the voices of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, even down to the sounds of mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and ants.

They hear all sounds, both those of the noble ones and those that are not noble; yet they do not give rise to a mind of attachment toward the sounds of the noble ones, nor do they give rise to a mind of aversion toward the sounds that are not noble.
Hearing the voice of an ordinary person, one does not give rise to the thought of inferiority; hearing the voices of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, one does not give rise to the thought of superiority.
Hearing the voices of those who are not noble ones, upon listening one does not feel aversion;
hearing the voices of noble ones, upon listening one does not feel attachment.

Regarding all sounds, one does not give rise to thoughts of beauty or ugliness; although hearing all sounds, they are entirely like echoes in space. Being free from "I" and "mine," because of their tranquil emptiness, one does not cling to the ear-base (*śrotrāyatana*) nor to the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*). This is called the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Good son! Regarding the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowledge of the minds of others: the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows his own mind as it truly is;

because he knows his own mind as it truly is, he knows the minds of all sentient beings as they truly are—namely, he knows greedy minds as they truly are, and minds free from greed as they truly are.”

A bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the mind of greed as it truly is and does not give rise to aversion; knowing the mind free from greed, he does not give rise to delight. Rather, he generates great compassion for sentient beings with minds of greed and great loving-kindness for sentient beings whose minds are free from greed.

In this way, one knows as they truly are a mind of anger and a mind free from anger; a mind of delusion and a mind free from delusion; a mind of attachment and a mind free from attachment; a mind of grasping and a mind free from grasping; a defiled mind and a mind free from defilement; a discursive mind and a non-discursive mind; a mind in samādhi and a mind free from samādhi; and one knows as they truly are a liberated mind and an unliberated mind.

In this way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows the minds of sentient beings as they truly are; toward sentient beings who have not yet attained liberation, he does not give rise to a mind of anger, and toward those who have attained liberation, he does not give rise to a mind of delight. Rather, he gives rise only to great compassion for those who have not attained liberation and great loving-kindness for those who have attained liberation.
Knowing all phenomena as they truly are to be nothing but this single mind, yet he does not give rise to craving or attachment toward that mind or this mind.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows the minds of others through his knowledge of others' minds, he knows the minds of all sentient beings as they truly are.

If those sentient beings were not granted the power of mindfulness by the Bodhisattva, they would be unable to know the Bodhisattva’s mind; even with the divine eye they could not know it, nor could any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas know it—how much less could ignorant ordinary people possibly know it?
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowledge of the minds of others.
"Good son! As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowledge of past lives, because they are fully endowed with all roots of goodness, they are able to know—"
One is able to know one's own past infinite lifetimes and the past infinite lifetimes of all sentient beings—
knowing one lifetime, two lifetimes, a hundred lifetimes, a thousand lifetimes, a hundred thousand million lifetimes,
up to infinite asaṃkhyeya lifetimes and infinite hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of lifetimes— and knows them well.

They skillfully know the formation of kalpas and the destruction of kalpas; they even skillfully know the formation and destruction of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and they skillfully know the formation and destruction of immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
They skillfully know the formation of great kalpas and the destruction of great kalpas, and they skillfully know the hundred [great kalpas].

He skillfully knows kalpas; he skillfully knows a thousand great kalpas, a hundred thousand great kalpas, and hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of great kalpas.

This knowledge of past lives of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is something that all the world’s devas, humans, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—except for the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, and those bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages—are utterly bewildered by.

In this way, the Bodhisattva knows: "In that place, I was born with such a lineage, such a complexion, such a name, such food and drink, such a lifespan, such a dwelling, such a height, such a breadth, such beauty or ugliness, and such suffering or pleasure. Dying there, I was born in another place; dying there, I am born here—with such a birth, such a lineage, such a complexion, such a name, such food and drink, such a lifespan, such a dwelling, such a height, such a breadth, such beauty or ugliness, and such suffering or pleasure."
Just as one knows one's own body, so too should one know the bodies of all sentient beings;
even down to mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and ants, one should know them in this same way.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowledge of past lives is unimpeded, unattached, non-abiding, unobstructed, and unhindered; it does not miss its proper time, is conjoined with great loving-kindness and great compassion, is profoundly deep and inconceivable, and is far removed from both active afflictions and the latencies of affliction. Adorned with all-purity, merit, and wisdom, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowledge of past lives.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowledge of the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi*)?

It is the unimpeded accomplishment of all merit and wisdom, which is spontaneous and non-conceptual. Through the superior power of one's own body—having practiced giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, samādhi, and samāpatti for immeasurable, incalculable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and trillions of kalpas—and through the superior condition of the Tathāgata’s pure celestial nature, this bodhisattva manifests that psychic transformation spontaneously and without obstruction, surpassing all worlds and bringing benefit to sentient beings.”
This bodhisattva can abide in whatever way they wish their mind to abide; they can manifest whatever realm they wish their mind to manifest.
This bodhisattva’s supernormal power of mastery manifests everywhere without obstruction, according to their will.

This bodhisattva should manifest the physical form of a single sentient being to those who can be transformed by such a manifestation; for their sake, the bodhisattva manifests the physical form of a single sentient being while appearing as the physical forms of all sentient beings. According to the capacity of each sentient being to receive the vessel of the Path, they manifest various transformation bodies to appear before them, performing various deeds, speaking various words, and displaying various modes of deportment.

When this bodhisattva, with a mental resolve, desires to manifest the physical forms of all sentient beings as the physical forms of all Buddhas, he is immediately able to manifest the physical forms of all sentient beings as the physical forms of all Buddhas.

When this bodhisattva, with a mental resolve, desires to manifest the physical forms of all Buddhas as the physical forms of all sentient beings, he is immediately able to manifest the physical forms of all Buddhas as the physical forms of all sentient beings.

If this bodhisattva intends to cause the kalpa of formation to appear as a kalpa of destruction, he immediately manifests the kalpa of formation as a kalpa of destruction, and those sentient beings see the kalpa of formation as a kalpa of destruction.

If this bodhisattva intends to cause the kalpa of destruction to appear as a kalpa of formation, he is able to manifest the kalpa of destruction as a kalpa of formation, and those sentient beings see the kalpa of destruction as a kalpa of formation. In this way, he manifests all instances of formation and destruction as either formation or destruction.

When this bodhisattva thus intends to manifest one eon as the first watch of a single day, he is able to manifest it accordingly; those sentient beings then perceive that eon as the first watch of a day.
When this bodhisattva manifests one eon as the first watch of a day, it becomes so for them, and those sentient beings likewise perceive it as such.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal power of transformation at will (*nirmāṇarddhi-vidhi-jñāna*).

As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal power of manifestation before one's eyes (*abhimukharddhi-vidhi-jñāna*): this supernormal power of manifestation before one's eyes is that which, based on inconceivable merit and superior wisdom, manifests spontaneously and without mental effort; it accomplishes all tasks without impairment and is able to manifest before one's eyes. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal power of manifestation before one's eyes.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s spontaneous supernormal power of mastery?

If there are sentient beings who should perceive various forms and colors and various modes of conduct through such faith and such views, this bodhisattva—without deliberation and without discrimination—spontaneously manifests these forms; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s spontaneous supernormal power of mastery.”

“If there are sentient beings in as many worlds as there are who should see the appearance of a Buddha in the world in order to be liberated, this Bodhisattva immediately manifests the appearance of a Buddha in those many worlds—descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, being born from the womb, renouncing the household life, practicing austerities, proceeding to the site of enlightenment to subdue Māra, attaining perfect awakening, turning the wheel of Dharma, and manifesting Great Nirvāṇa—in this manner teaching and transforming those sentient beings.”

“Good son! Such immeasurable spheres of the psychic power of supernormal transformation (*ṛddhi*) possessed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom of the supernormal power of supernormal transformation.”
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows? Good son!”
The bodhisattva remains far removed from the four outflows (*āsrava*):
namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Having remained far removed from such outflows as these, the bodhisattva mahāsattva no longer undergoes rebirth.

This bodhisattva no longer undergoes rebirth, yet is able to manifest birth in all places in accordance with sentient beings who are ready to be transformed; this is called the bodhisattva’s spontaneous and unceasing practice of the bodhisattva path.
These are called the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. "Good son!
What are the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
These are the clear knowledge of the divine eye, the clear knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. "Good son!
What is meant by 'knowledge'?"
There is the knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurjñāna*) and the clarity of the divine eye.
What is meant by "divine"?
It refers to the knowledge of the divine eye belonging to those pure devas and the supreme, sublime celestial beings.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva ultimately attains that knowledge of the divine eye—referring to the "pure devas," namely śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgatas;
and the "supremely sublime higher devas," meaning that the Tathāgatas are superior to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and [worldly] devas.
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the divine eye of those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, this is called the first clarity. "Good son,
what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s clarity of the knowledge of past lives?"

"Good son! Regarding the past, future, and present, there is no realm that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not know, do not see, or do not awaken to. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains those realms and that clarity of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). This clarity is unlike that of any Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha; this is called the second clarity."
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows?

It is when the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is far removed from the four outflows and the habitual tendencies of afflictions—namely, the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, the outflow of views, and the outflow of ignorance.”

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva realizes the Path of Seeing, they immediately become detached from such afflictions as well as the habitual tendencies of those afflictions; they do not merely realize the abandonment of the dharmas of the afflictive hindrances, nor are they the same as Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the like.

Having attained the exhaustion of outflows, one is without obstruction regarding all places of birth and in the teaching and transforming of all sentient beings; this is called the Bodhisattva’s clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*). "Good son!
What are the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s eight liberations (*vimokṣa*)?
That which is called "possessing internal form and seeing external forms" is named the first liberation;
"possessing the internal perception of form and seeing external forms" is named the second liberation;
and "perception of purity through faith" is named the third liberation.

This Bodhisattva transcends all perceptions of form, ceases all perceptions of sensory resistance, and does not attend to perceptions of diversity; knowing infinite space, they enter the meditative state of infinite space—this is called the fourth liberation.
This Bodhisattva transcends all perceptions of infinite space, knows infinite consciousness, and enters the meditative state of infinite consciousness—this is called the fifth liberation.
This Bodhisattva transcends all perceptions of infinite consciousness, knows nothingness, and enters the meditative state of the sphere of nothingness—this is called the sixth liberation.

This bodhisattva, transcending the sphere of nothingness, knowing the peace of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters into the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the seventh liberation.

This bodhisattva, transcending all practices of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, extinguishing all sensation and perception, enters into the practice of the attainment of cessation; this is called the eighth liberation.
“Good son! What is meant by ‘having form and seeing form’?

That which has form is entirely born of causes and conditions. To see that it is empty and devoid of a life-principle (jīva), and to be able to see in this way so as to attain liberation from bondage—this is called liberation.”
"What is meant by 'having the perception of internal forms while seeing external forms'?

To see that they are empty, devoid of a life-principle, and all produced through causes and conditions—to be able to see in this way and thereby attain liberation from bondage is called emancipation."
“What is the purity of faith? As for purity:
if one discriminates between pure and impure characteristics, it is called wrong view; because one attains liberation through the purity of faith, it is called emancipation.”

"Transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing all perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one perceives 'space is infinite' and thus enters the sphere of infinite space."
The immeasurable space is empty and void; one who can know it thus attains liberation from bondage, which is called "deliverance.
Transcending all space, one knows infinite consciousness and thereby enters the practice of infinite consciousness.
Immeasurable consciousness, boundless consciousness—this boundless consciousness is itself emptiness. One who can know it thus attains liberation from bondage; this is called emancipation.

"Having transcended the cognition of infinite consciousness and knowing that nothing exists, one enters the practice of nothingness—wherein 'existence' refers to the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion."
One who enters the practice of non-existence extinguishes those afflictions; being able to know in this way, one attains liberation from bondage, which is called "deliverance.
Having transcended non-existence, one knows that the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful, and thus enters the practice of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
That which is not characterized by perception is empty and quiescent by nature;
that which is not without perception exists by virtue of causes and conditions.
To be able to see in this way is to attain liberation from bondage, which is called emancipation.
“Transcending all states of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and extinguishing all sensation and perception, one enters the practice of the attainment of cessation.

When a bodhisattva perceives in this way—that perception is like a mirage and sensation is like a bubble; that perception is itself sensation and sensation is itself perception; and that there is no knower and no life-principle—one who can perceive thus attains liberation from bondage, which is called emancipation.”
“Good son! What are the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? They are as follows:
possessing form, one sees forms; having attained mastery over those forms, one knows them, and having attained mastery over those forms, one sees them. This is called the first base of mastery.

"With a perception of internal forms, one sees external forms—whether beautiful or ugly—and having attained mastery over those forms, one knows them; having attained mastery over those forms, one sees them. This is called the second base of mastery."

“Having the perception of internal forms, one sees external forms that are immeasurable—whether beautiful or ugly—and having attained mastery over those forms, one knows them; having attained mastery over those forms, one sees them. This is called the third base of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).”
“With the perception of internal forms, one sees external forms that are few—whether beautiful or ugly—and attains mastery over those forms while knowing them;
one attains mastery over those forms while seeing them. This is called the fourth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).”
“With the internal body possessing the perception of form, one sees external forms that are blue—seeing them as blue in color, blue in hue, and blue in luster.
Just as an *umakā* flower is seen as blue in color, blue in hue, and blue in luster;
so too is it with the Bodhisattva: with the internal body possessing the perception of form, he sees external forms that are blue, seeing them as blue in color, blue in hue, and blue in luster.”
Having attained mastery over those forms, one knows them; having attained mastery over those forms, one sees them—this is called the fifth *abhibhvāyatana*.
Internally perceiving the form-attribute of having physical form, one sees external forms that are yellow—seeing them as yellow, yellow in color, and yellow in luster.
For example, just as a *gaṇikāra* flower is seen to be yellow, with a yellow color and a yellow luster;
so too is it for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva: perceiving the internal body as having form, they see external forms that are yellow, seeing them as yellow in color and possessing a yellow luster.
Having attained mastery over those forms, one knows them; having attained mastery over those forms, one sees them. This is called the sixth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Internally perceiving the appearance of form, one sees external forms that are red—seeing red as red, with a red color and a red luster.
For example, just as when one looks at a pāṇḍuśīrṣa flower that is red, one sees the red color, the redness, and the red luster;
so too, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having the perception of internal form, sees external forms that are red, seeing the red color, the redness, and the red luster.
Having attained mastery over those forms, one knows them; having attained mastery over those forms, one sees them. This is called the seventh sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
"Internally perceiving the sign of form, one sees external forms that are white—seeing them as white in color, white in appearance, and emitting white light."
Just as, for example, the *uśanas-tārā* (the morning star) perceives white as white—perceiving it as white in color and white in light—the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this:
possessing the perception of internal form, they perceive external forms that are white, perceiving them as white in color and white in light.
"One attains mastery over those forms and knows them; one attains mastery over those forms and sees them. This is called the eighth sphere of mastery.
These are called the eight spheres of mastery of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
The Sūtra on the Collection of the Buddha’s Teachings, Scroll Two;
The Sūtra on the Collection of the Buddha’s Teachings, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
“Good son! What are the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? They are:

the earth universal base, the water universal base, the fire universal base, the wind universal base, the space universal base, the blue universal base, the yellow universal base, the red universal base, the white universal base, and the consciousness universal base. These are called the ten universal bases.”
If this bodhisattva wishes to cause all realms to enter into a single realm, then all realms enter into a single realm—namely, they enter the earth element;
if he wishes to cause all realms to enter into a single realm, then all realms enter into a single realm—namely, they enter the water element;
if he wishes to cause all realms to enter into a single realm, then all realms enter into a single realm—namely, they enter the fire element.
If one wishes to enter all elements into a single element, one enters that single element; that is to say, one enters the wind element.
If one wishes to enter all elements into a single element, one enters that single element; that is to say, one enters the space element.
If one wishes to enter all bases of mastery (*āyatanas*) into a single base of mastery, one enters that single base of mastery; that is to say, the blue base of mastery.
If one wishes to enter a single base by means of all bases, one enters that single base, namely the yellow base;
if one wishes to enter a single base by means of all bases, one enters that single base, namely the red base;
if one wishes to enter a single base by means of all bases, one enters that single base, namely the white base.
If one wishes to enter a single sphere by means of all spheres, one enters that single sphere, namely, the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*).

If one wishes to enter a single sphere by means of all earth, water, fire, wind, space, blue, yellow, red, white, and the sphere of consciousness, one enters that single sphere; therefore, this is called "entering one by means of all spheres."
Entering into one [base] immediately accomplishes all bases; therefore, they are called the "all-bases.
These are called the ten all-bases of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva. "Good son!
What are the ten masteries of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? They are:

mastery over life, mastery over mind, mastery over material things, mastery over karma, mastery over birth, mastery over supernormal powers, mastery over conviction, mastery over vows, mastery over wisdom, and mastery over the Dharma. These are called the ten masteries of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Good son! Attaining the supreme nectar is called mastery over life;
being able to know that all things are but this one mind is called mastery over the mind.
Producing various precious jewels from the palms of one's hands and taking even space as a treasury is called mastery over objects (*vastu-vaśitā*);

being far removed from all afflictions (*kleśa*), the latent tendencies of afflictions (*vāsanā*), and the underlying propensities of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) is called mastery over karma (*karma-vaśitā*);
turning at will within meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*) is called mastery over birth (*upapatti-vaśitā*).
To act spontaneously among all conditioned phenomena is called mastery over the will (*vaśitā*);
to attain the contemplation of mastery within all spheres of entry is called mastery over faith (*adhimukti-vaśitā*);
and at the very moment the mind arises, to manifest and accomplish all matters before one is called mastery over aspiration (*praṇidhāna-vaśitā*).
All actions of body, speech, and mind are rooted in wisdom; this is called mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
To manifest the attainment of the equality of the *tathatā*-dharma-dhātu and the stainless wisdom of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is called mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*).
"Furthermore, noble son!
Because he has attained mastery over life, he counteracts all fear of death in the world;
because he has attained mastery over the mind, he counteracts all fear of afflictions in the world."
Because they have attained mastery over objects, they counteract all fears of worldly poverty;
because they have attained mastery over karma, they counteract all fears of worldly misconduct;
because they have attained mastery over birth, they counteract all fears of the evil realms of existence.
Because they have attained mastery over the fulfillment of wishes, they counteract the fear of all worldly pursuits;
because they have attained mastery over faith, they counteract the fear of the karmic retribution for slandering the Dharma in all worlds;
because they have attained mastery over vows, they counteract the fear of the bonds of mental afflictions in all worlds.
Because they have attained mastery over wisdom, they counteract all worldly fears of the thorns of doubt;
because they have attained mastery over the Dharma, they counteract all worldly fears of the great assemblies.
"Furthermore, noble son!
To remain far removed from the transgression of taking life and to harbor no mind of anger or harm toward any sentient being is the cause for mastery over life.

To possess unimpeded great loving-kindness toward sentient beings experiencing happiness and unimpeded great compassion toward sentient beings experiencing suffering is the cause for mastery over the mind."
Equanimity that relinquishes all affairs and dedicates them toward great enlightenment is the cause for mastery over things;
entering into all performed actions—namely, pure actions of body, speech, and mind—is the cause for mastery over karma;
taking the bodhicitta as the foundation to encompass all roots of goodness and the ten paths of wholesome action is the cause for mastery over birth.

Offering all forms of worship, reverence, prostration, and praise; giving away elephants, horses, and carriages to sentient beings—these are the causes for mastery over wish-fulfillment (*rddhi-vaśitā*).
Teaching and transforming all sentient beings within the Three Jewels is the cause for mastery over faith (*adhimukti-vaśitā*).
Bestowing pure actions of body, speech, and mind upon all sentient beings is the cause for mastery over aspiration (*praṇidhāna-vaśitā*).
To remain far removed from craving for offerings, veneration, and food, and to be able to bestow the food of Dharma upon all sentient beings, is the cause of mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*).

To impartially teach and transform all sentient beings, to proclaim that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is equal for all sentient beings, and to declare that all sentient beings and all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) rather than a body of food, is the cause of mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*).
This is called the ten masteries attained by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
"Good son! What are the ten truths of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas?"

What are called the conventional truth, the ultimate truth, the truth of characteristics, the truth of distinctions, the truth of contemplation, the truth of phenomena, the truth of arising, the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, the truth of the knowledge of entering the path, and the truth of the collection of Tathāgata-knowledge—these are named the ten truths.

“Good son! As for the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it refers to that which is limited and defined by names and numbers, explained to others as something narrow and inferior rather than extensive; this is called the conventional truth.”

"The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) refers to the profound dharmas associated with emptiness; it is without limit or boundary, a state that is never severed, not produced by other causes and conditions, equal and of a single characteristic, devoid of high or low, possessing neither the characteristic of agitation nor of stillness—the characteristic of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas. This is called the ultimate truth."

"Regarding the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*): that which is oppressive is the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*); that which arises is the characteristic of origination (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*); that which is pure is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*); and that which is the vehicle is the characteristic of the path (*mārga-lakṣaṇa*). This is called the truth of characteristics."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

To know that the self-nature of all phenomena is characterized by non-self, characterized by the realization of the path, and characterized by the actualization [of that realization]—this is called the Truth of Characteristics."

To thus know that all phenomena have the characteristic of intrinsic purity, the characteristic of being intrinsically detached, the characteristic of intrinsic emptiness, and the characteristic of being intrinsically neither arising nor ceasing; and to realize the characteristic of the Path and to act upon the characteristic of realizing the Path—this is called the Truth of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*).

"Regarding the truth of differentiation: all phenomena are of a single characteristic, yet they are explained as differentiated based on dependent causes and conditions. This 'single characteristic' refers to the characteristic of emptiness; that emptiness is explained through the differentiation of the dependent."

"Furthermore, all phenomena are signless, wishless, and without activity; they are neither born nor extinguished. All their various distinctions are the characteristic of emptiness—they are entirely empty and possess the characteristic of non-contradiction. This is called the truth of distinction."
"What is the contemplation of the truths?

Contemplation means thorough observation; it consists of repeated seeing, reflection, knowing, viewing, awakening, and realized wisdom that is not in contradiction with its object—this is called the contemplation of the truths."

"Regarding the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*): it refers to the knowledge of phenomena. 'Phenomena' refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). To know that these aggregates, elements, and bases arise solely through causes and conditions, being devoid of a substantial entity (*vastu*) and a life-principle (*jīva*), and to realize the Path by knowing them thus—this is called the truth of phenomena."
"What is the Truth of Arising?

It refers to that by relying upon which one knows the severance of afflictions, by relying upon which one practices the severance of afflictions, and by relying upon which path one severs afflictions; thereby attaining the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities, further realizing all dharmas, and obtaining the supreme sovereign dharmas of all Tathāgatas—this is called the Truth of Arising."

Regarding the truth of the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unborn (*kṣayānutpādajñāna-satya*): it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are exhausted. Whether those conditioned phenomena are exhausted or not exhausted, they are exhausted by means of both exhaustion and non-exhaustion.
If there were an exhaustion of that which is already exhausted, then there would be an exhaustion of exhaustion; therefore, they are neither exhausted nor non-exhausted.
Therefore, the state where exhaustion is neither arising nor ceasing is called the Truth of the Knowledge of the Non-arising of Exhaustion (*kṣayānutpādajñānasatya*).
What is the Truth of the Knowledge of Entering the Path (*mārgapraveśajñānasatya*)?

By means of what knowledge, by means of what path, by means of what accumulation of merits, and by means of what accumulation of wisdom, one knows that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing; and relying upon those phenomena, one enters it oneself and causes others to enter it—this is called the Truth of the Knowledge of Entering the Path.
"What is the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom?

It refers to the interval between the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) and the Tathāgata stage, wherein one accumulates the truth of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and attains the realization of that spontaneous path of Tathāgata-wisdom; this is called the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom."
"These are called the ten truths of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Good son, what are the nine successive attainments of samāpatti of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"

“The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, detached from all desires and unwholesome, evil dharmas, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of detachment, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna.”
"Good son! 'Free from all desires' refers to the objects of craving and attachment associated with the first dhyāna; to be far removed from those dharmas is called being free from all desires.

'Free from all evil and unwholesome dharmas' refers to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, greed, anger, and wrong views arising from attachment, aversion, and delusion—these are called evil and unwholesome dharmas. To be far removed from those dharmas is called the first dhyāna."
That which possesses vitarka is so called because it is associated with vitarka. What is vitarka?
Upon what object does it depend?
Conforming to the first dhyāna, this awakening has various synonymous names, namely: knowledge, awareness, reflection, investigation, concentration, and so forth; these are called "awakening."
What is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)?

It is the mental application that accords with the initial dhyāna, consisting of the investigation and reflection upon the perception of desire and the awareness of meditative concentration; this is called contemplation.

Based on the practice of renunciation, together with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one accomplishes the first dhyāna; based on the practice of renunciation, together with joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*), one accomplishes the first dhyāna. This is called the practice of entering the first dhyāna with joy and bliss.
"Practice" refers to that which is termed upholding, guarding, mindfulness, joy, bliss, knowledge, and so forth; this is called practice.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in the first dhyāna and attains the superior aspiration for the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they therefore enter dhyāna to seek the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to attain a mind that seeks an even more superior endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), develops a lack of firm attachment toward that first dhyāna; for this reason, the bodhisattva relinquishes that first dhyāna to seek the second dhyāna.

This bodhisattva, having departed from that mind of vitarka and vicāra belonging to the first dhyāna, extinguishes that mind, detaches from that mind, purifies that mind, and brings that mind to stillness; this is for the purpose of entering the second dhyāna and accomplishing the mental application of the second dhyāna.

This bodhisattva, having transcended applied and sustained thought, with internal purity and a mind focused on a single point, free from applied and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.
"Inner purity" refers to the antidote to those factors that obstruct the second dhyāna.
When the bodhisattva is tranquil and those factors are pure and free from turbidity, this is called inner purity.

"One-pointedness of mind" means that all initial and sustained application (*vitarka* and *vicāra*) of the first dhyāna are extinguished, becoming tranquil and of a single flavor, like the great ocean.
Good son! For example, just as all waters entering the great ocean become of one and the same flavor—namely, the salty taste.

In this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the second dhyāna, he extinguishes all vitarka and vicāra of that first dhyāna; it is tranquil and of a single flavor, without vitarka and without vicāra. This is called attaining the samādhi of non-vitarka and non-vicāra.

This bodhisattva gives rise to joy based on that samādhi—meaning he gives rise to a joyful mind toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—and by relying on that joyful mind, all virtuous merits are spontaneously fulfilled.

"This bodhisattva, for the sake of that supreme light of the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)—a light that becomes increasingly radiant, increasingly sublime, and increasingly supple—attains a mind of superior aspiration."

Because this bodhisattva relies on that superior aspiration for the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he does not dwell in nor take delight in that second dhyāna, but further seeks the practice of the superior third dhyāna.

This bodhisattva gives rise to such a thought, knowing that this mind of joy obstructs the third dhyāna and obstructs the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore, the bodhisattva departs from joy and practices equanimity, mindfulness, and clear awareness, experiencing bliss with the body—a bliss which the noble ones also describe as "equanimous" and "mindful. Having distanced himself from the joy of rapture, he enters the practice of the third dhyāna.
Having attained the bliss of samādhi, this bodhisattva becomes weary of that joy and gives rise to this thought:
"This joyless bliss is impermanent; it is a bliss subject to exhaustion and cessation. It is not eternal, not constant, not true bliss, and not ultimate bliss."
Having understood this, that bodhisattva progressively attains an even more superior desire for the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Relying on that superior desire for the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, that bodhisattva takes no pleasure in suffering or pleasure; having abandoned both suffering and pleasure, and with the prior cessation of sorrow and joy, they enter the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and pure mindfulness.

This bodhisattva attains the samāpatti of the fourth dhyāna—a supple mind, a masterful mind, a tranquil mind, a luminous mind, and an upright mind—and relinquishes all those sources of happiness to all sentient beings.

When this bodhisattva brings about immediate peace and happiness for all sentient beings, the light of the realization of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) immediately manifests before them.
Because this bodhisattva has attained the manifestation of that light of the realization of the non-arising of phenomena, their practice becomes swift.

"This bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of attachment toward the sublime and excellent bliss within that fourth dhyāna; remaining detached from that bliss, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he perceives only the manifestation of empty space before him."
This bodhisattva transcends all marks of form, extinguishes all marks of resistance, and does not attend to various marks; knowing infinite space, they enter the practice of infinite space.
This bodhisattva contemplates form in this way, briefly in two kinds:
first, the four great elements; second, that which depends upon the four great elements.
The four great elements refer to earth, water, fire, and wind.
That which depends on the four great elements refers to form, fragrance, taste, and tangibility.
Thus, there are broadly eight kinds of form; apart from all these characteristics of form, there is no characteristic of form.
Because those signs of form are extinguished, it is said that one has transcended all signs of form.
Whatever phenomenon possesses a sign of form must necessarily possess a sign of resistance.
Therefore, having transcended all signs of form and extinguished all signs of opposition, one does not attend to nor engage with various diverse signs.
Because they transcend various distinct characteristics and do not dwell upon various distinct characteristics, they perceive only the characteristic of empty space.
Therefore, the bodhisattva knows that immeasurable empty space is precisely the entry into the practice of boundless empty space.
When this bodhisattva enters the samādhi of the sphere of infinite space, he gives rise to this thought:
"Space is infinite, space is boundless, space is shoreless; according to whatever phenomena are infinite and so forth, those phenomena have no prior limit, no middle limit, and no subsequent limit."
"In this way, he contemplates all phenomena as having no prior, middle, or subsequent limit.

When this bodhisattva enters such a samādhi, he immediately gives rise to a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings, and the wisdom of equality regarding all phenomena manifests before him. At that time, within the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), the bodhisattva first attains the manifestation of the light of supreme progress."
“Having transcended all marks of infinite space, this bodhisattva directly realizes the mark of infinite consciousness and enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
This bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:
‘These marks of infinite space are merely conceptualizations and discriminations of consciousness.’”
When this bodhisattva attains such a mind, he knows that all things are merely the marks of consciousness (*vijñapti*), and that this consciousness is immeasurable and boundless.

This bodhisattva enters such a samādhi and attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), yet it is not the ultimate accomplishment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.

This bodhisattva, having transcended all signs of infinite consciousness, directly realizes the sphere of nothingness and enters the practice of the sphere of nothingness, which is the absence of even the slightest thing.
That which is "nothing" means the absence of that which belongs to it.
What is that which exists?
It refers to the conceptualizations of greed, hatred, and delusion; various conceptualizations and false conceptualizations. All conditioned phenomena arise from the mind of false conceptualization.
Because that which belongs to it does not exist, it is called "non-existent" (an-asti).
Regarding "not even a little": as previously stated, within phenomena, minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), subtle characteristics, and minute characteristics are termed "minor characteristics."
Because there is not even the slightest mark of that, it is said that "nothing exists.
Because it transcends all marks, whether coarse or subtle, it is said that "there is nothing" and "not even the slightest exists.
When this bodhisattva abides in such a samādhi, he attains a further superior light of the non-arising dharma-patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) which manifests before him.

"This bodhisattva, having attained that patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), does not delight in that samādhi of non-existence and non-substantiality; rather, this bodhisattva further seeks a superior samādhi, giving rise to a mind of sublime aspiration."
This bodhisattva further seeks the superior practice of higher samādhi and gives rise to this thought:
"Even this state of non-existence and the absence of subtle marks of activity are themselves subtle marks, because they are false conceptualizations."
"Next, one contemplates that which is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic.
What dharma is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic?
That which is 'non-characteristic' is emptiness; that which is 'not non-characteristic' arises from causes and conditions."

At that time, the bodhisattva attains the samādhi of "neither-sign nor non-sign" which manifests before him; this bodhisattva transcends all states of nothingness and, with diminished signs, enters the practice of the samādhi of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
When the bodhisattva dwells in that state, he gives rise to this thought:
"In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is nothing to be delighted in.
Thus, the bodhisattva distances himself from that state.
"When this bodhisattva distances himself from those states, all dharmas immediately manifest as neither arising nor ceasing.

This bodhisattva knows that all dharmas neither arise nor cease; he perceives that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is quiescent. This bodhisattva neither proceeds nor abides; at that time, the bodhisattva attains the supreme, pure, and unsurpassed *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*."
From this point onward, this bodhisattva attains the spontaneous and uninterrupted bodhisattva path.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s ninefold sequential entry into samāpatti.
“Good son! What are the ten powers of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? They are:

the power of faith, the power of internal realization, the power of cultivation, the power of patience, the power of wisdom, the power of detachment, the power of the wisdom of hearing, the power of eloquence, the power of merit, and the power of practice according to reality.”
“Good son! What is the power of faith?
As for the power of faith, it is that when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has faith in various dharmas, within each of those dharmas, their mind immediately achieves the power of decisive faith.”
In this power of faith, no devas, humans, or māras in any world can disturb or shake this bodhisattva; this is called the power of faith of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Good son! What is the internal power of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
When a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of desire, they cultivate the contemplation of impurity, whereby that mind of desire is immediately extinguished;”
When a mind of anger arises, by practicing great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), that anger is extinguished;
when a mind of delusion arises, by practicing the contemplation of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), that delusion is extinguished.
If this bodhisattva is reviled, struck, or bound by others, they give rise to this thought:
"This sound is like an echo; verbal abuse and the like are like a dream.

At that time, the bodhisattva attains the wisdom of equality and, with faith, understands that beating, reviling, imprisonment, and so forth are solely the result of one's own karma; by being able to see things in this way, [the afflictions] are immediately extinguished.

This bodhisattva knows what things exist within this body—namely, things such as oppression and mutilation—which are like the moon reflected in water; at that time, the bodhisattva attains the wisdom of equality, and by knowing them in this way, they are immediately extinguished.
To state the essentials: that a bodhisattva can know that all gates of affliction are themselves gates of purity—this is called the inner power of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. "Good son!
What is the power of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

It refers to the power of the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*) and the power of the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārgabhūmi*), by which those obstructive dharmas that serve as counteragents cannot obstruct that bodhisattva.

In the stage of practice through faith and in the stage of the path of vision, no one among the gods, humans, Māras, or Brahmās in all the worlds can disturb them; this is called the power of cultivation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of patience?
It is when a bodhisattva is reviled by others but does not retaliate, because he has attained the power of wisdom that perceives all things as equal to echoes.”
If a bodhisattva is struck by another and does not retaliate, it is because they have attained the power of wisdom that perceives equality with a reflected image;
if a bodhisattva is troubled by another and does not retaliate, it is because they have attained the power of wisdom that perceives equality with an illusion;
if a bodhisattva is provoked to anger by another and does not retaliate, it is because they have attained the power of wisdom that perceives internal purity and equality.
They cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, because they have attained the power of wisdom regarding the purity and equality of worldly phenomena;
they cannot be defiled or overcome by any afflictions, because they have attained the power of wisdom regarding the equality of the causal conditions of their accumulation.
To state the essentials: when this bodhisattva perceives that all gates of defiled dharmas are themselves gates of purity, this is called the power of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Good son! What is the power of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

It is that the bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas) are empty, neither arising nor ceasing; it is by means of such wisdom that he can gather great bodhi.”

Within that wisdom, all Māras, non-Buddhists, and those with false views—even when manifesting in the form of a Buddha—cannot move him, nor disturb him, nor cause him doubt; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of wisdom.
“Good son! What is the power of detachment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

If a bodhisattva remains in one place and all sentient beings come to him to revile and abuse him with harsh speech, or to slander him, and likewise revile the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha Jewel; or if they seize the bodhisattva, or cut or mangle him—the bodhisattva, at that time, does not give rise toward those sentient beings to harm or anger, nor does he arouse a mind of affliction (*kleśa*), a mind of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), or a mind of habitual afflictions (*vāsanā-kleśa*).”

If there are sentient beings who come to transform a bodhisattva, inciting them to commit various evils, the bodhisattva at that time transforms them so that they follow him, causing them to attain a firm mind toward the Triple Gem; this is called the power of detachment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the wisdom of hearing? Good son!”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses a vast learning that is retained through hearing, a sea-treasury of the wisdom of hearing, and an accumulation of the wisdom of hearing; thus, this Bodhisattva achieves such power of the wisdom of extensive learning.

If the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm, harboring various doubts, were to approach the Bodhisattva and simultaneously pose questions that differ from one another, at that time the Bodhisattva’s mind would remain unmoved, answering with a single voice to sever all their doubts.

In this way, regarding hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of various questions over hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, the bodhisattva answers them all at once with a single voice; this is called the power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom derived from hearing.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of eloquence?
