When a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma amidst an assembly of hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of beings, that bodhisattva does not deliberate or discriminate as to which specific beings delight in which specific dharmas; rather, the bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to those beings in accordance with their needs.”

When a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, they do not lose the meaning of the words; nor do they repeat themselves, speak too slowly or too quickly, use harsh tones, or speak in excessive or insufficient measure. This is called the power of eloquence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Good son! What is the power of merit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Whether a bodhisattva is beneath a tree, in his own home, or in an open space, even if all the māras and their retinues approach that bodhisattva to cause destruction or to create disturbance, those māras and their retinues will be unable to destroy or disturb that bodhisattva’s practice.”
Those hosts of Māras were themselves struck with terror; they were shattered and dispersed, seeing themselves utterly destroyed and without any savior.

The weapons held by those hosts of Māras—swords, blades, spears, lances, long hooks, battle-axes, discuses, nooses, bows, arrows, halberds, and pikes—such things as these, like clouds and rain, were instantly transformed into various kinds of flowers through the power of the merit of that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. These were the so-called *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *roca* flowers, *mahāroca* flowers, *tāla* flowers, *mahātāla* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *sumana* flowers, *utpala* flowers, and *padma* flowers; such various flowers fell like clouds and rain to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.

Whatever various kinds of coarse and fierce speech those hosts of Māras uttered—which would cause terror in those who heard it—all such sounds were instantly transformed into various subtle and wonderful sounds of praise through the power of this Bodhisattva’s merit.

At that time, because of the power of this bodhisattva’s merit, those various coarse and evil objects of the six sense-fields belonging to the māras were immediately extinguished and ceased to appear.

At that time, as soon as the Bodhisattva thought of them, all manner of sublime objects immediately appeared in the sky. Relying on the superior causal conditions of his own merit, the Bodhisattva took that very space as a treasury; within his own palms, he brought forth all kinds of supreme treasures which manifested before him, causing all sentient beings to enjoy them. All these excellent and wondrous jewels in the Bodhisattva’s palms were accomplished through the power of his own merit.
"Good son! Even if one were to speak of the power of this bodhisattva’s merit for the duration of an eon, it could not be exhausted; this is called the power of merit of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
“Good son! What is the power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice according to reality? Good son!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of power of practice according to reality.
What are the ten? They are:

the power of practice of giving, the power of practice of ethical discipline, the power of practice of patience, the power of practice of diligence, the power of practice of meditative concentration, the power of practice of wisdom, the power of practice of skillful means, the power of practice of aspiration, the power of practice of strength, and the power of practice of knowledge. These are called the ten kinds of power of practice according to reality corresponding to the pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Good son! All other immeasurable powers of correct practice belonging to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are entirely subsumed within these ten kinds of power of correct practice."
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the practice of giving? Good son!”
A bodhisattva mahāsattva has not a single thing that they are stingy about and do not relinquish;
the sole exception being matters that would cause harm or distress to sentient beings.

Whatever state of mind a bodhisattva employs when practicing giving, that mind of generosity cannot be believed by any sentient beings other than the Tathāgatas and those bodhisattvas who have attained forbearance (kṣānti), let alone be understood by them.
This is called the bodhisattva’s power of the practice of giving.
"Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s power of the practice of ethical discipline?
"Good son! There are ten kinds of power in a bodhisattva’s practice of upholding the precepts. What are these ten?

These are: the practice of upholding the precepts of the śrāvakas; the practice of upholding the precepts of the pratyekabuddhas; the practice of upholding the precepts of the bodhisattvas; the practice of upholding the precepts for gathering all wholesome dharmas; the practice of upholding the precepts for seeking spiritual friends and never abandoning them; the practice of upholding the precepts for protecting and gathering the sublime Dharma; the practice of upholding the precepts for constantly benefiting others; the practice of upholding the precepts for dedicating toward great enlightenment; the practice of upholding the precepts for constant tranquility and entry into samādhi; and the practice of upholding the precepts for severing afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.

"Good son! Bodhisattvas are skillfully able to discern the subtle and secret observance of the precepts. For this reason, the precept-observance practiced by those bodhisattvas cannot be known by anyone who has not attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); this is called the power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of observing the precepts."
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s power of the practice of patience?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva has three kinds of patience:”
These are: the patience of enduring all sufferings, the patience of not retaliating against the evils inflicted by others, and the patience of knowing that all phenomena are unarisen.
Good son! As for the patience of enduring all sufferings, it is because one knows that one's own karma is what creates them.
Patience that does not retaliate for evil is so called because one has attained the mind of a single child toward all sentient beings;
patience regarding all phenomena is so called because one has attained the wisdom of non-arising regarding all phenomena.
These are called the three kinds of patience of a bodhisattva.
Good son! This is called the power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of patience.
“Good son! What is the power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s diligent practice? Good son!”

In whatever place and by whatever practice a bodhisattva acts, for the sake of accomplishing the power of cultivation of those wholesome dharmas, they give rise to this thought regarding each respective dharma:
"I shall accomplish these wholesome dharmas so that all sentient beings may likewise attain them."
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the practice of diligence.
"Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the practice of meditative concentration?"

"Good son! A bodhisattva does not perceive even a single dharma that is not quiescent; they perceive all dharmas as quiescent by their very nature. They extinguish all discursive thoughts and remain far removed from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). They are neither born nor extinguished, neither moving nor disturbed."

This bodhisattva does not perceive their own mind as concentrated or another’s mind as distracted; they do not perceive a samādhi that exists apart from their own body or apart from the bodies of others. Yet, they are able to cultivate all meritorious qualities with unremitting diligence. This is called the power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s cultivation of meditative concentration.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the practice of prajñā? Good son!”

A bodhisattva does not perceive a single dharma that is apart from the collection of causes and conditions; they do not perceive a single dharma apart from emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and liberation; nor do they perceive a single dharma apart from the liberation of space, yet they are able to cultivate the factors conducive to awakening with unceasing diligence, and they transform sentient beings without resting. This is called the power of the cultivation of prajñā by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of the practice of skillful means? Good son!”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not perceive a self, yet constantly guards his own secret conduct;
he does not perceive sentient beings, yet constantly teaches and transforms them without ceasing; he does not perceive afflictions, yet constantly guards the activities of his sensory faculties.
When the Bodhisattva perceives all forms, he does so as never departing from the form of the Buddha, and thus constantly seeks to behold all Tathāgatas.
Rūpa, when a bodhisattva hears all sounds, they do not depart from the sound of the Dharma and constantly seek to hear the Dharma without ever becoming weary or satisfied;
they do not perceive the world, yet they are always weary of and detached from all worlds;
they do not perceive nirvāṇa, yet for the sake of attaining nirvāṇa, they relinquish all internal and external things; and they do not perceive a Buddha or bodhi.
Yet, constantly aspiring to attain Buddhahood and bodhi, they perpetually make hundreds of thousands of millions of vows and practice them before their eyes;
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of skillful means in cultivation.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the practice of vows? Good son!”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not perceive a single dharma increasing, nor does he perceive a single dharma decreasing; yet he is able to rejoice in the roots of goodness performed by all sentient beings and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, he dedicates all his own roots of goodness together with those of all sentient beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, making this declaration:

"By means of these roots of goodness, I shall certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; by means of these roots of goodness, I shall accomplish such and such a Buddha-land; by means of these roots of goodness, I shall obtain such and such a great assembly."
"In this way, the great vows of the bodhisattva are accomplished and cannot be destroyed.
This bodhisattva cultivates and maintains pure precepts that are unbroken, without leakage, unstained, and undefiled, and are praised by the wise."

When this bodhisattva dwells within such pure observance of the precepts, all the great vows they have made are fully accomplished; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the practice of vows.
“Good son! What is the power of practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
If there should be sentient beings who manifest in the body of a Buddha and approach the bodhisattva with the intent to cause him to regress from the mind of bodhi, saying these words:”
"Where could such a Dharma of Bodhi exist? Thus they spoke various words of subversion. Yet that bodhisattva cannot be made to regress, nor can he be turned away by such subversion;

he remains mindful of Bodhi, mindful of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), mindful of the subduing of Māra, mindful of turning the wheel of Dharma, and mindful of great compassion. Toward those beings who subvert him and those with false teachings, he does not give rise to an evil mind; rather, through compassion, he returns to instruct those people, establishing them in wholesome dharmas. Furthermore, that bodhisattva does not lose the powers of pure faith, diligence, right mindfulness, samādhi, and prajñā.

By relying on that power of non-retrogression, this bodhisattva causes immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings to attain the Buddha’s bodhi and enter the Buddha’s bodhi; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of the practice of power.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the practice of wisdom? Good son!”

The bodhisattva knows all phenomena as they truly are: that there are no sentient beings, and that they are neither born, nor age, nor become ill, nor die; seeing only phenomena, free from the notions of "I" and "mine."
By relying on such power of knowledge regarding all dharmas, this bodhisattva causes immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings to enter into that wisdom.
Even all the Māras and non-Buddhists of the entire world cannot turn back that mind of *tathatā* (suchness) belonging to this bodhisattva, let alone divert it toward worldly dharmas.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s power of the practice of wisdom.
"Good son! These are called the ten kinds of powers of practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
“Good son! What are the ten knowledges of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? They are:

the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path; the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering, the knowledge of phenomena regarding the origin, cessation, and the path; the knowledge of the aggregates, the knowledge of the elements, the knowledge of the sense bases; the knowledge of the past and future; and the knowledge of the path and its fruits. These are called the ten knowledges of all bodhisattvas.”
“Good son! What is the knowledge of suffering?
It refers to the knowledge of suffering within suffering, the knowledge of the origin within suffering, the knowledge of cessation within suffering, and the knowledge of the path within suffering.”
Furthermore, son of good family!

Regarding the knowledge of suffering as empty, the knowledge of emptiness and signlessness, the knowledge of suffering as wishless, and the knowledge of suffering arising from causes and conditions—these constitute the knowledge of suffering within such suffering that arises solely as suffering.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Knowledge of the wisdom of non-existence, knowledge of the wisdom of craving, and knowledge of the wisdom of grasping—these are called the wisdom of suffering.
Son of good family!
What is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*)?

Whichever phenomena arise, that which knows their origination within that knowledge is the knowledge of origination; that origination is itself only suffering—this is called the knowledge of origination.
Furthermore, son of good family!
To know craving as the origin is called the knowledge of the origin.
Son of good family!
What is the knowledge of cessation?

It is the knowledge that the past has nowhere from which it comes, the knowledge that the future does not arise, and the knowledge that the present does not abide; this is called the knowledge of cessation.
Furthermore, good son!
To know that past dharmas do not perish, and to know that future and present dharmas do not perish—this is called the knowledge of extinction. Good son!
What is the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?

It refers to seeking the knowledge of the path and knowing the knowledge of the path within the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path; this is called the knowledge of the path.
"Good son! What is the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering, and the knowledge of phenomena regarding the origin, cessation, and the path?
A bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:"
"These—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—are solely phenomena (dharma).

Thus, one knows the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering, and the knowledge of phenomena regarding the origin, cessation, and path; this is called the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering, up to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path.
“Good son! What is the wisdom of the aggregates (skandha-jñāna)?

It refers to the wisdom that perceives the five aggregates as being like illusions and dreams, the wisdom of their unity, the wisdom of their accumulation, and the wisdom of their conjunction; this is called the wisdom of the aggregates.”

Furthermore, knowing that form is like a mass of foam, knowing that feeling is like a water bubble, knowing that perception is like a mirage, knowing that mental formations are like a plantain tree, and knowing that the aggregate of consciousness is like an illusion—this is called the knowledge of the aggregates.
“Good son! What is the knowledge of the elements (dhātu-jñāna)?
It refers to the earth element being the dharma-element, yet the dharma-element does not possess the characteristic of solidity;”
In this way, the water element is the dharma-realm, yet the dharma-realm does not have the characteristic of moisture;
the fire element is the dharma-realm, yet the dharma-realm does not have the characteristic of heat;
the wind element is the dharma-realm, yet the dharma-realm does not have the characteristic of motion. To know it thus is called knowing the elements.
Furthermore, good son! Knowledge of subtle wisdom is called the knowledge of nature (*dharmatājñāna*).
Knowledge of the root of all phenomena is called the knowledge of the realm (*dhātujñāna*).
Furthermore, good son!
The knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path are called the knowledge of the realms (*dhātu-jñāna*). Furthermore, good son!
There are two realms:
namely, the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).
Knowledge regarding these conditioned and unconditioned [realms] is called "knowledge of the realms" (*dharmajñāna*).
Furthermore, good son!

The eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element are the dharma-realm; yet the dharma-realm is not a characteristic of seeing, nor is it a characteristic of being seen, nor is it a characteristic of being known.

Likewise, the ear-element, the sound-element, and the ear-consciousness-element are the dharma-realm; yet the dharma-realm is not a characteristic of hearing, nor is it a characteristic of being heard, nor is it a characteristic of being known.

The nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element are the dharma-element; yet the dharma-element is not the characteristic of hearing, nor is it the characteristic of being heard, nor is it the characteristic of being known.

The tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element are the dharma-element; yet the dharma-element is not the characteristic of tasting, nor is it the characteristic of being tasted, nor is it the characteristic of being known.

The body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element are the dharma-element; yet the dharma-element is not the characteristic of aggregation or combination, nor is it the characteristic of touch, nor is it the characteristic of a mirage.

The mind-element, the dharma-element, and the mind-consciousness-element are the dharma-element; yet the dharma-element does not possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, or ceasing. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowledge of the elements.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s entry into knowledge?

It refers to entering into extensive knowledge, profound knowledge, universal knowledge, binding knowledge, piercing knowledge, fearful knowledge, deceptive knowledge, impermanence knowledge, and obstructive knowledge; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s entry into knowledge.”
Furthermore, good son!
The bodhisattva knows how to enter a village that is like an empty village—just as that empty village does not itself know that it is an empty village.
In this way, those sense-bases (āyatana) do not themselves know that they are empty, like an empty village.
If a bodhisattva knows them thus, it is called the wisdom of entry.
Furthermore, son of good family!

In this way, the bodhisattva understands the twelve bases (*āyatana*), namely: the eye-base, the form-base, the ear-base, the sound-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the taste-base, the body-base, the tangible-base, the mind-base, and the mental-object-base. These bases are without self and without what belongs to a self.
If a bodhisattva knows in this way, it is called entering into wisdom.
"Good son, what is the wisdom of the past and future?
It means that a bodhisattva knows the past and knows the future; this is called the knowledge of the past and future.

Furthermore, son of good family, knowing that the future has no agent and knowing that the past has ceased and perished—this is called the knowledge of the past and future of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Good son! What is the wisdom regarding the path and the fruit?
It is the wisdom within the six pāramitās; this is called the wisdom of the path.”
The wisdom within the ten stages and the stage of the Tathāgata is called the wisdom of the fruit.
That wisdom within both the path and the fruit is what is meant by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom within both the path and the fruit.
“Good son! These are called the ten knowledges of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

When this Dharma-gate of the Collection of Dharmas was being taught, seventy-six thousand bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having well accumulated their past karmas, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vikramamati addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpādita to say: "Good son,
you should now expound the collection of dharmas corresponding to the various pāramitās of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
Why is this? Son of good family!
This is the most supreme collection of the Dharma taught, namely, the teaching of the various pāramitās:
"What are the various pāramitās?
What is the collection of dharmas of the pāramitās?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Asaṃprasthita spoke to the Bodhisattva Vikrama-mati:
“Good son! The various pāramitās are:
the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, prajñā-pāramitā, upāya-pāramitā, praṇidhāna-pāramitā, bala-pāramitā, and jñāna-pāramitā.”
“Good son! These are called the various pāramitās.
What is the collection of the dharmas of the pāramitās?”
That which is called not perceiving giving is named the *dānapāramitā*, yet one constantly relinquishes all internal and external things;
that which is called not perceiving the observance of precepts is named the *śīlapāramitā*, yet one constantly cultivates and maintains all pure precepts, the *dhūta* virtues, and so forth;
that which is called not perceiving patience is named the *kṣāntipāramitā*, yet one constantly practices the conduct of patience and peace.
Not perceiving diligence is called the *vīrya-pāramitā*, yet one constantly cultivates all roots of goodness without rest;
not perceiving meditative concentration is called the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, yet one always honors the mind of tranquility;
not perceiving wisdom is called the *prajñā-pāramitā*, yet one constantly cultivates the methods of the wisdom derived from hearing.

Not perceiving skillful means is called the perfection of skillful means, yet one constantly manifests in commonality with all non-Buddhists for the sake of initiating the roots of goodness conceived by all sentient beings;
not perceiving vows is called the perfection of vows, yet one constantly seeks all roots of goodness and, together with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

not perceiving powers is called the perfection of power, yet one constantly seeks the body of Nārāyaṇa and the Vajra-mighty ones in order to teach and transform sentient beings and subdue their arrogance.
The wisdom that does not perceive [objects] is called the perfection of wisdom (jñānapāramitā), yet one constantly practices all arts, crafts, and the five sciences (pañcavidyāsthāna).
O son of good family!
This is called the collection of dharmas associated with the various pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, son of good family, the bodhisattva does not seek any karmic fruition, yet never abandons the mind of giving; at all times, he relinquishes all things."
Without making conceptual distinctions regarding the observance of precepts, one is able to sacrifice body and life without violating pure morality;
while remaining unshakable by any phenomena, one constantly stays far removed from thoughts of anger and malice;
and while seeking nothing among all dharmas, one constantly keeps all roots of goodness in mind.
Without discriminating regarding the tranquil mind, they constantly practice meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and samādhi;
they harbor no doubt regarding any phenomenon, yet they constantly seek the wisdom of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
they do not seek after any phenomena, yet their minds are ever mindful of the various dharmas of the roots of goodness.
While abiding in a mind of perpetual tranquility, they constantly practice all vows;
having severed all pride and arrogance, they constantly practice to achieve a firm adamantine body;
while skillfully knowing all sūtras and śāstras, they constantly seek out all venerable spiritual friends.
“Good son! This is called the collection of dharmas associated with the various pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Furthermore, good son!”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s mind always delights in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), yet he manifests in accordance with beings who are stingy and envious;
his mind always delights in the cultivation and maintenance of pure precepts, yet he manifests in accordance with beings who violate the precepts;
his mind always delights in the practice of patience (*kṣānti*), yet he manifests in accordance with beings who are unable to endure and are subject to perversions.
Their minds always delight in the practice of diligence, yet they manifest in accordance with sentient beings who are indolent, lazy, and inverted;
their minds always delight in meditative concentration and samādhi, yet they manifest in accordance with sentient beings who are distracted by many affairs and inverted;
their minds always delight in the wondrous wisdom of prajñā, yet they manifest in accordance with sentient beings who lack faith in wholesome states and are foolish and mute.
Their minds always delight in skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), yet they manifest as not seeking any of their own undertakings;

their minds always delight in the roots of goodness of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna-kuśalamūla*), yet they manifest conduct that accords with world-weariness and detachment for the sake of sentient beings;
their minds always delight in possessing power, yet they manifest in accordance with those sentient beings who are powerless.
Their minds always delight in supreme wisdom, yet they manifest in accordance with those sentient beings who lack it.
Good son! This is called the collection of dharmas associated with the pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, noble son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) attains a hand of wish-fulfilling jewels and takes empty space as his treasury;

one who practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) transcends all evil realms and attains mastery over birth and death, as well as a supple mind and a mind of sovereign compliance."

Those who practice the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) attain the adornment of the Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpa-kāya), achieving the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, such that those who see them never tire of doing so;
those who practice the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) attain the four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya) and the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid);
and those who practice the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) attain mastery over all sounds and mastery over all actions performed.
One who practices the perfection of wisdom attains non-obstruction regarding all phenomena, because all phenomena are equal to bodhi;
one who practices the perfection of skillful means attains spontaneity in the actions performed, because they attain spontaneity in the actions of body, speech, and mind;
one who practices the perfection of aspiration attains mastery over past lives throughout all births, as well as conduct that accords with reality and deeds that accord with what is to be done.
One who practices the perfection of power cannot be disturbed by any afflictions, any demons, or any non-Buddhists, because they thereby attain the most exalted body among all in the world;
one who practices the perfection of wisdom is said to be able to transcend the aggregates (*skandha*), death, afflictions, and the celestial Māras.
"Good son! This is called the collection of dharmas associated with the various pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Furthermore, good son!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva praises generosity, yet does not regard that generosity as pure;
he praises ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, vows, powers, and the praise of knowledge, yet does not regard those as pure.

Why is this? Although one may cultivate all such dharmas, because they can be relinquished, all these dharmas exist only through the conceptualizing mind; therefore, one must completely relinquish both the conceptualizing mind and the dharmas produced by that conceptualizing mind.

Therefore, the bodhisattva does not dwell together with the mind of discrimination or the mind that discriminates all phenomena; he does not give rise to such thoughts for the sake of purity. Rather, the bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: knowing the realm that is non-discriminative and free from conceptual proliferation, he realizes the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Vegeṭamati said: "Good son,
regarding what dharma is the term 'bodhi' spoken?"
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said: "Good son,
that which is called 'bodhi' refers to the dharma that is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation."
“Good son! To perceive a self is called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); this is not bodhi.
To be far removed from the view of a self and to be without conceptual proliferation is called bodhi.”
"Good son! Attachment to 'mine' is called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); this is not bodhi.
To be free from 'mine' and devoid of conceptual proliferation is called bodhi."
To conform to aging, sickness, and death is called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); this is not bodhi.
To not conform to aging, sickness, and death—being tranquil and free from conceptual proliferation—is called bodhi.
Avarice, envy, breaking the precepts, malice, indolence, distraction, and delusion—these, along with the conceptual proliferation of ignorance, are not bodhi.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—the dharma that is free from conceptual proliferation—is called bodhi.
Wrong views, evil conceptualizations, and evil vows are called frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*); these are not bodhi.
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the dharma that is free from frivolous proliferation—is called bodhi.
Furthermore, good son!
One may say that all dharmas are bodhi, and one may also say that all dharmas are not bodhi. He asked:
"For what reason are all dharmas called bodhi,
and why are all dharmas not bodhi? He replied:
"To be attached to all phenomena as 'I' and 'mine' is not bodhi;
to awaken to the equality of all phenomena and to know the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena is called bodhi."
Furthermore, son of good family!
That which is called "bodhi" is termed "quiescence";
quiescence is termed the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena.
He asked: "Good son! Regarding what you call 'true thusness' (tathatā), in reference to what phenomena is 'true thusness' spoken?"
He replied: "Good son! That which is called *tathatā* (suchness)—*tathatā* is termed emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and that emptiness is neither born nor extinguished."
He asked: "If it is thus, all phenomena are empty.
Therefore, all phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished."
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said: "So it is, so it is.
O son of good family!"
"As you have said, all dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished.
He asked: "If this is so, for what reason does the Tathāgata say that conditioned dharmas are all subject to production and extinction?"
The Buddha said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise and perish;
what does this statement mean? The Bodhisattva Anutpāda replied, “Noble son!

Because ignorant ordinary beings are attached to the phenomena of arising and ceasing, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, out of great compassion, protect them from fear by conforming to worldly convention and thus declaring that all phenomena arise and cease; yet, in reality, all phenomena neither arise nor cease.
Therefore, good son!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should know all buddhas, should know the dharmas of all buddhas, should know all sentient beings, should know all dharmas, should know his own self, and should know the dharmas of the body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpāda, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Buddha and the appearance of the Buddha in the world, The true essence of all Buddhas’ dharmas—
A bodhisattva, in accordance with those dharmas, Knows them through non-negligence.”
The various aggregates of wholesome, untainted qualities—of which the Buddha, the World-Knower, is supreme—are accomplished in dependence upon the minds of sentient beings.
He is the one who knows all phenomena; he is the one who awakens to all phenomena.
This person reaches all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
awakening has no giver, nor is there anyone who takes it.
Truly knowing the dharmas of one's own self is what is called "the awakened one who awakens."
If one can know that one’s own body Is merely a sign and lacks reality, This one can know as the Buddha does, And know the dharmas of awakening.
All sentient beings are but signs; They are spoken of through false conceptualization.
The Bodhisattva knows things as they truly are, as having characteristics like dreams and illusions.
Those who falsely perceive or falsely realize cannot know this practice;
only one who has tamed the horses of the sense faculties can rely upon meditative concentration to know it.
This person has neither enemy nor friend, Nor what is to be done or not to be done;
Furthermore, there is no dharma of grasping or abandoning— This is called the true accumulation of Dharma.
Because one can correctly know all phenomena, one speaks of the meaning of the Dharma-aggregate;
because one does not correctly know all phenomena, one speaks of unwholesome dharmas.
Regarding the dharma of craving and the departure from craving, there is the vision of purity and equality.
Seeing that desire and delusion are likewise thus— this is called the true accumulation of the Dharma.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, one gives rise to great compassion,
yet perceives no sentient beings, provided one is not separated from emptiness.
If one knows the Dharma in this way— the state of equality and stainlessness—
attaining the wondrous island of the awakened state, that wise one achieves perfect enlightenment.
Like a worldly illusionist who resolves to deliver illusory beings, [so does the Bodhisattva].
That illusion does not cling to illusion, for it has never existed.
Knowing the three realms are like an illusion, one generates the great bodhicitta;
in order to deliver all sentient beings, one truly knows those very beings.
One's own person is like space;
the self-nature of sentient beings is empty. Seeing the Dharma in all places, one attains the patient acceptance that dwells on the supreme continent.
One does not proceed toward any phenomena, nor does one return from any phenomena.
By neither proceeding nor returning, one dwells on the continent of pure conduct.
If one abides thus in reality, with a mind of the equal dharma-realm, the Buddhas will immediately bestow upon one the prediction: "This one shall surely attain great enlightenment."
One's own self and the Buddha are likewise; having received the Buddha’s prediction and seen the equality of that Dharma, one is immediately predicted by all Buddhas.
Attaining the state of non-obstruction, one realizes cessation while wandering in the world.
In all places there is no fault, for one takes great compassion as one's body.
If a bodhisattva possesses wisdom and desires to gather such a Dharma,
and practices this Dharma-conduct, they will certainly attain this gathering of the Dharma.

When the Bodhisattva Asaṃprasthita spoke these verses, sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and eight thousand devaputras became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anutpāda addressed the Bodhisattva Vikramamati, saying:
"Good son, a bodhisattva should practice the collection of the Dharma of the true truths."
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas take the wisdom of the ultimate truth as their accumulation of the Dharma. Good son!
"What is the ultimate truth?
Son of good family!

When a bodhisattva resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and even at the cost of sacrificing their own body and life does not abandon that resolve nor abandon all sentient beings—this is called the ultimate truth of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

"Good son! If a bodhisattva has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet at times abandons the mind [of awakening] and abandons sentient beings, such a bodhisattva is to be censured; this person is said to be a supreme liar."
He asked: "How is it that a bodhisattva, having resolved their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, does not again abandon that mind, nor abandon all sentient beings?"
He replied: "If a bodhisattva knows the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path, that bodhisattva no longer abandons that mind."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas know the ultimate truth; therefore, their bodhicitta does not regress. He asked:
"What is suffering? How does one know suffering? He replied:
“Craving for the five aggregates and being oppressed by what is not desired—this is called suffering.

When a bodhisattva knows that suffering is empty, devoid of a life-principle, without self or what belongs to a self, and arises solely through the conjunction of causes and conditions, this is called knowing suffering.”
When a bodhisattva perceives that suffering is merely the accumulation [of causes], being false, insubstantial, and devoid of a life-principle, this is called knowing the accumulation (*samudaya*).

When a bodhisattva knows that suffering does not come from the past limit, does not go to the future limit, and does not abide in the present limit—being without beginning and without end, its essence primordially quiescent, its essence empty, and its essence tranquil—knowing it thus is called knowing cessation (*nirodha*).
Question: "Regarding that which is called 'cessation' (nirodha), what dharma is being described? Answer:
"Good son! That which is called 'extinction' cannot be spoken of. He asked:
“Good son! If cessation cannot be spoken of, for what reason do you speak of ‘cessation’? He replied:

“Good son! What is called ‘extinction’ refers to adventitious afflictions, various obstacles, unrealities, and dharmas of false discrimination. When a bodhisattva does not discriminate those unreal dharmas, at that time it can be said that extinction has been extinguished.”
Furthermore, illusory dharmas are fundamentally such that there is nothing to be extinguished; therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent.
He asked: “Good son!
The Tathāgata says that a bodhisattva does not realize extinction; if a bodhisattva were to realize extinction, that bodhisattva would fall into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
For what reason does the Tathāgata speak thus?
He replied: "Good son, what is called 'realization' (sākṣātkriyā) is termed 'direct perception' (pratyakṣa)."
However, the dharma of cessation cannot be perceived; for this reason, the Tathāgata says that the dharma of cessation is invisible.
If a dharma is invisible, that dharma also cannot be realized.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that a bodhisattva does not perceive extinction and does not realize extinction.
Based on this meaning, the Tathāgata says that a bodhisattva does not realize extinction.
Because the śrāvakas grasp at the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), they realize cessation (nirodha).
To know by what mindfulness, what contemplation, and what practice one thus knows, thus sees, and thus attains certainty—this is called knowing the path.
"Furthermore, good son! That which is called 'suffering' is named 'self. That self has characteristics;
if one thus collects [these characteristics], it is called 'knowing the collection.'"
When a bodhisattva perceives that accumulation, they do not perceive a single dharma capable of accumulating; knowing thus is called knowing cessation.
If one can contemplate in this way and seek in this way, it is called knowing the path.
"Furthermore, good son! In whatever phenomena the mind clings to with attachment, that is called suffering. Why is this?
"Good son! The Tathāgata has always said:
'Whatever the mind clings to is called suffering; whatever place the mind clings to is unreal.'"
Therefore, when attachment arises from the mind, it is called "origination";
when suffering does not attach to the mind, it is called "cessation.
By means of what wisdom one does not become attached to that wisdom, it is called "knowing the path."
“Good son! I shall now speak according to my wisdom of the ultimate truth; even if all bodhisattvas were to speak for one kalpa or for immeasurable kalpas, they could not exhaust it.”

When this wisdom of the knowledge of the true reality was taught, sixty thousand bodhisattvas, through the cultivation of wisdom based on the true reality, attained the stage of non-retrogression; and in the sky, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, having become free from dust and removed from defilement regarding all phenomena, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
The Sūtra of the Collection of the Buddha’s Teachings, Scroll Three;
The Sūtra of the Collection of the Buddha’s Teachings, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vigorous Wisdom addressed the Bodhisattva Non-Arising, saying: "Good son!
What is the wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s application of mindfulness to the mind?"
"What is mindfulness? And what is the application of mindfulness to the mind?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpāda spoke to the Bodhisattva Vikrama-mati, saying:

“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the knowledge of non-arising regarding all phenomena, this constitutes the knowledge of the application of mindfulness of the mind; among all forms of knowledge, the knowledge of non-arising is the most supreme.”

By means of that knowledge of non-arising, all bodhisattvas are named for their activity of the knowledge of non-arising; they are undisturbed in all places, straightforward in all places, and immovable in all places. Like the waters of the great ocean, they are immeasurable, such that no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas are able to know them.
By means of what mental application (*manasikāra*) is one able to hear, retain, and uphold all that is taught by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, without losing it?
This is the mental application of the Bodhisattva which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, know as being present before them; this is the mental application of such a Bodhisattva.
"That Bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness has ten bases.
What are the ten? They are:

the application of mindfulness to the body, the application of mindfulness to feelings, the application of mindfulness to the mind, the application of mindfulness to phenomena; the application of mindfulness to the Buddha, the application of mindfulness to the Dharma, the application of mindfulness to the Sangha, the application of mindfulness to ethical discipline, the application of mindfulness to relinquishment, and the application of mindfulness to the devas. These are called the ten applications of mindfulness."
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to the body?
The bodhisattva settles the mind in this way:”

"This body does not come from a prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) nor does it go to a subsequent limit (*aparākoṭi*); it does not abide in a prior limit or a future limit. It arises solely from the mind of false discrimination (*abhūtaparikalpa-citta*). There is no agent (*kāraka*), no life-principle (*jīva*), and no prior, middle, or subsequent limits. It does not abide and has no root; there is no teacher and no grasper, yet it is merely described through adventitious (*āgantuka*) words as having a physical form, substance, or sense-bases."

"If one contemplates the body in this way, this body is not solid; it is born from the impurity of the union of the father's semen and the mother's blood, having a foul and putrid nature as its substance. Greed, hatred, and delusion act as bandits to cause turmoil, destruction, and instability; and the countless hundreds of thousands of millions of diseases constitute its dwelling place."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva dwells in mindfulness regarding the body in this way:

'This body is a collection of various parts from head to foot, namely: the feet, toes, heels, ankles, calves, shins, thighs, knees, hip bones, waist and spine, chest and ribs, abdomen and sides, arms, hands, fingers, elbows, wrists, shoulders, upper arms, cheeks, jaws, neck, nape, skull, eyes, and ears. Thus, these things are accumulated to form the body; karma and existence act as its creator, while hundreds of thousands of kinds of false discriminations—consisting of various afflictions and secondary afflictions—serve as its dwelling place.'"

This body contains many kinds of impurities, namely: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, blood, flesh, skin, bones, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, the two internal organs (the raw and the cooked), spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, fat, grease, brain and membranes, yellow and white phlegm, nasal mucus, saliva, tears, and excrement and urine—all of which are foul, filthy, and loathsome.
"This collection consists of such immeasurable impure things; among these, what is the body?
Thus the Bodhisattva contemplates the body and reflects:
"This body is without reality, just like empty space."
This is called the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness like space.
By thus settling the mind, one perceives all phenomena as being like space.

When a bodhisattva knows the body in this way, there is within all phenomena neither a moving mind nor a dwelling mind; because this bodhisattva is neither moving nor dwelling, it is called abiding in the application of mindfulness.
Abiding thus in mindfulness, one can know in this way: as is the body of Bodhi, so it is with this; herein, one cannot give rise to a mind of revulsion. Why is that?
All these are wrong mindfulness and not right mindfulness; regarding what phenomena does one give rise to a mind of revulsion?
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s application of mindfulness to the body.
"Furthermore, noble son!
What is the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to sensation? Noble son!"
The Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:
"That which is called 'receiving' is termed 'awakening.
That awakening is of three kinds:"
That is to say: the inverted, the non-inverted, and that which is free from both.
Furthermore, "inverted experience" refers to the distracted mind and the inverted mind of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Those ordinary worldlings take impermanent feelings to be permanent, painful feelings to be pleasant, selfless feelings to be a self, and impure feelings to be pure; this is called inverted feeling.

Non-perverted feeling means feeling impermanence as impermanent, feeling suffering as suffering, feeling non-self as non-self, and feeling impurity as impure; this is the feeling of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and it is called non-perverted feeling.
One who is detached from those two types of sensation experiences impermanence as neither permanent nor impermanent;
experiences suffering as neither suffering nor non-suffering;
and experiences non-self as neither self nor non-self.
Feeling that which is impure, neither pure nor impure—this is called the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to feeling.
Thus the bodhisattva experiences feeling, yet does not perceive a feeler, does not perceive one who is capable of feeling, and does not perceive that which is felt.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"The Tathāgata has always taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are feeling (*vedanā*).
If all phenomena are taken as feeling, then among these, which phenomenon is itself the feeler?"

That which is not an experiencer cannot be considered an experiencer, because that which is experienced is not itself the experiencer; furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) cannot experience conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), for apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena have no experiencer.

"In this way, the Bodhisattva does not perceive a subject that receives within what is received, nor does he perceive one who receives; yet he is able to teach others regarding that which is received.
This Bodhisattva perceives that which can be received as being just like Bodhi itself. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s application of mindfulness to sensation (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna)."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
What is the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to the mind?
Son of good family!"
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"That which is felt is merely mind; yet the mind does not abide, it cannot be grasped, and it is formless.
What dharma is ungraspable and formless?"
"What is that dharma which he experiences like?
It is neither mind nor known by the mind; it is neither mind nor seen by the mind.
He then further reflects:
"Regarding which mind arises from causes and conditions?
He perceives that all those minds exist through the power of others.
This bodhisattva does not see awakening as existing apart from the mind; he knows that this very dharma of the mind is itself awakening. At that time, the bodhisattva attains mastery over the mind.
Because one has attained mastery over the mind, one attains mastery within the Mahāyāna.
At that time, one attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
At that time, this bodhisattva dwells within the Great Vehicle and does not rely on the power of others; this is called the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to the mind.
"Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna)?"

"Good son! A bodhisattva gives rise to right mindfulness toward whatever phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome phenomena, phenomena that are censurable or uncensurable, phenomena with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane phenomena, the phenomena of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, or the phenomena of ordinary persons or non-ordinary persons."

This bodhisattva gives rise to right mindfulness regarding each and every phenomenon; they are skillfully able to know them, their wholesome karma is supple, and they are well able to practice cultivation. They have excellently cultivated the ultimate, excellently cultivated self-mastery, and excellently cultivated sovereignty, knowing that the dharma of equality is neither produced nor extinguished.
This bodhisattva does not perceive a single dharma apart from non-arising and non-ceasing; he does not perceive a single dharma apart from emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"All dharmas possess no life-principle, because their intrinsic nature is quiescent."
All phenomena are without self, because their intrinsic nature is non-dual;
all phenomena are without obstruction, because their intrinsic nature is like space;
all phenomena are without discrimination, because they are far removed from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
All phenomena are quiescent, because they are devoid of the nature of affliction;
all phenomena are beyond speech, because their intrinsic nature is ineffable;
all phenomena are inexhaustible, because their unconditioned nature is pure.
All phenomena are incalculable, for they transcend all numerical measures;
all phenomena are upright, for they transcend all conceptual proliferation;
all phenomena are rootless, for they lack seeds.
All phenomena are without fault, because their fundamental nature is inherently pure;
all phenomena do not come, because they are formless;
all phenomena do not go, because they have no abiding place.
All phenomena are luminous because their intrinsic nature is empty;
all phenomena are empty because they arise from causes and conditions;
all phenomena are without contention because they are free from conceptual discrimination.
All phenomena depend on the power of one's own wisdom, for they are awakened to according to what is contemplated;
all phenomena are bodhi, for they are the domain of wisdom;
all phenomena are merely names, for they lack any substantial reality.
All phenomena are free from all views, because they cannot be seen;
all phenomena are neither bound nor liberated, because they lack form and characteristics;
all phenomena do not depart, because their essence is suchness.
All phenomena constitute a single realm, because they do not differ from the true dharma-realm;
all phenomena are non-differentiated, because the ultimate truth is equal.

"Thus, when a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena and practices all phenomena, they do not perceive distinctions among sentient beings, do not perceive distinctions among phenomena, do not perceive distinctions among vehicles, do not perceive distinctions among buddha-fields, do not perceive distinctions among dharmas, and do not perceive distinctions among the sublime Dharma. They see neither bondage nor liberation; they see neither the world nor nirvana. They neither abandon nor grasp; they neither proceed nor abide; they neither accept nor reject, yet they dwell in tranquility and dwell in immovability."

When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, perceive such a Bodhisattva of tranquil liberation within those various Buddha-lands, they immediately bestow upon that Bodhisattva the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
"Furthermore, noble son!
What is the bodhisattva’s recollection of the Buddha? Noble son!"
The Bodhisattva practices the recollection of the Buddha and the recollection of all sentient beings, thinking:
"I shall bring all sentient beings to the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Abiding thus in these foundations of mindfulness, this bodhisattva reflects: 'The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities; I shall certainly accomplish those Buddha-dharmas.'"

Furthermore, one can recollect that those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess such a mindfulness that is inconceivable, vast, pure, and stainlessly luminous; it is free from all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), and has severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of affliction. With wisdom as its primary faculty and wisdom as its sovereign, it reaches the sovereign state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of all Buddhas—the sovereign dharma realized by all. It is far removed from all cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and afflictions; it cannot be fathomed by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Taking non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*) as its essence, it takes spontaneous non-obstruction as its non-action, non-obstruction, and non-abiding, illuminating the minds of all sentient beings like space, without discrimination. Such is the mindfulness of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

When a bodhisattva recollects the jewels of mindfulness of those Buddhas, the wealth and treasures of the Buddha-Tathāgatas, and the storehouses of the Buddha-Tathāgatas—recollecting such dharmas as these is called "recollection of the Buddha."
“Good son! The Buddhas do not think, nor is it that they do not think; in all places, they are spontaneously without discrimination.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, possess such a thought; when a Bodhisattva contemplates that thought, it is therefore called ‘recollection of the Buddha.’”
The Buddhas are without the characteristic of differentiation regarding all sentient beings and all phenomena; to be mindful of that mindfulness is therefore called "mindfulness of the Buddha.

The Buddhas are neither conceptualizing nor non-conceptualizing, neither grasping nor non-grasping, neither departing nor non-departing, and neither arising nor ceasing; to be mindful in such a manner is therefore called "mindfulness of the Buddha."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are adorned with great merit and wisdom; they take great loving-kindness and great compassion as their practice;
and having made the deliverance of the multitudes of sentient beings their salvation, they act as great physicians to extract the thorns of affliction."
Giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, they always abide in tranquility; they do not dwell in the realm of samādhi, yet they transcend both the mundane world and nirvāṇa.

Having reached the further shore beyond all afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions, they become the sustenance for the great multitude of beings and the refuge of the great multitude of beings; they extinguish all physical births and attain the Dharma-body.
The body dwells within the realm of the Dharma; the mind is without obstruction in all places;
at all times, it benefits all sentient beings without error in body or speech; its predictions are never false;
its bodily, verbal, and mental actions are beyond reproach in all matters; and it remains far removed from greed, hatred, delusion, and the like.
He cuts through all afflictions, subdues all demons and externalists, and does not engage in dispute with any in the world.
He is deeper than the great ocean of all worlds, more weighty than all the precious Mount Sumerus,
more immovable and unshakable than the great earth, more supple than water, and more radiant than fire.
It is unattached to wind, stainless as space, swifter than thought, and surpasses the wish-fulfilling jewel by its willpower;
it is the equality of all-knowledge, non-dual, free from all points of attachment toward all sentient beings,
and exerts tireless diligence to deliver all sentient beings.

With immeasurable physical forms, immeasurable voices, immeasurable merits, and inconceivable realms, they have attained the ultimately inconceivable Dharma-body, which transcends the spheres of mind, intellect, and consciousness. By means of the mind of clear conduct, they sever the unwholesome dharmas of the three evil destinies. With supreme great compassion, they share all their merits with all sentient beings; toward all beings they are like parents, regarding enemies and kin with equality, and whether incensed with perfume or otherwise, they give rise to neither sorrow nor joy toward sentient beings.
Abiding in all places, they possess immeasurable great radiance; having reached the ultimate further shore,
these beings of great mind and the noble wealth of the Great Dharma accomplish the practice of great illumination, become great Dharma masters capable of expounding the Great Dharma,
and become great men who ultimately achieve the marks of a great man— thus it is for all.
Invincible by the world, he is the light that illuminates all worlds;
he practices great skillful means within the sphere of great goodness, possessing ultimate great liberation and an ultimate great body.
Taking the great multitude of beings as his retinue, he is surrounded by these great-bodied beings without obstruction; they see him, hear him, and make offerings to him.

Practicing and drawing near [to the Dharma], they distance themselves from self-centered pleasure and attachment; they delight in extinguishing the suffering of others and take joy in the True Dharma.

They regard the Dharma as their wealth, the Dharma as their food, the Dharma as their clothing and sustenance, the Dharma as their foundation, and the Dharma as their sovereignty; they become great Kings of Dharma and bestow the gift of the Dharma.
Lord, you who always delight in the Dharma of relinquishment, who are ever heedful, and who always rejoice in tranquility;
you who serve as a bridge for all sentient beings— like a great royal road that is level and free of obstructions,
like the light of the Great Sun that destroys all darkness, and like the great Brahma King’s wisdom-vajra— you are this pure arrow of the Great Dharma.
One never tires of beholding the form-body (rūpakāya).
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess such immeasurable merits as these.

When a bodhisattva has reflected upon those merits, they practice for the sake of accomplishing those merits and maintain right mindfulness for the sake of accomplishing those merits; therefore, this is called "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānusmṛti).
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s station of mindfulness of the Buddha. "Good son!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s station of mindfulness of the Dharma?"
“Good son! A bodhisattva reflects thus:

‘The immeasurable merits of all Buddhas are born from the Dharma, transformed by the Dharma, attained through the Dharma, increased by the Dharma, exist because of the Dharma, have the Dharma as their sphere, rely upon the Dharma, and are accomplished through the Dharma.’”
Again, he reflects thus:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess the adornments of the marks and signs; these too are born from the Dharma, transformed by the Dharma, attained through the Dharma, and perfected through the Dharma."

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities; these also arise from the Dharma, are transformed by the Dharma, are attained through the Dharma, and are perfected through the Dharma.

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, possess eighteen unique qualities; those qualities likewise arise from the Dharma, are transformed by the Dharma, are obtained through the Dharma, and are perfected through the Dharma.
All worldly and supramundane happiness—all such matters of joy—arise from the Dharma, are transformed by the Dharma, are obtained through the Dharma, and are accomplished by means of the Dharma.

Therefore, as I seek the Bodhi of all Buddhas, I should revere the Dharma; I should rely on the realm of the Dharma, practice according to the Dharma, reach the ultimate through the Dharma, and remain steadfast in the Dharma.
This is called the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Furthermore, son of good family,
the bodhisattva reflects in this way:
“The Dharma dwells equally within all sentient beings; the Dharma does not give rise to discrimination by perceiving some beings as superior and others as inferior.
I, too, am like the Dharma: my mind is without discrimination, equal and without distinction.”
The Dharma does not initiate activity through seeing forms, for the Dharma is without partiality;
I, too, am like the Dharma, my mind being equanimous.
The Dharma does not initiate activity through seeing time, for the Dharma has no coming or going, and one understands the inner mind by itself.
I, too, am in accordance with the Dharma, my mind being impartial.
The Dharma does not perform its activity toward superior beings while failing to do so toward inferior beings, for the Dharma is neither high nor low;
I, too, am in accordance with the Dharma, my mind being impartial, giving rise to no discrimination.
The Dharma does not bring benefit to pure sentient beings while failing to bring benefit to impure sentient beings, because the Dharma is free from the distinctions of high and low;
I, too, am likewise, for my mind is impartial and gives rise to no discrimination.

The Dharma does not bring benefit to the noble ones nor fail to bring benefit to those who are not noble, because it is free from the mentalities that distinguish between fields of merit and non-fields of merit;
I am likewise thus, my mind being equanimous and giving rise to no discrimination.

The Dharma does not provide benefit by day and fail to provide benefit by night, nor does it fail to provide benefit by day and provide benefit by night; for the Dharma constantly provides benefit without ceasing.
I am likewise: my mind is equanimous, and I do not give rise to discrimination.
The Dharma does not exceed the proper timing for transforming sentient beings;
I am likewise so, my mind being equanimous and free from discrimination.
The Dharma does not fail to bring benefit to those who harbor anger, nor does it seek to bring benefit only to those who are not angry, because it is unattached in all circumstances.
I am also like this: my mind is equanimous and does not give rise to discrimination.
Dharmas neither increase nor decrease; dharmas are immeasurable and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), like space, neither exhausting nor increasing.
I am also like this: my mind is equanimous and does not give rise to discrimination.
Sentient beings do not protect the Dharma, nor does the Dharma protect sentient beings;
I am likewise, for my mind is equanimous and gives rise to no discrimination.
The Dharma serves as a refuge for the entire world.
I am also like this: my mind is equanimous and does not give rise to discrimination.
Since phenomena have no place where a mind of anger or malice can arise—because they possess the characteristic of non-malice—I am also like this:
my mind is equanimous and does not give rise to discrimination.
The Dharma does not abide in the latent tendencies of affliction, because the Dharma is far removed from those latent afflictions;
I am likewise, my mind being equanimous and free from the arising of discrimination.
The Dharma does not fear the world nor seek nirvana, for the Dharma is eternally free from discrimination;
I am likewise, my mind being equanimous and giving rise to no discrimination.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva maintains right mindfulness regarding the Dharma; therefore, it is called 'mindfulness of the Dharma.
Good son! This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s station of mindfulness of the Dharma."
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the Saṅgha? Good son!”

The Bodhisattva reflects thus: "The Saṅgha is called those who speak according to the Dharma; they are called those who practice the Dharma; they are called those who contemplate the Dharma; they are called those who are fields of merit through the Dharma; they are called those who uphold the Dharma; they are called those who rely upon the Dharma; they are called those who make offerings to the Dharma; they are called those whose actions accord with the Dharma; they are called those whose sphere accords with the Dharma; they are called those who achieve accomplishment through the practice of the Dharma; they are called those of the true Dharma; they are called those of the straightforward Dharma; they are called those of the truly pure Dharma; they are called saviors of sentient beings; they are called those of great compassion; they are called those whose sphere is ever-quiescent; they are called those who always take refuge in the Dharma; and they are called those who always purify their own conduct through the Dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva reflects in this way: 'The Tathāgata has said that the Saṃgha is not of only one kind;

namely, the Saṃgha of conventional truth, the Saṃgha of ultimate truth, the Saṃgha of shame and remorse, the Saṃgha without shame or remorse, the Saṃgha of noble ones, the Saṃgha of the disciplined, and the Saṃgha of those who do not regress.'"

"Furthermore, noble son! A bodhisattva practices by gathering the Saṃgha of conventional truth; practices by making offerings to the Saṃgha of ultimate truth; practices by causing the Saṃgha of shame and remorse to attain liberation; practices by reproving the Saṃgha lacking in shame and remorse; practices by making offerings to, honoring, and attending upon the Saṃgha of noble ones; practices toward the Saṃgha of those who are disciplined just as one would toward a Buddha; and practices by preaching the Dharma to the Saṃgha of those who are non-retrogressive."
"Furthermore, good son! A bodhisattva reflects in this way:
'The Sangha is called that which does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, for they are the sons of the Buddha;'"
The Sangha can bestow the retribution of desired fruits, for it is a field of merit;
the Sangha is free from afflictions, for it is fearless;
the Sangha has relinquished all attachments, for it has attained liberation.
The Sangha is called "tranquil" because it has tamed the mind;
the Sangha is called "unmixed" because it is free from afflictions;
the Sangha is "distant from unwholesome dharmas" because it possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame.
The Sangha is called those who speak in accordance with truth, because they are capable of being transformed;
the Sangha is called those who know their own selves, because they are free from arrogance;
the Sangha is called those who are tranquil, because they are free from prideful thoughts.
The Saṃgha is called "contentment," because it is free from perverted thoughts;
the Saṃgha is called "the severance of discrimination," because it is free from affliction;
the Saṃgha is called "reaching the wondrous island," because it has attained the state of fearlessness.
The Sangha is called "seeing reality" because they are free from negligence;
the Sangha is called "the further shore" because they are able to reach that wondrous island on the further shore;
the Sangha is called "not evil" because they practice the conduct of an araṇya-dweller.
The Sangha is called "the Swift," because they ultimately proceed to the site of enlightenment;
the Sangha is called "those who know the Three Trainings," because they practice the conduct of disciples;
the Sangha is called "those who practice within the sphere of the Four Mindfulnesses," because they excel all other practitioners of mindfulness.
The Saṃgha is called the realm where one practices the four right efforts, because of the practice of diligence;
the Saṃgha is called the realm where one practices the four bases of psychic power, because of being free from weariness;
the Saṃgha is called the realm where one practices the five faculties, because of being indestructible.
The Sangha is called the cultivation of the sphere of the five powers, because they subdue the thorns of all afflictions;
the Sangha is called the cultivation of the practice of the seven factors of enlightenment, because they are without obstruction;
the Sangha is called the cultivation of the sphere of the eightfold noble path, because of right view.
The Sangha is called the realm of practicing the ultimate truth, because it has attained a place of refuge;
the Sangha is called the realm of practicing all meditative concentrations, because its mind is stabilized;
the Sangha is called the realm of practicing the convergence of causes and conditions, because it is able to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The Sangha is called great compassion, because it is the state of non-retrogression;
the Sangha is called the accumulation of all merits, because in a single lifetime one attains Great Enlightenment.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Having thus recollected the Saṃgha, the bodhisattva reflects:
'The Saṃgha possesses such immeasurable merits; I desire to attain them all, and I shall also cause all sentient beings to ultimately achieve them.'"
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s recollection of the Saṃgha. Good son!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the precepts?
Son of good family!
The bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"Whatever mundane or supramundane, most excellent and wondrous fruits of retribution there may be, all such fruits of retribution are obtained through the observance of the precepts. Why is this?"
"By relying on the fundamental power of pure precepts as the cause. "Good son!
It is like all grasses, trees, and forests, which rely upon the earth as their foundation."

In this way, all mundane and supramundane sublime fruits depend upon the precepts as their foundation. When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in the observance of the precepts, they are able to serve as a great field of merit for all devas and humans, and furthermore, they are able to fulfill the meritorious virtues of those who practice giving.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva abides in the precepts, he gives rise to a heart of joy;
because his heart is joyful, he does not give rise to distress or affliction.
Because one is free from anxiety and distress, the mind attains exultation;
because one attains exultation, one attains physical and mental composure;
because one attains physical and mental composure, the mind attains happiness.
Because the mind attains joy, one attains samādhi;
because one attains samādhi, one attains knowledge of things as they truly are;
and because of this knowledge of things as they truly are, the bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I now understand this Dharma-gate of the samādhi of suchness as it truly is, in order to bring all sentient beings to fulfillment."

This bodhisattva, having cultivated through the mind of great compassion, fulfills the higher training in ethics, the higher training in concentration, and the higher training in wisdom by relying upon that mind of great compassion, and thereby attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Therefore, I now cultivate and maintain the sublime precepts, remaining unshakable and heedful.
I maintain these precepts while keeping all sentient beings in my mindfulness."
Why is this? If a bodhisattva does not maintain the precepts with mindfulness for the sake of all sentient beings, it is not the bodhisattva precept.
Therefore, I now cultivate and uphold the pure precepts in order to enable all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness.
"Furthermore, good son! A bodhisattva reflects thus:
'When a bodhisattva leaves the household life to practice and maintain the pure precepts, they are then able to remain far removed from all worldly affairs.'"
When a bodhisattva dons the dyed robes, they are able to fulfill the relinquishing of all cherished things;
when a bodhisattva upholds the pure precepts, they are able to fulfill the purity of body, speech, and mind;
when a bodhisattva cherishes and maintains the precepts, they are able to fulfill the six supernormal powers.
When a bodhisattva sits in meditative seclusion and maintains the precepts, they can fulfill the factors of enlightenment;
when a bodhisattva hears the sublime Dharma and practices the pure precepts, they can fulfill the four types of unimpeded knowledge;
when a bodhisattva seeks out extensive learning and wisdom while practicing the pure precepts, they can fulfill the mind that is free from self-exaltation.
When a bodhisattva draws near to spiritual friends and practices pure precepts, they can fulfill all merits;
when a bodhisattva practices the precepts of the perfection of giving, they can fulfill the knowledge of all modes of knowledge;
when a bodhisattva practices pure precepts according to the Dharma as it has been heard and taught, they can fulfill the role of a great Dharma teacher.
When a bodhisattva contemplates and upholds the Dharma as it has been heard, they are able to fulfill and attain dhāraṇī;
when a bodhisattva recollects the bodhicitta while practicing pure precepts, they are able to transcend all evils and attain fulfilled morality;
when a bodhisattva practices pure precepts without giving rise to a harmful mind, they are able to fulfill and never lose the bodhicitta.
"When a bodhisattva maintains the pure precepts without losing the bodhicitta, they will be able to fulfill the mind that does not lose the Three Jewels. The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"If one can protect those who maintain the precepts, then all that is worthy of protection in the world can be protected."
"This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of morality (śīla-smṛti).
Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of relinquishment (tyāga-smṛti)?"
"Good son! A bodhisattva reflects thus:
'All things that can be relinquished are entirely subsumed within two kinds of relinquishment:'"
That is to say, the relinquishment of dharmas and the relinquishment of material wealth. "Good son!

When a bodhisattva practices the giving of the necessities of life, they are able to fully perfect the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, purify buddha-fields, and transform sentient beings."

The bodhisattva’s relinquishment of dharmas is also able to fulfill the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities, and is able to sever both the afflictions and the habitual tendencies of the afflictions.

"Furthermore, good son! When a bodhisattva is able to relinquish the mind of stinginess regarding material requisites, and through the causes and conditions of relinquishing the Dharma, they are able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"Furthermore, the renunciation of material wealth can purify the physical body born of parents, while the renunciation of the Dharma can purify the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, the merit of renouncing material wealth can cause one to relinquish the physical body born of parents."
Who possesses this power of relinquishment?
With the exception of Bodhisattvas of the first stage, it exists in none among all worldly beings.
One who practices the dharma of relinquishment can achieve the supernormal power of mental mastery.
Who possesses this power?
None in all the worlds except for the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages.
Furthermore, the relinquishing of material wealth can transform sentient beings, while the bestowing of the Dharma can enable them to attain liberation.
"Furthermore, the relinquishing of material wealth can lead to the accumulation of merit, while the giving of the Dharma can cause one to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, the relinquishing of material wealth can only give half; the giving of the Dharma gives everything."

"Furthermore, the gift of material wealth can bring about liberation through the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*), while the gift of the Dharma can accomplish liberation through the departure from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
