Furthermore, if one who practices relinquishment (*tyāga*) can relinquish false conceptualization (*abhūta-vikalpa*), this relinquishment is the most supreme and foremost—namely, the relinquishing of the mind of false conceptualization."
"Why is this? Because a bodhisattva abandons false conceptualization, they are therefore called 'pure.
The bodhisattva asked:
"What dharma is meant by 'false speech'? He replied, "Good son!
"To speak of what is false and deceptive means to discourse on unreal dharmas of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). He asked:
"What is meant by 'unreal conceptual proliferation'?"
He replied: "If a person thinks thus:
'I am greedy, I am angry, I am deluded; I am defiled, I am pure, I am impure; I wander in the world, I enter into nirvāṇa.'"
"All such things as these are entirely unreal, false, conceptual constructions, and the dharma of frivolous proliferation. Why is this? All things are merely dependent origination;

they are without self and without what belongs to a self; they are without sentient beings, without persons, without life-force, without a soul, without a long-lived one, without an agent, and without an instigator."
Those various causes and conditions are empty and quiescent in their intrinsic nature, being far removed from mind, mentation, and consciousness;
those various causes and conditions cannot conceive, cannot discriminate, cannot be defiled, cannot be purified, cannot traverse the world, and cannot enter nirvāṇa.
Therefore, because the bodhisattva can know such illusory phenomena and does not entertain the thought,
"This is truly existent," they abandon such a mind; hence, it is called "renunciation."
“If a bodhisattva can maintain mindfulness of such dharmas as these, it is called ‘mindfulness of relinquishment.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are three kinds of relinquishment for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: namely, relinquishment, great relinquishment, and superior relinquishment.”
"What is the renunciation of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?

It refers to food and drink, parched grain, granaries, clothing, vehicles, lamps, incense, flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, banners, canopies, standards, curtains, carriages, necklaces, crowns, gold, silver, precious jewels, and all such things that are not means for harming or injuring sentient beings. With the sole exception of matters that could harm sentient beings, there is nothing among all other objects that he does not relinquish; this is called the renunciation of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
"What is the great relinquishment (*mahātyāga*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
Son of good family!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has perfected relinquishment, he is able to give away what he holds dear: his wife, children, sons and daughters, those of all ages, male and female servants, attendants, ministers, officials, subjects, houses, gardens, groves, kingdoms, and royal thrones. This is called the great relinquishment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
“What is the superior renunciation (*adhyāśaya-tyāga*) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
Son of good family!

Because a bodhisattva accomplishes both renunciation and great renunciation, he accomplishes superior renunciation—namely, being able to relinquish hands, feet, ears, noses, heads, eyes, marrow, brains, blood, flesh, tendons, bones, lips, tongues, teeth, skin, nails, and hair. Being able to relinquish all such things as these is called the superior renunciation of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
"Furthermore, noble son,
a bodhisattva contemplates such relinquishment, great relinquishment, and supreme relinquishment, thinking:
'I shall ultimately accomplish relinquishment, great relinquishment, and supreme relinquishment.'"
At that time, he was named the Bodhisattva Mindfulness of Renunciation.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of renunciation."
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the devas? Good son!”
The Bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the pure heavens—namely, mindfulness of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas.
How does one practice this mindfulness?

To be mindful of that practice, to be mindful of merit, to be mindful of non-arising, to be mindful of the objects experienced, to be mindful of initial practice, to be mindful of cultivation, and to be mindful of accomplishment—this is called mindfulness of the devas.
"Furthermore, good son! A bodhisattva is mindful of the devas.
How does he practice mindfulness of the devas?
By practicing virtuous deeds, one obtains superior karmic retribution. What are these virtuous deeds?

They are the ten paths of wholesome action, which involve distancing oneself from the paths of unwholesome action. Through the causal conditions of these virtuous deeds, one obtains the various celestial forms, exquisite pleasures, purity, and the superior, wondrous fruit of the sense faculties.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward those sublime and wondrous karmic rewards, they generate great compassion and share those excellent fruits of happiness with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"I wish to cause sentient beings to attain the sublime bliss of the heavens.
Furthermore, in order to bring those roots of goodness to fulfillment, he exerts great diligence and gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings born in the evil realms.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I should instruct all sentient beings to practice wholesome deeds so that they may be reborn in the heavens, and there, within those celestial realms, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva instructs all sentient beings to cultivate wholesome deeds so as to be reborn in the heavens, ensuring they do not fall away from those sublime fruits of heaven; from that celestial bliss, they then attain the unsurpassed bliss—namely, the tranquil and wondrous bliss of the Tathāgata.
"This is called the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the devas. Good son!
These are called the ten applications of mindfulness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpāda, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"One does not perceive suffering as suffering, for by perceiving suffering one sees it as emptiness.
If one does not depart from suffering, the dharma of emptiness cannot be attained."
Those who wish to perceive emptiness should perceive the meaning of suffering;
for they take suffering to be the meaning of emptiness, because that emptiness is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Suffering has no agent, because suffering is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Apart from suffering, who is the agent?
Furthermore, there is no before or after.
There is no real accumulator; if one could truly accumulate suffering, [it would not be possible].
Where does this arise?
Since suffering has no agent,
suffering comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
With what phenomena is it conjoined?
Where can there be freedom from suffering?
It is taught that craving is the origin; for if one can accumulate [craving], one accumulates suffering.
Craving is truly without craving; how could that which is free from craving accumulate?
Since suffering has no place from which it comes, who is there to encounter the future?
To speak of cessation as definitive is to be free from the phenomena of coming and going.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is extinguished; they are fundamentally pure and luminous.
All phenomena are equally quiescent, for they are free from the limits of past and future.
If a phenomenon were to arise first, it would necessarily undergo cessation later.
How can cessation arise apart from arising?
Without arising, there is no such cessation.
Seeking wisdom in this manner is called the untainted path.
The Dharma is said to be like a raft, illustrated by the necessity of abandoning even the raft.
If one abandons even the teachings, why should that teaching be clung to?
Abandoning the path and dwelling on the sublime island—this is called attaining liberation.
It is said that the characteristic of liberation consists in not contending with any phenomena,
because one has realized the path of suchness regarding all phenomena.
Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, fat, skin, blood, flesh, and bone—

Tears, saliva, feces, and urine; liver, gallbladder, brain membranes, heart, lungs, large intestine, and small intestine—this accumulation is called the body, a dwelling of false discrimination; thus do the wise contemplate it.
There is no real agent, nor is there one who experiences;
like an empty village, such is this illusory body.
It is said that "feeling" is the act of experiencing, but who is it that experiences that feeling?
The feeler is detached from feeling; no distinction can be found between them.
The wise person reflects thus:
"That wise one contemplates feeling; its characteristic is like bodhi—quiescent, pure, and luminous."
Not seeing the mind within the body, nor seeing the mind within the mind, such a person is free from feverish affliction; though free, they do not rejoice.
Seeing that phenomena are nothing but mind, they remain far removed from conceptual discrimination.
Not abandoning the practice of True Suchness (tathatā), one thereby attains the unobstructed realm.
All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;
free from all numerical categories and the mark of exhaustion, they are equal like space.
Knowing these phenomena as they truly are, the wise have no mark of going;
knowing phenomena, they likewise do not abide, for they dwell in equanimity.
If one can maintain such mindfulness, one remains unshakable amidst all phenomena.
This person has reached the other shore, like the field of merit of all Buddhas.
Knowing that all phenomena are the Buddha, they are stainless in every respect;
having gathered pure and white dharmas, they bring peace and security to all sentient beings.
Mindfulness of tranquility and sublime form, as well as mindfulness of all merits—
when a bodhisattva fulfills all dharmas, they will surely attain the unsurpassed path.
This bodhisattva makes offerings to the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
With mindfulness unmoving within the Dharma, through the constant state of meditative concentration,
And having firmly bound the armor of steadfastness, one contemplates the realm of the sublime Dharma;
Thus attaining unsurpassed bodhi, this is the firm practice of the Bodhisattva.
Just as with the Dharma, so it is with me; if one forms such a thought:
"This thought of the Dharma should be known, namely that all Bodhisattvas are free from 'I' and 'mine';"
"As the Dharma is, so am I.
If one can reflect in this way, it is called cultivating mindfulness of the sublime Dharma.
The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is the unsurpassed field of merit.
They shall surely attain the Bodhi of the Buddhas; I constantly keep such persons in mind.
Like the ocean, they are immeasurable; I keep such persons in mind and dedicate all these merits so that all may become Buddhas.
Skillfully cultivating the non-retrogressive precepts, I contemplate those virtuous practices;
may all their merits be given entirely to sentient beings,
dedicated toward the unsurpassed path, so that they may attain ultimate bliss.
This is called the mindfulness of the precepts, which can bring happiness to sentient beings.
It relinquishes both material resources and dharmas, and likewise abandons all afflictions.
Performing meritorious deeds for the sake of sentient beings, one dedicates them toward the unsurpassed path.
Thus accomplishing equanimity and mindfulness, He does not abide in the two paths;
Free from signs, he acts spontaneously, Shining like the sun wherever he is.
All ordinary and noble beings Attain their state through wholesome karma.
By means of those various causes and effects, he practiced great compassion and bestowed them upon all.
Through such sublime deeds, for the sake of granting supreme bliss,
he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment right there in that celestial realm.
At that time, the two great beings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Aśaṅkita-prasthāna and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vikrāntamati, together with their immeasurable retinues, went to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and, honoring the World-Honored One’s intention, withdrew to sit to one side; together with his retinue, they also sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When we two were preaching the Dharma-gathering atop the sublime jewel terrace of the Victorious Pavilion, all Tathāgatas fully knew, saw, and awakened to all phenomena without any obstruction.
“World-Honored One!
Does the collection of the Dharma taught by the two of us accord with the Buddha’s intention?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the two bodhisattvas, saying:
“Good son! It is as you have said:
the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, fully know, see, and awaken to all phenomena without any obstruction. Good son!”
The collection of teachings expounded by you two is well-aligned with my intention. Good sons!
All the speech of all bodhisattvas is, in every case, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Excellent, excellent! Son of good family,
you have now skillfully expounded this collection of the sublime Dharma.
If there are bodhisattvas who wish to expound the *Dharmasaṃgīti*, they should do so as you have spoken.
Sons of good family!
The sublime *Dharmasaṃgīti* that you have spoken constitutes the very work performed by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
"Noble son! I give my approval to the collection of teachings spoken by you two.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpādita to these words:
“Good son! For what reason are you named ‘The Unarisen’?
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who brings all actions of body, speech, and mind to rest; who does not cling to any activity performed; who seeks not even a single dharma, does not abandon afflictions, and has no desire to attain dharmas; who perceives the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all past and future dharmas as equal, and does not perceive any dharmas as inferior, middling, or superior—for this reason, it is called ‘non-origination.’”
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra!
All dharmas are without origination, because they are fundamentally non-existent. Śāriputra!
"If dharmas had a beginning, they would have an origin.
Since all dharmas are beginningless, how can one say that they have an origin?
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
“If the Dharma is thus, how can you speak of the accumulation of the Dharma?
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda replied,
“Venerable Śāriputra!...”
"I preach the collection of the Dharma without any arousal [of thought].
The Bodhisattva Without Arousal said to Śāriputra: "Śāriputra!..."
What do you think?
Is that which you have asked a question that has been raised,
or is it a question that has not been raised?
If one says there is that which initiates a question, by what causes and conditions is it initiated?
Yet, there is no dharma-initiated phenomenon apart from dharmas, nor is there any questioning apart from dharmas.
"Venerable Śāriputra!
If there is no one who raises questions, that constitutes entering the collection of the Dharma taught by me.
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
“Good son! I have a question to ask, and you likewise have something to say;
why then do you speak of ‘non-arising’?”
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said: "Venerable Śāriputra!
That which you have asked and that which I have spoken are both like an illusory teaching."
In this way, it should be understood that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the Tathatā-dharmadhātu as it has been described.
Venerable Śāriputra! As for an illusory person, they have no mind and no mental factors.
All sentient beings are likewise thus: they have no mind and no mental factors.
If this is so, how can there be any arising? Venerable Śāriputra!
Just as there is that which is spoken by a magician’s illusions,
so too should it be understood that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to speak based upon the *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā*.
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
“Good son! It is like the illusory feats produced by a magician; they are neither real nor unreal.”
"If it is thus, you too should be so— neither real nor unreal.
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said, "Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have realized that all dharmas are like illusory forms; therefore, they say that all dharmas are false and like illusions.
Śāriputra said, "So it is, son of good family!"
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, realize that all phenomena are like illusions and teach that all phenomena are like illusions.
The Bodhisattva Arousing Nothingness said,
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
Just as that illusion is neither real nor unreal, so too are all phenomena: they are neither real nor unreal; one should understand them in this way.
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said: “Śāriputra,
if all phenomena were either real or unreal, one should not say that all phenomena are like illusory appearances.”
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
"Good son, for what purpose do you practice the bodhisattva path?"
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said: "Venerable Śāriputra!
When I practice the bodhisattva path, I do not act for the sake of an objective, nor do I act for the sake of what is not an objective."
Why is this? If there is a bodhisattva who practices for the sake of [conceptual] objects, such a bodhisattva acts with a point of view.
If one acts while holding a point of view, such a bodhisattva does not accord with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

Why is this? If one practices while harboring any view, such a person cannot even conform to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), let alone enter directly into it.
If one is separated from the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), then one does not accord with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
If one practices conduct for the sake of nothing other than [worldly] gain, such a person walks upon a false path.
"One who practices a deviant path has no true meaning.
The Venerable Śāriputra said,
"O son of good family!"
"If one does not act for the sake of the ultimate meaning, yet it is not that one does not act for the sake of the ultimate meaning—
in such a case, where does a bodhisattva practice?
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda replied, "Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"Wherever all ordinary worldlings of the path of hair (mārga) may go, there the Bodhisattva likewise goes. Śāriputra said,
"O son of good family!"
"Where do ordinary worldlings travel?
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda replied, "Venerable Śāriputra!"

Wherever the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, travel, there the foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) also travel; yet these foolish ordinary beings do not know that "the Buddhas travel everywhere, and I too travel there."
The Venerable Śāriputra said:

"Good son! If ordinary worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) do not know the sphere of activity of all Buddhas, how can you say that wherever the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, go, ordinary worldlings go to that same place?"
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said: "Venerable Śāriputra!
Are you now able to know the realm of the Buddha?"
Śāriputra said: "Good son!
I merely grasp according to those words; how could I know the realm of the Buddhas?"
"Good son! However, all śrāvakas hear sounds from the Tathāgata and, through discrimination, claim to know them. Good son!"
"The realm of all Buddhas is immeasurable and boundless, yet there is no realm of ordinary beings apart from the realm of all Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva Asamudgata said,
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."

If there were a realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) distinct from the realm of the Buddhas, then how could Śāriputra’s previous statement—that ordinary beings on the path of hair (*keśamārga*) do not know the realm of the Buddhas—be true?
The Venerable Śāriputra said: “Good son!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, transcend the world, whereas ordinary worldlings of foolish nature wander within the world; therefore, these ordinary worldlings do not know the realm of the Buddhas.”
The Bodhisattva Aproduita said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, what do you think?"
"Do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have anything to be attained, anything in which to abide,
or anything to be benefited? Śāriputra replied,
"O son of good family!"
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have no dharma they do not know; having known all dharmas and awakened to all dharmas, they are able to benefit sentient beings within the realm of conditioned phenomena.
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said:
"If Śāriputra understands it in this way, for what reason do you say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, transcend the world?
Is this not something the Venerable Śāriputra has spoken without due reflection?"
Śāriputra! If the Tathāgata has transcended the world, then the Tathāgata has nothing to be attained, nothing in which to abide, and no benefit to be performed. Śāriputra!
"What you have said is already refuted.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Anutpādita:
"O son of good family!..."
"I have already been ruined previously; it is not only now. In the past, I once regressed from my roots of goodness and the mind of omniscience.
Son of good family!
I deeply rejoice in your eloquence of inspired speech; may all sentient beings likewise attain such eloquence."

When this Dharma collection was being spoken, eighty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); sixty thousand devaputras became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye;

five thousand bhikṣus turned away from the mind of a śrāvaka and resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The Buddha bestowed predictions upon those bhikṣus that each would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within various buddha-fields.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Aśaṅkita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully know the dharmas of the graspable and the grasper?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! If a bodhisattva knows all dharmas, at that time the bodhisattva skillfully knows the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka)."
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said:
“World-Honored One,
how does one rightly know all dharmas?”
The Buddha said:
"One sees all phenomena as being like a dream, an illusion, a city of the Gandharvas, a mirage, a fire-wheel, the moon in water, a transformation, and a reflection in a mirror."
The Bodhisattva Asaṃudgata said:
“World-Honored One!
What are all dharmas that are seen as being like a dream, an illusion, a city of the Gandharvas, a mirage, a fire-wheel, the moon in water, a transformation, and a reflection in a mirror?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
What are called ‘all phenomena’ (sarvadharma) refer to the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects.”

"Good son! This is called seeing all phenomena as like a dream, a magical illusion, a city of the Gandharvas, a mirage, a fire-wheel, a transformation, the moon in water, and a reflection in a mirror."
The grasper refers to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
the graspable refers to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives, knows, and awakens to all phenomena—both the subjective grasper and the objective grasped—and is also able to skillfully explain them; for this reason, he is called the Omniscient One.
If one is an omniscient one, such a person is free from the underlying tendencies of affliction (*anuśaya*);

if one can be free from the underlying tendencies of affliction, such a person is without self and without what belongs to a self, being non-conceptual like space, and attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
because of attaining this mind of equanimity, they attain a mind of tranquility in all circumstances.

Because he has attained a mind of tranquility, he is named the one whose practice of the Dharma is naturally firm and steadfast; the one who acts as the leader among all sentient beings; the one who is without obstruction regarding all phenomena; the one of great loving-kindness and great compassion; the one who is immovable; and the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Bodhisattva Anutpāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva wishes to attain the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, how should they practice?”
The Buddha said:

“A bodhisattva who wishes to attain such dharmas as those of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, should give rise to a mind of equanimity like the great earth, because they are able to endure all the unwholesome actions and malicious speech of all sentient beings.”
Furthermore, one should give rise to a mind of equanimity like pure water, for it is able to wash away the subtle defilements of false discrimination belonging to oneself and all sentient beings.
Furthermore, one should generate an impartial mind that is like a fierce fire, for it can burn away the fuel of afflictions—both one's own and those of all sentient beings—with the fire of wisdom.
Furthermore, one should generate an impartial mind whose characteristic is like the wind, for it is able to remain free from all attachments.
Furthermore, one should give rise to a mind of equality like space, because there is no obstruction in any place. "Good son!
Just as the lion king, so too is the bodhisattva, because he is neither startled nor terrified in any place."
Just as a dragon-elephant, so too is the bodhisattva, for he bears the heavy burdens of all sentient beings with a tamed mind.
Just as a great rain, so too is the bodhisattva, for he pours down the wondrous rain.
Just as the sun’s light, so too is the bodhisattva, for they illuminate all sentient beings with the light of wisdom.
Just as the bright moon, so too is the bodhisattva, for all sentient beings who see them wherever they may be feel love and joy.
Just as a great caravan leader, so too is the bodhisattva, for he leads sentient beings toward the great jewel island of omniscience.
Just as a skilled physician, so too is the bodhisattva, for he is able to cure the disease of afflictions in all sentient beings.
Just as one who extracts a thorn, so too is the Bodhisattva, for he is able to extract the doubts and delusions of all sentient beings regarding all phenomena.
Just as a maritime navigator, so too is the Bodhisattva, for he is well-versed in omniscience and understands the significance of all directions.
Just as a ship, so too is the bodhisattva, for they are able to skillfully ferry across all sentient beings of the world from the great ocean of existence.
Just as various waters, rivers, ponds, and the like, so too is the bodhisattva, for they are able to nourish and moisten all sentient beings.
Just as the great royal highway, so too is the bodhisattva, for they are able to provide equal passage for all sentient beings.
Like an island of jewels, so too is the bodhisattva, for they are able to fully possess all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Just as a wish-fulfilling gem grants all that is needed to those who seek it, so too is the Bodhisattva, for they can bestow upon sentient beings the infinite benefits of whatever Dharma they seek.
Just as a fine horse, so too is the Bodhisattva, for they can carry the burden of sentient beings who are weary and suffering.
Just as the great ocean is, so too is the bodhisattva, for his wisdom is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom.
Just as Mount Sumeru is, so too is the bodhisattva, for he is unshakable regarding the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Just as all trees of exquisite jewels, so too is the bodhisattva, for they are fully endowed with supreme adornments.
Just as Jāmbūnada gold, so too is the bodhisattva, for they are rare and difficult to find.
Just as Śakra, King of the Gods, so too is the bodhisattva, for he is able to attain superior sovereign power over all phenomena.
Just as Mahābrahmā, so too is the bodhisattva, for he is fully endowed with tranquility and all dignified deportments.
Just as the four world-protecting heavenly kings and others, so too is the bodhisattva, for he is able to protect and uphold the supreme and wondrous Dharma.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch, so too is the bodhisattva, for he is able to practice the ten wholesome courses of action.
Just as a great minister, so too is the bodhisattva, for he is able to guard the secret teachings of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
A bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of renunciation, for he dwells well in the dharma of a śramaṇa.
The Bodhisattva dwells within the dharma of the śramaṇa because he has brought the actions of body, speech, and mind to tranquility.
The Bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya because he has accomplished meditative concentration (dhyāna), samādhi, samāpatti, the supernormal powers (abhijñā), and liberation through clear knowledge.
The Bodhisattva dwells in meditative concentration because he has attained the profound emptiness of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The Bodhisattva dwells in a place of tranquility because he is able to teach and transform *gandharvas*, *kiṃnaras*, and *mahoragas*, and because he accomplishes incantations, sublime medicines, and the dharmas of the sages.
The Bodhisattva dwells securely in clear wisdom, because he has fully accomplished the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividyā*).
The Bodhisattva abides in supreme tranquility, because he has attained the six sublime powers of transcendence (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
The bodhisattva abides in the wisdom of extensive learning, because he is able to skillfully know the distinctions among the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
The bodhisattva abides in the presence of a teacher, because he is able to skillfully know all treatises.
The Bodhisattva dwells on the stage of the Dharma-preacher because he is able to teach and transform others by remaining free from offerings of food and drink.
The Bodhisattva dwells well within the Vinaya because he is able to distance himself from all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
The bodhisattva dwells in the state of *māyā* because he is able to remain tranquil in all places;
the bodhisattva dwells in a supple mind because he is able to remain far removed from all seeking.
“A bodhisattva does not abide in a restless mind, because they are able to remain far removed from the affliction of greed.
A bodhisattva does not abide in a haughty mind, because they are able to remain far removed from the affliction of hatred.”
A bodhisattva does not abide in malicious speech, because they are able to remain far removed from a deluded mind.
A bodhisattva does not abide in confused speech, because they are able to achieve the perfect guarding of their words.
"A Bodhisattva dwells as a Great Teacher because he is able to practice the Mahāyāna Dharma.
A Bodhisattva dwells well as one who bears the heavy burden because he is able to accomplish the mind of great enlightenment (mahābodhicitta)."
Just as there is great water, so too is the bodhisattva, because they provide benefit, profit, and sustenance for sentient beings.
Just as there is a great city, so too is the bodhisattva, because they fulfill the merit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"Just as a servant, so too is the bodhisattva, for he labors diligently on behalf of all sentient beings out of great compassion.
Furthermore, son of good family!"
The bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of gentleness toward beings who are evil; a mind of reverence toward beings who are arrogant;
a mind of straightforwardness toward beings who are deceitful and crooked; a mind free from the conduct of the dense forest toward beings who practice the conduct of the dense forest;
a mind of rescue and deliverance toward beings who do not practice; and [a mind of compassion] toward beings who lack a sense of shame.
One gives rise to a sense of shame; one gives rise to a sense of remorse toward those who lack it;
one gives rise to a mind free from cowardice toward those who engage in false doctrines; and one does not give rise to fear when dwelling among the great assembly.
One cannot be defiled by worldly dharmas, cannot be destroyed by any demons, and cannot be overcome by the false doctrines of external paths.
I prostrate, giving rise to a mind of reverence toward those worthy of honor; always giving rise to a mind of making offerings toward teachers and elders;
giving rise to a mind of wonder toward those of great learning; giving rise to a mind of rare appreciation toward those who have attained meditative concentration;
giving rise to a mind of profound practice toward those who are wise; and giving rise to a mind of love and respect toward all Dharma masters, as one would toward the Buddha.
All bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of refuge, a mind of ultimate certainty toward all Tathāgatas,
and a firm mind toward those who practice according to reality; they are neither startled nor terrified by any afflictions,
do not realize nirvāṇa, and, giving rise to great compassion, engage in worldly conduct to deliver sentient beings.
They do not preach the Dharma or teach others with a defiled mind, because they always remain far removed from all offerings and honors;
they are free from perverted minds, because they know, as it truly is, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity;
they possess a liberated mind, because they are able to distance themselves from sensory objects.
They achieve birth according to reality, because they are born into the family of the noble ones as it truly is;
they achieve wisdom according to reality, because their minds are constantly inclined toward renunciation;
they achieve noble conduct, because they know suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are.
They achieve the marks of a great man because they are fully endowed with the observance of precepts, extensive learning, and heedfulness;
they achieve a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings because they skillfully understand that the world is selfless;
and they achieve the non-perverted Dharma because they are sealed with the seal of the noble ones.

They achieve the mind of the site of enlightenment because they are sealed with the seal of non-retrogression. All these bodhisattvas constantly achieve pure mental conduct and achieve conduct of universally adorned majestic demeanor. They do not delight in speaking of worldly technical skills or language; they do not delight in associating with evil associates; they do not delight in matters of making offerings or showing respect; they do not delight in speaking of worldly idle chatter; they do not delight in speaking of the affairs of various lands; they do not delight in speaking of the affairs of kings; they do not delight in speaking of bandits and thieves; they do not delight in speaking of women; they do not delight in speaking of auspicious gatherings; they do not delight in speaking of military expeditions and battles; they do not delight in factions, strife, or litigation; they do not delight in various evil countries, cities, towns, villages, or difficult border regions; and they do not delight in associating with those who engage in music, song, dance, theater, or jesting.
"Furthermore, noble son! One does not delight in being with those who are stingy or envious;

one does not delight in being with those who break the precepts, hold wrong views, accumulate many evils, are heedless, or treat the Dharma lightly; one does not delight in being with those who harbor much resentment or have perverted and distracted minds; nor does one delight in being with those who are foolish or mute—one does not associate with any such persons at all."

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always delight in the courageous practice of giving—namely, the gift of Dharma, the gift of material goods, and the gift of fearlessness—and they sever the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion. As great and wondrous practitioners, they delight in dwelling away from the clamor and confusion of crowds; they delight in silence and always delight in solitude—in such places as high mountains, rocky peaks, ravines, grassy thickets, forests, clear springs, and flowing streams. They delight in such secluded and tranquil locations.”

During the first and last watches of the night, they abandon sleep and practice with diligent effort, giving rise to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as various dhyānas, samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and sovereign supernormal powers. Countless, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Dharma gates manifest before them; they see countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, attain hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of samādhis and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of dhāraṇī gates, and are able to transform and guide hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings.
“A bodhisattva should accomplish such states of mind as these, and will then be able to attain that sublime Dharma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpādita-uttara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one can practice in accordance with reality, because this is the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is the vehicle upon which those who practice according to the teachings ride.
If one can be diligent and not negligent, such a person is said to be practicing in accordance with reality.
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, one who practices according to reality is said to be one who has resolved upon the vow for bodhi; one who is diligent is said to be one who fulfills that vow for bodhi.
Moreover, one who practices according to reality is said to be one who practices giving; one who is diligent is said to be one who does not seek recompense.”
Furthermore, the practitioner who trains according to reality upholds the pure precepts, while the one who is heedful accomplishes the non-retrogressive precepts.

Furthermore, the practitioner begins the cultivation of the practice of patience, while the one who is heedful attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, the practitioner seeks all roots of goodness without weariness, because one who is heedful relinquishes all worldly activities.
Furthermore, while the practitioner first cultivates meditative concentration, one who is heedful does not remain fixed in that concentration.
Furthermore, the practitioner fulfills wisdom; the one who is heedful does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
Furthermore, the practitioner guards the sublime Dharma; the one who is heedful does not perceive [the inherent existence of] all phenomena.
Furthermore, while the practitioner causes all sentient beings to attain great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), the one who is heedful does not perceive those sentient beings as separate entities.
Furthermore, while the one who practices according to reality accumulates all roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), the one who is heedful dedicates them toward great enlightenment.
Furthermore, for one who practices according to reality, awakening (bodhi) is the true dharma; one who is heedful knows all dharmas as they truly are, according to the characteristics of awakening.
Furthermore, one who practices according to reality attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), while one who is heedful vows to take up birth.

Furthermore, one who practices according to reality proceeds to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and manifests all supreme adornments, while one who is heedful knows *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as they truly are.
Furthermore, one who practices according to reality knows awakening as it truly is; one who is heedful has well-cultivated all past karmas.
Furthermore, one who practices according to reality reaches great parinirvāṇa; one who is heedful well knows that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is quiescent extinction.
“World-Honored One!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are well able to practice in this way and remain heedful will find it no difficulty to attain bodhi.
World-Honored One!”
For this reason, World-Honored One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate practice according to reality and heedfulness. This,
World-Honored One,
is called the Collection of Subtle and Wondrous Dharmas.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, upon hearing the Dharma-collection spoken by the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and various bodhisattvas, give rise to faith and are able to practice it, these bodhisattvas possess the sublime Dharma-collection.”
Why is this? If one does not have faith in the Dharma, there will be no accumulation of the Dharma; if one does not practice with diligence, there will likewise be no accumulation of the Dharma.
If a person can give rise to a sense of rare wonder and a mind of suchness toward the teachings spoken by the Noble Ones, that Bodhisattva possesses the accumulation of the sublime Dharma.
"Bhagavān! If a person does not praise themselves nor disparage others, that person possesses the accumulation of the sublime Dharma. Bhagavān!"

If a person possesses a mind of noble compassion toward the noble and a mind of inclusive care toward those who are not noble; if a person does not perceive their own superiority nor perceive the inferiority of others; if a person gives rise to an impartial mind toward equal phenomena and likewise gives rise to an impartial mind toward unequal phenomena; if they give rise to an impartial mind toward the equal and an impartial mind toward both the equal and the unequal, without discriminating between the equal and the unequal—such a person possesses the accumulation of the sublime Dharma.

If a person, upon hearing but a single phrase, is able to understand hundreds of thousands of millions of phrases, you should know that this person possesses the *Sūtra of the Collection of the Sublime Dharma*.

If a person hears the Dharma without stillness or distraction; if a person hears the Dharma without being bound or liberated; if a person hears the Dharma without practicing or dwelling; if a person hears the Dharma without increase or decrease; if a person hears the Dharma without joy or anger; and if a person hears the Dharma without abiding in the world or entering nirvāṇa—O World-Honored One!
If one can thus enter into the collection of the Dharma, it should be known that this person possesses the sublime collection of the Dharma.
World-Honored One,
does the collection of the Dharma that I have now expounded accord with the collection of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said, “It is so, Śāriputra.”
"Śāriputra! What you have said accords with the Buddha's intention.
*Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! If a bodhisattva...”
If one thinks, "I am able to preach the Dharma-Collection," such a bodhisattva will be unable to preach it.
Why is this? Those who possess the view of a self give rise to such thoughts:
"I am able to preach the Dharma, and that person listens to the Dharma."

"If a person is far removed from the mark of self, that person does not see 'I' as the one who can preach the Dharma, nor 'another' as the one who can hear the Dharma; they do not see those two, yet it is not that they do not see the two."
World-Honored One!

All phenomena that exist are not truly existent. Whatever phenomenon one may give rise to a discriminating mind regarding and claim to be truly existent, one should know that such a phenomenon is false and lacks reality.
The bodhisattvas do not give rise to the discrimination that those phenomena truly exist within that dharma.
Why is this? Because they do not give rise to the discrimination that these are truly existent.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all phenomena are false and unreal, like the speech uttered by a conjured person.
World-Honored One!
That which is false is truly non-existent yet appears to exist; such phenomena accord with emptiness, do not contradict causes and conditions, and accord with non-arising and non-ceasing.

Such a person does not contradict the dharma of emptiness and all causes and conditions; they accord with non-arising and non-ceasing, abandon various forms of discrimination, sever the self and the view of self, and remain far removed from all false views.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all dharmas are illusory, yet they can accord with the world by speaking of them as existing.
If one can thus speak of illusory dharmas so that others may understand them, this is called a "speaker who can expound the collection of dharmas."
"What kind of teaching do you say constitutes the 'collection of dharmas'?
To teach that all dharmas have but a single characteristic— such a collection of dharmas is called the subtle and sublime collection of dharmas,
World-Honored One!"
"Is this collection of the Dharma that I have now taught in accordance with the collection of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said, "It is so, Maudgalyāyana!"
"What you have said accords with the Buddha’s intention.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
World-Honored One!
If a person preaches the *Dharmasaṃgīti* for the sake of seeking merit, what they say is to be censured. Why is this?
Because of attachment to a self.

If one is attached to the characteristics of a self and what belongs to a self, then the unwholesome actions, meritorious actions, and immovable actions performed by such a person are deeds not free from false views; it should be known that such a person can neither benefit themselves nor others.
“World-Honored One!
If a person cannot know such a collection of dharmas, that person does not give rise to unwholesome actions, meritorious actions, or immovable actions.
If a person can know the collection of dharmas, that person neither accumulates the five aggregates, nor is it that they do not accumulate them.”
He gathers the eighteen elements, yet it is not that he does not gather them; he does not gather the twelve bases, yet it is not that he does not gather them.
This person does not grasp at sentient beings, yet it is not that he does not grasp them; he does not grasp at dharmas, yet it is not that he does not grasp them.
He does not grasp at reality, nor does he grasp at unreality; he does not grasp at objective spheres, yet he is not apart from objective spheres. This is...
One does not grasp at greed, hatred, or delusion, nor is one separated from greed, hatred, or delusion; one does not grasp at the mundane world, nor does one grasp at nirvāṇa;
one does not grasp at dispute, nor does one grasp at silence; one does not grasp at emptiness, nor does one grasp at false views;
one does not grasp at signlessness, nor does one grasp at applied and sustained thought; one does not grasp at wishlessness.
Nor is it non-apprehension; one does not apprehend the dharmas of the Buddhas, nor does one apprehend the dharmas of ordinary beings;
one does not apprehend dharma, nor does one apprehend non-dharma; one does not apprehend the noble Saṃgha, nor does one apprehend the Saṃgha of external paths.
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva knows all dharmas and does not seek an ultimate point of rest. Why is this?
This bodhisattva knows that there is no dharma whatsoever that is not ultimately so.
This bodhisattva does not seek liberation, for the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is quiescent, and there is nothing that is not liberation.
This bodhisattva does not delight in a single dharma, nor does he feel aversion toward a single dharma.
This bodhisattva knows that all Buddha-dharmas are neither his own dharmas nor the dharmas of others.
One does not grasp at a single dharma, nor does one abandon a single dharma; if there were grasping or abandoning, that would be censurable.
One neither acts nor dwells; if there were acting or dwelling, that too would be censurable.
One is neither joyful nor sorrowful; if there were sorrow or joy, that too would be censurable.
“World-Honored One!
What has been thus spoken is called the Collection of Dharma.
World-Honored One!”
“Is this Dharma collection that I have now taught in accord with what the Tathāgata has spoken? The Buddha said, “Pūrṇa!”
"What you have said accords with the Buddha’s intention.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If a person possesses the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) and the notion of non-phenomena (*adharmasaṃjñā*), and preaches the Dharma based on these two notions, such a person is said to dwell within ignorance (*avidyā*). Why is this?
If a person perceives what is not the Dharma as it truly is, that is the true Dharma.
World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva perceives what is not the Dharma as it truly is, that is suchness.
World-Honored One!
As for the true Dharma, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; the Dharma does not depend on persons.
World-Honored One!
The Dharma is neither distant nor near to people; the Dharma is likewise neither distant nor near in terms of location.
World-Honored One!
The Dharma has no such thought:

"I practice toward superior sentient beings but do not practice toward inferior or middling sentient beings; I practice toward inferior or middling sentient beings but do not practice toward superior sentient beings."
"World-Honored One!
A dharma does not obtain its name by way of having characteristics, nor does it obtain its name by way of being without characteristics. Why is this?"
World-Honored One!
When the noble ones perceive all marks as bondage, they likewise perceive the markless as bondage.
World-Honored One!
The Dharma is neither detachment nor practice.
World-Honored One!
One who is able to know the Dharma remains far removed from both detachment and practice.
World-Honored One!
The Dharma is neither given to others nor taken by oneself; yet, according to what is desired, its benefits differ, because there is no agent.
World-Honored One!
The Dharma does not give rise to thoughts of affection toward the Buddhas, nor do ordinary worldlings give rise to thoughts of enmity;
World-Honored One, this is because it is free from the conceptualization of non-discriminative proliferation.
World-Honored One!
The Dharma is neither near the Buddha nor far from ordinary beings; yet, according to their respective practices, the Dharma they attain differs.
World-Honored One!
“Such a teaching as this is called the ‘Collection of Dharma.
World-Honored One,
does the Collection of Dharma that I have explained accord with the Collection of Dharma taught by the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said,
“Mahākātyāyana! What you have said accords with the Buddha’s intention.”
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a person seeks tranquility yet preaches the collection of dharmas, such a person has no collection of dharmas.”
"Bhagavān! All dharmas do not depart from tranquility, because they are non-dual.
As for dualistic dharmas, they do not know duality, because they are far removed from mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and cognition (*jñāna*)."
The single dharma does not seek a second, because it is far removed from the dharma of seeking and desiring;
the single dharma is also non-dual, because it is without any conditioned activity.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
That which is quiescent is the non-dual dharma;
that which is the non-dual dharma does not depart from all dharmas.

“World-Honored One! All dharmas are of a non-dual nature because their intrinsic nature is empty. Their intrinsic nature is signless, wishless, and without activity; their intrinsic nature is neither born nor extinguished. They are not obtained through a mark of purity, yet they are obtainable; they are not obtained through a mark of impurity, yet they are obtainable. They are not obtained by the stingy, nor by the generous; not obtained by those who break the precepts, nor by those who uphold them; not obtained by the hateful, nor by those who practice patience; not obtained by the indolent, nor by those who exert diligence; not obtained by the distracted, nor by those in meditative concentration; and not obtained by the ignorant, nor by those possessed of wisdom.”
If one can thus not apprehend any dharmas, this is called truly attaining the Dharma. If there is anything apprehended among dharmas, then one cannot attain them;

if there is any sphere of activity, then one cannot attain them. One who dwells within the sphere of mental activity, who practices dualistic dharmas, who perceives existing dharmas, who relies upon dharmas, who seeks to realize dharmas, who seeks to leave behind afflictions, who seeks the ultimate, who perceives the Buddha, who perceives the Dharma and the Sangha, who perceives the world, or who perceives nirvana—such a person cannot attain this sphere.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a person seeks the Dharma, they should have no seeking toward any phenomena.
World-Honored One!"
"One who seeks nothing among all phenomena is said to truly seek the Dharma.
World-Honored One!
A Bodhisattva of right view perceives neither phenomena nor non-phenomena, yet regarding all phenomena, they reflect as follows:"
"To be far removed from the notion of 'mine' and to have no attachments is called the true Dharma;
to be far removed from what is false and unreal is called the true Dharma;
to be far removed from all seeking is called the true Dharma."
"If one knows that all phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation, this is called the true Dharma.
If there is a bodhisattva who can speak in this way, this is then called the "Gathering of the True Dharma."
“World-Honored One!
Does this collection of the sublime Dharma that I have now spoken accord with the Tathāgata’s collection of the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! What you have said accords with the Buddha’s intention.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That which is called ‘Dharma’ is named ‘non-contention.
If one can practice non-contention, such a person possesses the Dharma.”
“World-Honored One!
The eye and forms do not contend;
the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena likewise do not contend—this is called the Dharma.”
Furthermore, why are the two phenomena of the eye and form without contention?
Because they do not come together and because these two phenomena do not reach one another.
The same applies to the ear and sound, the nose and odor, the tongue and taste, the body and touch, and the mind and mental objects; for these also do not come together and do not reach one another.
"World-Honored One, that which does not arrive and does not conform to any dharma is entirely free from conflict and dispute.
World-Honored One, dharmas are non-dual; therefore, dharmas do not dispute."
World-Honored One!

All dharmas are non-dual; they do not know one another. They are without cognition or discrimination, free from manifold conceptualization, neither arising nor ceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither delighting nor loathing, and abiding neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa.
As for the true Dharma, it does not say that a person can obtain the Dharma, nor that the Dharma is obtained by a person.
World-Honored One!
All dharmas are neither weary nor joyful; they are neither defiled nor pure.
World-Honored One!
If a person says, "I know," "I perceive," or "I speak," such words are all false conceptualizations regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
"Bhagavān! Yet these sense-bases have no such thought:
'I am able to differentiate.'"
"If a person can know such a Dharma as this, one should know that this person does not contend with things;
if they do not contend with things, this person accords with the path and Dharma of the śramaṇa;

if they accord with the practices of the śramaṇa, this person neither goes nor comes, neither acts nor abides, neither advances nor retreats. Seeing all dharmas, they practice according to the Dharma; seeing all dharmas, they practice liberation; seeing all dharmas, they see the Dharma-realm; seeing all dharmas, they reach the ultimate, yet they do not perceive anyone who reaches the ultimate."
All phenomena that are perceived are merely names, merely false, and merely illusory. If one can thus perceive them as false and unreal, such persons are said to "see the Dharma."

“World-Honored One! To see the Dharma is called seeing the Buddha; to see what is not the Dharma is called seeing the Buddha. To see the Buddha is called seeing all sentient beings; to see what is not a sentient being is called seeing causes and conditions. To see what is not causes and conditions is called seeing emptiness; to see what is not emptiness is called non-seeing.”
World-Honored One!
This is called the right view regarding all dharmas.
World-Honored One!
"If one can thus correctly view all phenomena, it should be known that such a person can follow the intention of the Buddha, accord with the Dharma, and accord with the Sangha.
"World-Honored One!"

If bodhisattvas attain such patience regarding the dharma of non-contention, they do not even contend with those māras, much less give rise to conflict or contention with fellow bodhisattvas who practice the same path.
It is impossible for him to engage in conflict or dispute. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva sees that all speech can serve to accomplish his own practice; therefore, he should not engage in contention or litigation with others.
Because they are free from contention and dispute, Bodhisattvas ultimately attain the dharma of non-contention.
Because they have ultimately attained the dharma of non-contention, these Bodhisattvas are said to have attained all ultimate dharmas and to have attained equanimity regarding all dharmas.
Just as one sees one's own self as equal, so too does one see all phenomena; abiding in equality and attaining equanimity, for this reason it is called "attaining the ultimate."
All phenomena are equal, having neither going nor coming; therefore, this is called attaining the ultimate.
World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva thus attains the ultimacy of all phenomena, every word spoken by such a bodhisattva is a collection of the Dharma, entirely providing peace and happiness for all sentient beings.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is this collection of the Dharma that I have now spoken in accordance with the Tathāgata’s collection of the Dharma?"
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti, what you have said accords with the Buddha’s intention.”

"Subhūti! While you were now preaching this Dharma-collection, five thousand devaputras distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; five thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Subhūti! If there are bodhisattvas who hear this subtle and wondrous collection of the Dharma spoken by you, those bodhisattvas will immediately know that they have entered the great ocean of the Dharma; they will know that this body of theirs has not been spent in vain, and that they will certainly attain sublime bliss.
"Subhūti! This is called the foremost assembly of the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are called the ‘Collection of Dharmas’ by way of their names and letters. Why is this so?”
The nature of syllables has no characteristic of exhaustion; that which has no characteristic of exhaustion is itself the syllable.
World-Honored One, I say that speech is nothing but syllables.
"Bhagavān! As for syllables, they do not emerge from one's own body, nor do they emerge from another's body.
These various names do not form such thoughts:"
“I produce sounds,” O World-Honored One!
Yet all syllables neither increase nor decrease.
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva knows that all syllables and all dharmas are equal in their intrinsic nature.
World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva can thus ultimately know the sounds of all phenomena, for this reason the bodhisattva is not obstructed by sounds; whatever sounds they hear are all the voice of the Buddha, the voice of emptiness, the voice of signlessness, the voice of wishlessness, the voice of the dharma-realm, and the voice of the limit of reality.
For this bodhisattva, there is not a single dharma that can act as an obstacle to omniscience; this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma apart from the Buddha’s awakening.
This bodhisattva perceives all dharmas as entirely without obstruction, being able to see that all dharmas are identical to the Buddha’s awakening and are not in conflict with it.
This bodhisattva does not perceive any phenomena as advancing or retreating; this bodhisattva does not perceive any phenomena, yet constantly benefits all sentient beings.
Thus, the bodhisattva attains ultimate patience (*atyanta-kṣānti*) regarding all phenomena; by attaining this patience, they achieve profound eloquence in joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
What is this profound eloquence of inspired speech?
It is that which, according to the eloquence possessed by all bodhisattvas, cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

"This bodhisattva attains the eloquence of secure and blissful discourse—'secure eloquence' meaning that by means of such eloquence, they are able to cause all sentient beings to attain security and bliss."

“He shall attain the eloquence of appropriate discourse—‘the eloquence of appropriate discourse’ means that according to what each sentient being ought to hear of the Dharma, he preaches it extensively or concisely in accordance with their respective faculties and natures; this is called the eloquence of appropriate discourse.”
Furthermore, they attain swift eloquence—swift eloquence being that which, through the rapidity of its eloquent speech, teaches and transforms all sentient beings with speed.

Furthermore, he attains sharp and incisive eloquence—by which "sharp and incisive eloquence" is meant that he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings according to their superior faculties and keen intelligence, enabling them to attain swift liberation.
“Furthermore, they attain supreme eloquence in discourse—supreme eloquence meaning that whatever Dharma they preach is equal to that of the Buddha.

Moreover, their eloquence increases—increasing eloquence meaning that by means of a single word or phrase spoken with such eloquence, they can produce hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of ever-increasing levels of supreme eloquence.”
"One attains the eloquence of light and joyful speech.
What is this eloquence of light and joyful speech?
It is the eloquence that preaches the Dharma in accordance with the characteristics of what is known."
"Furthermore, he attains the eloquence of delight—eloquence of delight meaning that through such eloquence, those who hear the Dharma never grow weary of it.
Furthermore, he attains the eloquence of discipline—eloquence of discipline meaning that all his eloquence does not contradict the intent of the Buddha."
"Furthermore, they attain supple eloquence—supple eloquence being that eloquence which gives rise to no arrogance and possesses no heedless mind.
Furthermore, they attain tranquil eloquence—tranquil eloquence being that eloquence which, through its power, can bring both oneself and others to tranquility."

Furthermore, they attain the eloquence that accords with sounds—eloquence that accords with sounds meaning that, through such eloquence, they teach and transform sentient beings so that they enter the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

Furthermore, they attain the eloquence of detachment—this "eloquence of detachment" means that by means of their eloquence, they teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to attain the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

Furthermore, they attain supreme eloquence—by which supreme eloquence they employ eloquence to explain eloquence, and by whatever eloquence is appropriate, they teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to enter the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, they attain uncommon eloquence—uncommon eloquence being that which, through such eloquence, can expound the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique dharmas.

“Furthermore, they attain the eloquence of tranquility—eloquence of tranquility meaning that, by means of this eloquence, they are able to expound all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Furthermore, they attain the eloquence free from reproach—eloquence free from reproach meaning that, by means of this eloquence, they cause sentient beings to rejoice, have faith, and find delight.”

Furthermore, they attain the various powers of eloquence—by these powers of eloquence, they are able to completely subdue all Māras, external paths, and heterodox arguments according to their skill in speech.

“Furthermore, they attain the eloquence of skillful exposition—by ‘eloquence of skillful exposition’ is meant that whatever eloquence they possess for preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly, they give rise to no fear.
World-Honored One!”
"This is called the Collection of the Sublime Dharma.
World-Honored One,
does this collection of the Dharma that I have now spoken accord with what was taught by the Tathāgata?"
The Buddha said:
"Aniruddha! What you have said accords with the Buddha's intention."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva who wishes to preach the *Dharmasaṃgīti* should seek out and uphold those who receive and maintain the Dharma.”
Why is this? Because one obtains the Dharma from those who uphold it; therefore, one should seek it.
Seeking the Dharma with single-minded devotion alone is supreme.
Why is this? It is because one can attain the Dharma by revering the Dharma, but one does not obtain the benefits of the True Dharma by revering food;
one knows that while the relinquishing of body and life will certainly yield a future fruit, the retribution is not obtained within the object of contemplation itself.
He constantly seeks quiet places and does not delight in clamor; he associates with those who dwell in peace and security, not with those who break the precepts;
he associates with those who are respectful, not with those who are arrogant; he associates with those who practice for peace and happiness, not with those who are harsh and unruly;
he associates with those whose minds are supple, not with those who are rigid; he associates with those whose minds are tranquil, not with those who are attached.
The mind is that which inclines toward the disclosure of transgressions rather than the concealment of evils;
it inclines toward delighting in all forms of giving rather than stinginess and envy; it inclines toward upholding the precepts rather than breaking them;
it inclines toward patience rather than resentment and hatred; it inclines toward diligence rather than indolence; and it inclines toward meditative concentration.
One who is not distracted in mind, one who draws near to wisdom and is not foolish, one who draws near to the learned and is not of little learning,
one who draws near to right mindfulness and is not of wrong mindfulness, one who draws near to those who cultivate wholesome deeds and does not engage in unwholesome deeds,
and one who draws near to those who delight in the Buddha-dharma and does not delight in worldly dharmas.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, those who approach are those who delight in emptiness, not those who have fallen away through false views; they are those who draw near to the upholding of precepts, not those who merely seek refuge."
If a person can uphold the precepts, that person possesses the Dharma.
What, World-Honored One, are these precepts?
All precepts are entirely subsumed within three types of precepts. What are these three?
They are known as the higher training in ethical discipline (adhiśīla), the higher training in concentration (adhicitta), and the higher training in wisdom (adhiprajñā).
"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva is able to train in these three kinds of precepts, it should be known that this person has already trained in all Mahāyāna precepts."
“World-Honored One!
What is the superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
World-Honored One!”
A bodhisattva is able to uphold the *prātimokṣa* precepts, yet does not regard the *prātimokṣa* precepts as ultimate purity, because they rely on the practice of the bodhisattva precepts;
a bodhisattva accomplishes all states of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), yet does not regard such conduct as ultimate purity, because they abide in the state of bodhisattva dignified conduct;
and even regarding minor transgressions, they harbor fear and dread, because they rely upon bodhisattva wisdom.
What is the wisdom of a bodhisattva?
It is that a bodhisattva knows all phenomena as they truly are; because they do not fear any karma or afflictions, this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.
What is the sphere of the bodhisattva?
It is that which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), not a sphere of various conceptual discriminations.

Knowing the equality of precepts, one trains in the precepts; knowing the equality of emptiness, one trains in the precepts. Therefore, it is said: "Knowing the equality of emptiness, one trains in the precepts."

Knowing the equality of signlessness, knowing the equality of wishlessness, knowing the equality of non-activity, and knowing the equality of neither arising nor ceasing, one trains in the precepts; therefore, it is said that one trains in the precepts by knowing equality.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva forms this thought:
"I shall now cause all sentient beings to receive and uphold this prātimokṣa precept."
"This is called the Bodhisattva’s training in higher ethical discipline.
'World-Honored One,
what is the Bodhisattva’s training in higher concentration?'"
That is to say, the cultivation of the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the samāpattis.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects:
"I shall now, by means of this superior training in concentration, bring all sentient beings to fulfillment."
This is called the bodhisattva’s training in higher concentration.
What is the bodhisattva’s training in higher wisdom?
It is that the bodhisattva trains in the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects:
"I shall now cause all sentient beings to know and see these eighteen modes of emptiness.
This is called the bodhisattva’s training in higher wisdom.
“World-Honored One!
These three types of training of a bodhisattva are able to encompass all trainings.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If there is a bodhisattva who can protect sentient beings, such a bodhisattva is able to maintain pure precepts;
if they maintain pure precepts without attachment to that maintenance of precepts, such a bodhisattva relies upon those precepts to fulfill the hearts of all sentient beings.
"Bhagavān! A bodhisattva who has left the household life and maintains the precepts does not give rise to attachment toward any material things;
a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts in tranquility does not give rise to a mind of delight toward any speech."
A bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through the practice of peaceful sitting does not give rise to a mind of attachment toward any spoken sounds;
a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through meditative concentration does not give rise to a mind of attachment toward any sensory objects;
a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through liberation does not give rise to a mind of attachment toward any place of rebirth.
A bodhisattva who hears the Dharma and maintains the precepts does not give rise to a mind of attachment toward worldly discourse;
a bodhisattva who expounds the Dharma and maintains the precepts does not grow weary even when traveling hundreds of thousands of millions of *yojanas* to preach the Dharma;
a bodhisattva who protects the Dharma and maintains the precepts does not give rise to weariness amidst any afflictions, harms, or oppressions.
A bodhisattva who maintains the precepts with the thought of enlightenment practices all deeds solely for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, not for their own sake;
a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts with a profound mind desires that all sentient beings attain enlightenment first, seeking no realization for themselves;
a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts with an exalted and profound mind generates great joy in acts of benefiting others, rather than feeling joy in their own benefit.
A Bodhisattva who practices and upholds the precepts diligently cultivates each factor of enlightenment for immeasurable eons, being able to accomplish those dharmas without weariness;
a Bodhisattva who practices giving and upholds the precepts is even able to sacrifice their head, eyes, marrow, and brain to benefit sentient beings;
a Bodhisattva who upholds the śīla-precepts does not abandon sentient beings who have broken the precepts.
A bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through patience does not fear any disturbances caused by demons;
a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through diligence cultivates awakening for the sake of all sentient beings without weariness;
a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through meditative concentration gives rise to no attachment toward any sounds or any activities.
The Bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through wisdom perceives that the nature of all phenomena is equal, like the characteristic of bodhi;
the Bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through the practice of emptiness does not engage in worldly conduct;
the Bodhisattva who maintains the precepts through great compassion does not enter nirvana.
“World-Honored One!
Maintaining the precepts in this way is called the accumulation of the Dharma.
World-Honored One!”
"Is this Dharma collection that I have now taught in accord with what the Tathāgata has spoken? The Buddha said, "Rāhula!..."
"What you have said accords with the Buddha’s intention.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If a bodhisattva personally distances themselves from afflictions, they also cause sentient beings to distance themselves from afflictions—namely, the realm of all sentient beings, the realm of phenomena, and the realms of greed, hatred, and delusion.
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:

"Until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, the realm of phenomena is exhausted, and the realms of greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted, I shall teach and transform sentient beings during all that time without weariness."
The Bodhisattva further reflects:
"The intrinsic nature of all dharmas is quiescent extinction, yet sentient beings neither perceive nor know this. Why is this so?
All phenomena are empty and quiescent; therein nothing proceeds—namely, all false views and all disputes do not proceed thereat.
All phenomena are signless and extinguished; therein all discursive thought, reflection, and mental equanimity do not proceed thereat.
All phenomena are wishless and extinguished; therein all dharmas such as seeking, wishing, and desiring do not proceed thereat.
All phenomena are extinguished as being without self; therein, all attachments cease to function.
All phenomena are extinguished as being without a sentient being; therein, all various [conceptions] cease to function.
All phenomena are extinguished as being without a life-principle; therein, all birth and death cease to function.
When all dharmas are extinguished in the ultimate truth, there, all falsehoods do not function;
when all dharmas are extinguished through the cessation of the collection of causes and conditions, there, all notions of a life-principle (*jīva*) do not function;
when all dharmas are extinguished in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there, all thoughts and all formations (*saṃskāra*) do not function.
All dharmas are extinguished through the four right efforts; therein, no dharma is grasped, rejected, or practiced.
All dharmas are extinguished through the four bases of power; therein, no going or coming is practiced.
All dharmas are extinguished through the five faculties; therein, all high and low states are not practiced.
All phenomena are extinguished by the five powers; therein, all forms of subjugation do not function.
All phenomena are extinguished by the seven factors of enlightenment; therein, all signs of darkness do not function.
All phenomena are extinguished by the eightfold noble path; therein, evil karma and false reflections do not function at all.
All phenomena are extinguished within the ten powers; therein, all habitual tendencies do not function.
All phenomena are extinguished within the four fearlessnesses; therein, all alarm, dread, and apprehension do not function.
All phenomena are extinguished within the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; therein, all conditioned activities do not function.
When all phenomena are extinguished through wisdom, therein all ignorance does not function;
when all phenomena are extinguished as being without an agent, therein all formative activities (*saṃskāra*) do not function;
when all phenomena are extinguished as being without mentation, therein all consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not function.
All phenomena are extinguished through the absence of perception; therein, all name-and-form do not proceed.
All phenomena are extinguished through the absence of dependence; therein, all six sense-bases do not proceed.
All phenomena are extinguished through non-exhaustion; therein, all contact does not proceed.
When all phenomena are extinguished through the absence of wisdom, there is no occurrence of any sensation therein;
when all phenomena are extinguished through selflessness, there is no occurrence of any craving therein;
when all phenomena are extinguished through the absence of grasping, there is no occurrence of any clinging therein.
All phenomena are extinguished without body; therein, all forms of existence do not proceed.
All phenomena are non-extinguished; therein, all forms of birth do not proceed.
All phenomena are firmly extinguished; therein, all forms of aging do not proceed.
"All phenomena are neither exhausted nor extinguished; therein, all death does not occur.
World-Honored One!
This is called the gate of unobstructed wisdom of all bodhisattvas."
