When Bodhisattvas abide in this gate of unobstructed wisdom, they cannot be subdued by any demons, nor can they be refuted by non-Buddhist teachers; they know that no afflictions can defile them, they are constantly praised by all Buddhas, and they are revered by all devas.
“World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to reach such a gate of ultimate wisdom is said to have attained the great Dharma-treasury; is said to be not poor; is said to be the guardian of the secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; is said to be one whom all Buddhas and Tathāgatas can trust; is said to have done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished; and is said to have attained his own benefit—just as the great ocean cannot be measured and Mount Sumeru cannot be shaken.”
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Sublime and Wondrous Dharma.
World-Honored One!”
"Is the Dharma collection that I have now taught in accordance with what the Tathāgata has spoken?
The Buddha said, "Upāli!"
What you have now said accords with the Buddha’s intention. Upāli!
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who rely on this collection of dharmas to practice will be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among all karmas, the Bodhisattvas’ upholding and protection of the sublime Dharma is the most preeminent.”
World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva is able to practice and uphold the sublime Dharma, they will accord with Bodhi and all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, revere the Dharma.
World-Honored One,
what constitutes the protection and upholding of the sublime Dharma?

That which is called a bodhisattva being able to expound all the profound sūtras of the Buddhas, and being able to read, recite, contemplate, and practice them, is termed a bodhisattva’s upholding and protection of the sublime Dharma.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva embraces and practices [the teachings], this is called upholding the sublime Dharma.
World-Honored One!"
"What is the bodhisattva’s practice of gathering [beings]?

World-Honored One, all the physical, verbal, and mental actions of the bodhisattvas are for the benefit of all sentient beings; with great compassion as their primary motive and great loving-kindness as their preeminent quality, they protect sentient beings so that they may attain peace and happiness."
The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, with such a profound mind, reflects thus:
"By whatever practice one can bestow peace and happiness upon sentient beings, I should cultivate such practices."
"Therefore, one accomplishes the contemplation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); yet, while performing this contemplation, one does not seek to abandon the five aggregates.
One contemplates the elements (*dhātu*) as being like venomous snakes to cultivate practice, yet the mind does not seek to abandon the eighteen elements;
one contemplates the sense bases (*āyatana*) as being like an empty village to cultivate practice, yet the mind does not seek to abandon the twelve sense bases."

In this way, one cultivates practice by contemplating form as being like a mass of foam, yet the mind does not abandon the accomplishment of the physical body adornments of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;

one cultivates practice by contemplating sensation as being like a bubble, yet the mind does not abandon the accomplishment of the meditative concentrations, samādhis, samāpattis, and the sublime bliss of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
one cultivates practice by contemplating perception as being like a mirage, yet the mind does not abandon the accomplishment of the wisdom cultivation of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
One practices by contemplating formations as like a plantain tree, yet the mind does not abandon the practice of the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;

one practices by contemplating consciousness as like an illusion, yet the mind does not abandon the practice of purifying the actions of body, speech, and mind, with the perfection of wisdom as the foremost.

Practicing generosity without seeking karmic retribution; practicing ethical discipline to rescue sentient beings who violate the precepts; practicing patience to be able to subdue sentient beings; practicing diligence to accomplish all wholesome dharmas; practicing meditative concentration to achieve suppleness of body and mind; practicing wisdom to illuminate the characteristics of all phenomena; practicing the four foundations of mindfulness so that body and mind are free from defilement; practicing the four right efforts to attain unobstructed knowledge; practicing the five faculties to be able to accomplish the practice of progress; practicing the five powers so as not to regress from Bodhi; practicing the seven factors of enlightenment to be free from the net of doubt; practicing the eightfold noble path to be free from faults; and practicing the four Brahma-vihāras to attain sovereign mastery according to one's will.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva knows emptiness, they are able to embrace the sublime Dharma.
Moreover, 'emptiness' is a name for the absence of conceptual proliferation."
World-Honored One!
Where there is conceptual proliferation, there is no upholding of the sublime Dharma.
World-Honored One!
If one knows emptiness and signlessness, such a person is said to embrace the sublime Dharma;
if one grasps at signs, then there is no embracing of the sublime Dharma,
World-Honored One!

Because all phenomena are empty and signless, there is no aspiration; one who has no aspiration is able to embrace the sublime Dharma, whereas one who relies upon aspiration cannot embrace the sublime Dharma.

“World-Honored One! Those who perceive all phenomena do not grasp the sublime Dharma; those who rely on ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self’ do not grasp the sublime Dharma; those who possess pride do not grasp the sublime Dharma; those who rely on offerings, veneration, and praise do not grasp the sublime Dharma; those who rely on jealousy and stinginess do not grasp the sublime Dharma; and those who are attached to sensual desires, harm, and malice do not grasp the sublime Dharma.”
“World-Honored One!

One who upholds the sublime Dharma does so because the bodhisattva gives rise to no notion of differentiation regarding sentient beings, nor gives rise to any notion of differentiation regarding phenomena.”
"Bhagavān! In this way, a bodhisattva embraces the sublime Dharma. Bhagavān!"
When a bodhisattva perceives that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
when a bodhisattva perceives that all sentient beings neither depart nor arrive, this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
when [he] perceives that his own self is neither defiled nor pure, this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.
To take no delight in the teachings of the Buddhas and to feel no aversion toward the teachings of non-Buddhists is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;

to receive and uphold the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma without giving rise to a mind that perceives the characteristics of dharmas is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;

to not associate with any afflictions or secondary afflictions, nor to abide in any evil or unwholesome states while not giving rise to the perception of what is contrary to the Dharma, is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.
Having attained the mind of liberation, one does not give rise to the thought:
"I have attained liberation.
This is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.

To perform the deeds of a disciple toward all Buddhas, yet to cultivate practice without giving rise to the mind of body, speech, or thought—this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
to be entirely sovereign over all dharmas, yet not to give rise to the notion of dharma or non-dharma—this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
to cultivate practice by neither grasping nor rejecting any dharmas—this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.
To practice without seeking to acquire dharmas and without seeking to realize them is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
to give rise to no mind of attachment toward any object is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;

if a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind that is neither that of an ordinary person, nor a learner, nor an arhat, and severs the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion without any basis for dependence, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.
If a bodhisattva receives the prediction of enlightenment yet does not seek after the Buddha-enlightenment, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
if, when a bodhisattva approaches the site of enlightenment, they perceive the site of enlightenment in all places, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
if one is able to subdue all māras yet perceives neither the māras nor their retinues, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.
If one can attain the bodhi of a Buddha without realizing any dharmas that were previously non-existent, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
if one can turn the great wheel of Dharma without creating sentient beings and without destroying sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
if one can subdue all māras and heterodox teachers without engaging in strife, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.
If one can be born, yet not born anew and not born from the old, this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
if one can die, yet not be extinguished, this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
if one can transcend the triple world, yet have no place of departure, this is called the bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.
If one can be free from all speech and sounds such that there is no speech, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma;
if one can neither crave nor feel aversion toward any phenomena, this is called a bodhisattva’s embracing of the sublime Dharma.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
World-Honored One!”
"Is the collection of the Dharma that I have now taught in accordance with the collection of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata? The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
"The Dharma collection you have expounded has deeply captured my meaning.

When Ānanda spoke these sublime words on the Dharma collection, eighty thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and five hundred bhikṣus, having distanced themselves from all outflows (*āsrava*), attained liberation of mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
It is like discarding the husks and chaff to take the grain within.
World-Honored One, the bodhisattva is also like this: they discard what is not the Dharma and take up the true Dharma.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva abandons stinginess and greed to adopt generosity; abandons breaking the precepts to adopt upholding the precepts; abandons anger and resentment to adopt patience; abandons laziness to adopt diligence; abandons distraction to adopt meditative concentration; and abandons ignorance to adopt wisdom—this is called the Collection of Sublime and Wondrous Dharmas.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
That which involves seeking is contrary to the Dharma;
that which does not seek is non-grasping."
If one does not grasp, then there is no protection;
if there is no protection, then there is no defilement;
if there is no defilement, then there is no contention.
If one does not contend, then one is not stingy;
if one is not stingy, then one does not diminish;
if one does not diminish, then one does not act.
If one does not practice, then one does not regress;
if a bodhisattva does not regress, then all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, bestow upon that bodhisattva the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Dharma; this is called the Collection of the Sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva gives rise to such a thought as,
"I shall not regress from the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," then the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, will not bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon that bodhisattva.
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
All afflictions have seeking as their root.

"Bhagavān! To be far removed from all seeking is called being free from afflictions; because they are free from afflictions, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment.
Furthermore, Bhagavān!"
The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"Receiving a prediction of enlightenment is a worldly, false discourse. Why is this so?"
"The one who receives the prediction does not exist, and the one who bestows the prediction also does not exist; if both do not exist, where would the prediction be received?
"It is so, World-Honored One!"
Out of great compassion and in accordance with the world, there is this conventional expression:
"If a bodhisattva can know all such dharmas as these, they are called a bodhisattva who has received the prediction.
World-Honored One!
It is, for example, as if a magician were to bestow a prophecy upon a magical creation; yet that magical creation has no such thought as:
"I have received a prophecy," or "I shall attain perfect enlightenment.
World-Honored One!
The Bodhisattva is also like this, possessing a mind free from discrimination, just like that illusory transformation. Yet the Bodhisattva reflects:
"Awakening (bodhi) is not a characteristic that can be realized, nor is it a characteristic that can be abandoned."
Awakening is neither characterized by arising nor characterized by cessation;
awakening is not realized through the body nor realized through the mind;
awakening is not within, nor is it without, nor is it in between.
"Bodhi does not have such a thought as:
'I am bodhi, and the bodhisattva can realize me.
World-Honored One!"
This is called the "Collection of Sublime and Wondrous Dharmas.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva is without shame or remorse and free from anxiety or distress; in the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), there is neither increase nor decrease; in the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), there is neither darkness nor light; in the Stage of Blazing Fire (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), there is neither grasping nor abandoning; in the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), there is neither victory nor defeat; in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), there is no awakening through oneself and no awakening through another; in the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), there is neither going nor staying; in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), there is neither movement nor conceptual discrimination; in the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), there is neither accomplishment nor the desire for accomplishment; in the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), there is no awakening through oneself and no awakening through another; and in the Buddha Stage (*buddha-bhūmi*), one is able to perform all deeds while yet performing no deeds at all.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is naturally free from conceptual proliferation.
World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva thus attains the wisdom of conformity, they achieve mastery over the teachings they proclaim.
What is this mastery in proclaiming the Dharma?”
Because they do not cling to any speech,
they further attain pure mastery.
What is meant by pure mastery?
Because they are unstained in all circumstances,
they further attain mastery over eloquence.
What is mastery over eloquence?
This means that by relying on the words and phrases of a single dharma, one can speak without ceasing for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons without being able to exhaust them.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*). What is mastery over wisdom?
Because one is able to explain each individual dharma, word, and phrase as hundreds of thousands of millions of dharma-gates.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over birth.
What is mastery over birth?
Because they are born in whatever various places are conducive to benefiting sentient beings.
Furthermore, they attain mastery over samādhi.
What is mastery over samādhi?
In every moment of thought, if he wishes to enter samādhi, he is able to enter it immediately.
Furthermore, he attains mastery over maintenance (*adhitiṣṭhanā-vaśitā*). What is mastery over maintenance?
Because they manifest empowerment wherever they abide—whether in deer, wild animals, birds, beasts, plants, trees, or stone walls—they are able to preach the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over retinues.
What is mastery over retinues?
It is because one obtains an immeasurable retinue and an indestructible retinue.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over vision.
What is meant by mastery over vision?
It refers to seeing exquisite forms.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over hearing.
What is mastery over hearing?
It refers to hearing sublime sounds.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over the nose.
What is mastery over the nose?
It is that all fragrances perceived are exclusively the fragrance of the sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over the tongue.
What is mastery over the tongue?
It means consuming the flavor of the Dharma and not consuming the flavor of food.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over the body.
What is mastery over the body?
It is because one has attained the accomplishment of the Dharma-body and not the body sustained by food.
Furthermore, one attains mastery over the mind.
What is meant by mastery over the mind?
It is because one knows the conduct and knows the minds of even mosquitoes, gadflies, and ants.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Delightful-to-Beheld Spoke to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices in such and such a manner, sentient beings who see them through these very practices immediately give rise to joy.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva has nothing else to do but to transform and guide sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Fundamental, Supreme, and Wondrous Dharmas of Bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One!”
Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice and study the conduct of delighting in the Dharma.
World-Honored One,
what constitutes delighting in the Dharma?
Bodhisattvas have four kinds of cherished dharmas.
What are the four? They are:

the mind of equanimity that practices giving to all sentient beings without seeking karmic retribution; the protection of all sentient beings from evil conduct through pleasant speech; the accomplishment of their benefit and welfare; and loving all sentient beings as one loves oneself because of our shared commonality.
“World-Honored One!
These are called the four kinds of dharmas that a bodhisattva cherishes, which are cherished by all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can perform acts of cherishing.”
What are the four? They are:
possessing the wisdom of extensive learning because of being free from a mind of pride;
preaching the Dharma without attachment to signs because of being free from a mind seeking offerings and sustenance;
To conceive reverence for those venerable ones in order to seek wisdom;
and to exert diligence in order to transform and guide all sentient beings—these are called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can bring about the state of endearment.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can perform acts that inspire love and joy.
What are these four? They are:
the accomplishment of pure ethical discipline through the giving of the gift of Dharma;..."
One achieves contentment by dwelling in secluded places;
one attains meditative concentration by abiding in quietude and silence;
and one dwells well in cities and villages by not violating the sphere of proper dignified conduct.
These are called the four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can perform acts that bring about affection and joy.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas, namely: speaking truthfully because of eloquence;

speaking according to the Dharma because of teaching emptiness; speaking with patience because of an impartial mind; and speaking of tranquility because of guarding the sense faculties. These are called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can perform acts that bring about affection and joy.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can perform acts that inspire affection. What are these four? They are:
first, greeting with a friendly disposition because of one's skillful speech;"
Their intention is easily satisfied, because they know contentment with whatever little they obtain;
they achieve freedom from flattery and crookedness, because they act in accordance with their words and speech;
they are free from the dense forest of deceit, because they do not deceive any sentient beings.
These are called the four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can perform acts that inspire affection.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can perform acts that inspire affection. What are these four?
That is to say: one does not give rise to an evil mind because of inner tranquility;
one does not give rise to a deluded mind because of being free from external inversion;
and one does not give rise to a stingy mind because of contemplating the impermanence of all phenomena.
One does not give rise to a mind of arrogance because one knows all phenomena as they truly are.
These are called the four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can bring about what is pleasing.
Furthermore, there are four other kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can bring about what is pleasing.
What are the four? They are:
attaining a profound mind by being the first to inquire after others with courtesy;
and being free from attachment and defilement by attaining gentle and affectionate speech.
Because they relinquish all [worldly] minds yet never abandon the bodhicitta;
and because they abide in the ultimate truth with a profound mind while conforming to conventional truth.
These are called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can bring about things that inspire love and joy.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
The Bodhisattva attains the foremost emptiness, attains great supernormal knowledge and clarity, and attains great mastery;
he is skilled in knowing how to expound the collection of the Dharma, delights in the most profound teachings, accords with all sentient beings,
and ultimately attains the inconceivable and rare Dharma, attains the supple Dharma, and attains great supernormal knowledge.
One who has attained the rank of a Great Dharma Master; one who has attained the rank of a Great Dharma King; one who has accomplished great deeds;

one who acts as a refuge for the great multitudes of sentient beings; one who has attained great supernormal power and prowess—who, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, does not regress, yet gives rise to birth without being born, and undergoes death without dying; whose tasks are already accomplished, and who has realized Bodhi.
With a liberated mind, one exerts diligence; entering into nirvāṇa, one practices fulfillment;
seeking the unseekable, one cultivates all-knowledge and inquires of others.
“World-Honored One!
All oceans may be measured and known, but that ocean of the Great Vehicle wisdom of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be measured or known.
World-Honored One!”
Just as empty space, though pure, can be defiled by dust and grime, the mind of that bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be stained.
World-Honored One!
Although wind has no form, it might be grasped by the hand; yet the mind of that bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be attached to the objects of the six sense-fields.
“World-Honored One!
While the heat of the spring sun can be touched and felt by the hand, that mind of ‘self’ and ‘mine’ belonging to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be found.
World-Honored One!
"This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sunetra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Bhagavān! When a bodhisattva cultivates all dharmas, the arousal of the bodhicitta alone serves as their root. Why is this?"
"Bhagavān! All dharmas are entirely false and illusory; they are merely the conceptualization of the mind, lacking any substantiality in their essence.
Detached from all things, they are like illusions without foundation, manifesting according to whatever is sought."
It is far removed from agent and recipient; its nature does not abide, for it is free from all abidings.
World-Honored One!
All dharmas have no beginning and no end, because they are non-dual and free from duality.
World-Honored One!
All phenomena are without self and without what belongs to a self, because they have no master;
all phenomena are equal like that dharma-realm, because they are not adventitious.
“World-Honored One!
All phenomena have no master, because they are far removed from all cravings;
all phenomena are free from conceptualization and manifold discrimination, because they are far removed from the mind that grasps or rejects.”
All phenomena neither come nor go, for they are solely the domain of wisdom; this is because they are empty of a knower and lack a master.
“World-Honored One!

These hair-tip ordinary beings give rise to the notion of a self within the dharma of non-self, and give rise to the notion of a sentient being within the absence of sentient beings. The Bodhisattva reflects thus:”
"I shall cause all sentient beings to attain understanding through such sublime teachings.
World-Honored One!

This is called the bodhicitta, the mind of peace and security for all sentient beings, the joyful mind, the unsurpassed mind, the mind of the dharma-realm, the luminous mind, and the sustaining mind of sentient beings.
To arise based upon such a mind is called "generating the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
practicing the dāna-pāramitā is called the "mind of tranquility," and practicing the śīla-pāramitā is called...
Cultivating the perfection of patience is called the mind that is undiminished; cultivating the perfection of diligence is called the mind that does not regress;
cultivating the perfection of meditation is called the mind that is undisturbed;
and cultivating the perfection of wisdom is called the mind that does not discriminate false constructs. Cultivating...
Great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is called the gentle mind; practicing great compassion (*karuṇā*) is called the non-retrogressive mind;
practicing great sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is called the insatiable mind; practicing great equanimity (*upekṣā*) is called the stainless mind;
practicing great giving (*dāna*) is called the non-avaricious mind; and practicing the conduct of affection is called the mind free from the dense forest [of afflictions].
Practicing beneficial conduct is called the mind of equanimity; practicing sympathetic joy is called the supreme mind;
practicing the wisdom of emptiness is called the non-discriminating mind; practicing signless knowledge is called the non-conceptualizing mind;
practicing wishlessness is called the non-abiding mind; and practicing the conduct of enlightenment is called...
Cultivating the mind of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and practicing with diligent progress is called the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha;
cultivating the practice of non-destruction is called the mind of mindfulness of the Dharma; cultivating the mind of the dharma-realm is called the mind of mindfulness of the Sangha;
cultivating the immeasurable mind is called the mind of mindfulness of the precepts; and cultivating the mind of non-appropriation is called...
To practice the mindfulness of equanimity and the mindfulness of the deva realm is called "mindfulness of all roots of goodness"—

because it serves as the accumulation and adornment of all roots of goodness, and because that superior rebirth is attained through the generation of the bodhicitta and the accumulation of all roots of goodness.
“World-Honored One!
Based on my resolve for bodhicitta, I could speak of that single eon, or even immeasurable eons, without exhausting it.
In this way, all bodhisattvas gather immeasurable causes and conditions to give rise to bodhicitta.”
Therefore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva who wishes to seek out all wholesome dharmas should know and seek them within the arousal of the bodhicitta.
World-Honored One!
"This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sujāta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
World-Honored One!
All dharmas are well-born because their root is pure.
World-Honored One!
"What is the root of all phenomena?
World-Honored One!
All phenomena have emptiness as their root, because therein no views exist."
All dharmas have signlessness as their fundamental basis, because therein there are no discursive thoughts or investigations;
all dharmas have wishlessness as their fundamental basis, because therein there are no afflictions of the three realms;
all dharmas have non-action as their fundamental basis, because therein there is no agent.
All dharmas have selflessness as their fundamental basis, because therein the activity of a self is not perceived;
all dharmas have the absence of a sentient being as their fundamental basis, because therein the activity of a sentient being is not perceived;
all dharmas have the absence of a life-principle as their fundamental basis, because therein the activity of a life-principle is not perceived.
All phenomena are unarisen, because therein the view of eternalism is not practiced;
all phenomena are unceasing, because therein the view of nihilism is not practiced;
all phenomena are without substance, because therein the view of existence is not practiced.
All phenomena are equal to nirvāṇa, because in that state one does not engage in the view of existence;
all phenomena are like bodhi, because in that state one does not engage in the vision of a Buddha;
all phenomena are unconditioned, because in that state one does not engage in the vision of dharmas.
All dharmas are non-conjoined, because therein one does not perceive a "sangha.
World-Honored One,
this is called the sublime assembly of the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāśāstṛ addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva wishes first to bestow great enlightenment upon all sentient beings rather than realizing great enlightenment for themselves; if a bodhisattva performs all their deeds for the sake of all sentient beings rather than for themselves, yet perceives no sentient beings and does not abandon the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion—this is called a bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!
What are the great loving-kindness and great compassion of the bodhisattvas?
World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva does not perceive sentient beings yet does not abandon any roots of goodness, practicing those roots of goodness and dedicating them toward great enlightenment, this is called great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*);
if a bodhisattva does not abandon the tasks performed for all sentient beings, this is called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
If a bodhisattva perceives that worldly phenomena are themselves nirvana, yet does not abandon the diligence of cultivating the path, this is called great kindness;
if they do not forsake sentient beings, this is called great compassion.
If one generates the bodhicitta within oneself, this is called great kindness;
if one teaches and transforms all sentient beings, this is called great compassion.
If one relinquishes all internal and external things, this is called great kindness.

If one relinquishes internal and external roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings attaining the Buddha’s bodhi, dedicating them toward the unsurpassed path, this is called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
If one purely maintains all precepts, neither violating nor transgressing them, this is called great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*);
if, while maintaining pure precepts oneself, one causes the pure precepts of sentient beings to increase, this is called great compassion.
If one personally practices the peaceful conduct of patience and delights in it, this is called great kindness;
if one bestows peace and happiness upon all sentient beings, this is called great compassion.
If one is able to constantly practice the conduct of diligence within oneself in order to attain the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas, this is called great kindness;
if one causes all sentient beings to attain this diligence through the practice of great diligence, this is called great compassion.
If one constantly practices tranquility within oneself, this is called great loving-kindness;
if one causes all sentient beings to attain this tranquility through the practice of tranquility, this is called great compassion.
If one cultivates and fulfills wisdom for one's own sake, this is called great kindness;
if one uses one's own wisdom to increase the wisdom of all sentient beings, this is called great compassion.
If one neither practices nor does not practice, this is called great loving-kindness;
if one neither acts nor does not act, this is called great compassion.
If there is arising but no departing, this is called great loving-kindness.
If one departs without moving, this is called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
If one speaks without words, this is called great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*);
if one is attached without being bound, this is called great compassion.
If one is bound yet not apprehended, this is called great kindness;
if one enters nirvana yet does not perish, this is called great compassion.
If one brings forth one's own śarīra yet it is without bone, flesh, sinew, or blood, this is called great kindness.
If one cultivates the body such that the bones neither increase nor decrease, this is called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
If one practices relinquishment without relinquishing material things, this is called great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*);
if one protects all that is to be protected without seeking personal accomplishment, this is called great loving-kindness.
If one increases [virtue] without becoming conceited, this is called great compassion,
World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
The Bodhisattva takes the mind of tranquil meditative concentration as their supreme activity. Why is this?
Because when the Bodhisattva abides in a tranquil mind, the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas naturally manifests before them.
“World-Honored One!
Because Bodhisattvas revere tranquility and attain the peace and bliss of a concentrated mind, they achieve awakening and obtain all the gates of dhāraṇī.
World-Honored One!”
What is the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī?

It refers to being able to not forget whatever Dharma one hears, being able to receive and uphold whatever Dharma one hears, being able to comprehend whatever Dharma one hears, and causing all sentient beings to likewise comprehend it; this is called dhāraṇī.
By means of whichever dhāraṇī one does not increase [defilements] and does not discriminate;
by means of whichever dhāraṇī one is able to receive and uphold the eighty-four thousand dharma-doors without forgetting or omitting them;

and by means of whichever dhāraṇī one knows the mental activities of all sentient beings—because of knowing the minds of all sentient beings—one preaches the Dharma to each and every sentient being in such and such a way.

By means of whichever dhāraṇī enables one to hear the languages of all sentient beings—by hearing the voices of śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings, one attains great compassion (mahākaruṇā), and by hearing the voices of the noble ones (ārya), one attains great loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī);

by means of whichever dhāraṇī one hears and grasps a single phrase of the Dharma and can expound it for immeasurable eons—such is the bodhisattva’s eloquence of joyful speech (pratibhāna), which is unretained, inexhaustible, and without limit;
by means of whichever dhāraṇī one knows all vocal sounds as they truly are.
By means of whichever dhāraṇī one understands that all speech is the word of the Buddha;

by means of whichever dhāraṇī one hears the sounds of the Dharma being preached in the abodes of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions and retains them all—such a bodhisattva experiences no obstruction in hearing the Dharma from a second Buddha, just as they did from the first.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the bodhisattva’s upholding of the dhāraṇī.
World-Honored One!”

When a bodhisattva attains the power of dhāraṇī, according to whichever dhāraṇī manifests before them, they can explain all phenomena just as they would explain a single phenomenon, a single syllable, or a single phrase.
Thus he speaks of all dharma-realms; yet this bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of arrogance nor initiate acts of negligence, thereby attaining the *uttara-dhāraṇī*.
According to whichever *dhāraṇī* enables him to speak of all phenomena as they appear before the world and to perceive all that appears before the world, he attains the *saṃbhāra-dhāraṇī*.
According to whichever *dhāraṇī* enables him to sever the doubts of all sentient beings and to sever all afflictions, he attains the *uttara-saṃbhāra-dhāraṇī*.
Whichever dhāraṇī can cause all wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*) to increase and cause all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be exhausted, that is the *caryā-dhāraṇī*.

“World-Honored One! By means of whichever dhāraṇī one knows all phenomena and knows the radiance of all phenomena, this bodhisattva knows all phenomena as they truly are without making conceptual distinctions. They practice all phenomena, yet their own body and mind do not truly practice; they speak of all phenomena, yet do not speak of any words; they relinquish all phenomena, yet do not lose them; they increase all phenomena, yet do not increase a single thing; they diminish all phenomena, yet do not diminish a single dharma. They speak of all phenomena, yet there is no speech; they cause others to enter nirvāṇa, yet they are unmoved within the world; they cause others to attain the stages of the noble ones, yet they do not depart from the stage of ordinary beings; they subdue all māras, yet this is not an action arising from body, speech, or mind.”
"This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Sublime Dharmas of all Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“World-Honored One, all dharmas have liberation as their characteristic.
A bodhisattva does not discriminate between what is bondage and what is liberation.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Liberation is not other than the self, and the self is not other than liberation.
World-Honored One!
Liberation does not increase a single dharma, nor does it decrease a single dharma.
World-Honored One!
"Liberation, World-Honored One, comes from nowhere;
bondage, World-Honored One, likewise goes nowhere."
A bodhisattva who has attained liberation does not give rise to such a thought as,
"I have attained liberation.
His mind knows only this:
"Just as liberation is, so too are all dharmas.
World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva gives rise to such a thought:
"The world is a defiled dharma; nirvāṇa is a pure dharma.
Because of this, the bodhisattva does not attain liberation. Why is that?
Those who possess the view of a self give rise to this thought:
"World-Honored One!
If a person gives rise to such a thought:"
"I loathe the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, and seek entry into nirvana"—
this person does not attain liberation. Why is this?
There is the view of a self; those who possess the view of a self give rise to such a thought:
"World-Honored One!
A bhikṣu whose mind has attained liberation reflects in this way:"
"All dharmas have the characteristic of liberation, yet foolish ordinary beings, being ignorant and unaware of this, give rise to such thoughts.
It is for this reason that I shall cause all sentient beings to know these dharmas."
"World-Honored One!
When a bhikṣu who has attained liberation gives rise to this thought:
'These ordinary people seek liberation within the state of perpetual liberation that is all phenomena,' I give rise to a heart of great compassion toward those various beings."
Why is this? If a person seeks liberation, that person will not attain liberation.
For this reason, World-Honored One!
A bhikṣu who desires liberation should contemplate both the binder and the bound; he should know both the binder and the bound. Such a person does not differentiate liberation;
if one does not differentiate, that person attains liberation.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the ‘Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharmas of Bodhisattvas.
*Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
The Scripture on the Collection of the Buddha’s Teachings, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsamudramati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! World-Honored One! Regarding the bodhisattvas...”
One should not fear the afflictions (*kleśa*). Why is this?
Because where there are afflictions, wherever those afflictions exist, there is awakening (*bodhi*); for one who has severed the afflictions, there is no awakening.
"World-Honored One!
Emptiness and all afflictions—these two are one and the same; there is no distinction between them.
World-Honored One!"

Bodhi, all afflictions, and all sentient beings—these dharmas are likewise one and the same, without any distinction; it is only because ordinary fools of limited capacity fall into inverted views that they discriminate between "I am defiled" and "I am pure."

"Bhagavan! A bodhisattva practicing correctly does not sever afflictions nor grasp at pure dharmas; rather, this bodhisattva contemplates the gateway of all afflictions and thereby attains the various samādhis and the gateways of the various dhāraṇīs."
Therefore, World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva knows that the nature of all Buddha-dharmas is affliction (*kleśa*). When such afflictions are present in whichever sentient beings possess a distracted mind and a perverted mind, those hair-tip ordinary beings will inevitably enter the evil realms and undergo various sufferings. By correctly contemplating in this way, the bodhisattvas are able to attain the *bodhi* of all Buddhas.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
all bodhisattvas should practice in accordance with the逆流 (pratiloma), and not in accordance with the順流 (anuloma).
World-Honored One!
Those bodhisattvas who have attained liberation do so within *nirvāṇa*, not within the world.

Why is this? Because bodhisattvas should fear *nirvāṇa* and not fear the world, for by contemplating the world they attain great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and realize great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

If one discriminates between nirvana and feels weary of or afraid of the world, such a bodhisattva, by virtue of that weariness toward the world, will regress from the unsurpassed enlightenment of all buddhas.
"Bhagavān! Bodhisattvas develop great loving-kindness and great compassion for sentient beings in the world, not for those sentient beings who have attained nirvāṇa. Bhagavān!"
Regarding what is called "nirvāṇa," O World-Honored One, nirvāṇa is the cessation of the unreal mind of false discrimination.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to see nirvāṇa should contemplate the mind in which false discrimination has ceased; it is in such a state that one attains nirvāṇa.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One!”
“World-Honored One, a bodhisattva need not study many dharmas.
If a bodhisattva upholds one dharma and skillfully understands one dharma, all other Buddha-dharmas will naturally be as if held in the palm of their hand.”
"Bhagavān! What is this one dharma?
It is what is called great compassion."
If a bodhisattva practices great compassion, all the dharmas of the Buddhas are as if held in the palm of their hand.
World-Honored One!
It is like the wheel-treasure mounted by a universal monarch (cakravartin); wherever it goes, the fourfold army follows in accordance with it.
World-Honored One!
It is likewise with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: wherever they go, following upon their great compassion, all those Buddha-dharmas naturally follow along with that great compassion.
World-Honored One!
It is like the rising sun that shines brightly upon the myriad things, so that all sentient beings encounter no difficulty in performing their tasks.
World-Honored One!

It is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva: wherever the sun of great compassion shines upon the world, it is easy for the sentient beings there to practice all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
World-Honored One!
For example, just as all the sense faculties have the mind as their basis and are all able to grasp their respective objects according to the mind’s will, so it is,
World-Honored One!

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: relying upon great compassion, they maintain all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), naturally practicing within each factor and in whatever tasks are to be performed.
World-Honored One!
It is just as, for example, based upon that life-faculty (jīvitendriya), there exist the remaining faculties.
World-Honored One!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: all other factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) exist in dependence upon great compassion.
World-Honored One!
This is called the "Collection of Supreme and Sublime Dharmas."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas take the straightforward mind and the profound mind as their root.”
"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva lacks a straightforward mind and a profound mind, that bodhisattva is far removed from the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas. Bhagavān!"

For Bodhisattvas who have accomplished the straightforward mind and the profound mind, even if no Buddha is preaching the Dharma, the sound of the Dharma naturally issues forth from the sky above, from trees, and from stone walls and other such places.
World-Honored One!

Bodhisattvas with a straightforward mind and a profound mind can naturally recollect within their own thoughts; upon hearing the sound of the Dharma, they accord with the wondrous teachings of all Buddhas.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the straightforward mind and the profound mind.
World-Honored One!
It is like a person who, having feet, is able to travel.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
It is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: possessing a straightforward mind and a profound mind, they naturally practice the sublime dharmas of all Buddhas."
World-Honored One!
It is just as if a person were to possess the upper parts [of the body], they would have a lifespan.
World-Honored One!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: if they possess a straightforward mind and a profound mind, such a Bodhisattva possesses the Bodhi of all Buddhas.
World-Honored One!
“World-Honored One, just as a person who possesses life can accomplish all affairs,
so it is with a bodhisattva mahāsattva: if a bodhisattva possesses a straightforward mind and a profound mind, that bodhisattva will then achieve the fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas.”
World-Honored One!
For example, because there is that which can be burned, there is that which can burn;
apart from that which can be burned, there is no that which can burn.
World-Honored One!
It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: if they possess a straightforward mind and a profound mind, they are able to cause the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas to blaze forth;
if they are devoid of a straightforward mind and a profound mind, they will not cause the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas to blaze forth.
World-Honored One!
It is like when there are clouds, then rain can fall.
World-Honored One!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: because they possess a straightforward mind and a profound mind, there is the rain of the Buddhas' Dharma.
World-Honored One!
It is, for example, like a tree whose roots have rotted; it cannot produce sprouts, leaves, flowers, or fruit.
World-Honored One!
It is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: if they lack a straightforward mind and a profound mind, then all the wholesome dharmas of the Buddhas will no longer grow.
Therefore, World-Honored One,

a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the enlightenment of all Buddhas should properly adopt the straightforward mind and the profound mind, properly guard the straightforward mind and the profound mind, and properly purify the straightforward mind and the profound mind.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the ‘Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sūrakṣa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva need not guard the various dharmas.
World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva is able to skillfully guard his own mind, then because that bodhisattva skillfully guards his own mind, he will be able to accomplish the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas.
World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva guards all dharmas, that bodhisattva will be unable to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva does not guard all dharmas and enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), that bodhisattva is without fault; they do not contradict the Buddhas or bodhisattvas, and they are able to know the Buddha-dharmas within their own mind without guarding their own mind.
Seeing that this mind arises dependent upon causes and conditions, one sees in this way that all phenomena arise dependent upon causes and conditions;
seeing one’s own mind as like an illusion, one sees all phenomena as like an illusion, yet the mind cannot be found within, without, or in between the two;

seeing all phenomena in this way, they are seen to be just like the mind, devoid of the marks of form, incapable of being demonstrated or seen, without physical obstruction, ungraspable, non-illuminating, and non-abiding—seeing all phenomena, their characteristics are thus.
If one can see in this way, that bodhisattva is then able to attain a mind of equanimity;
because they have attained a mind of equanimity, such a bodhisattva no longer further grasps at dharmas.

This bodhisattva no longer dwells, no longer acts, neither grasps nor abandons, and seeks nothing; because they seek nothing, they do not grasp; because they do not grasp, they have no attachment; because they have no attachment, they are undefiled; thus, this bodhisattva is undefiled by all phenomena.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the ‘Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva does not speak such words as:
‘By what kind of speech can I provoke anger in others?’”
A bodhisattva does not speak such words as,
"By what kind of speech can I arouse a mind of affliction in others?
A bodhisattva does not speak such words:
"What kind of speech can cause others not to understand?"—
the Bodhisattva does not speak such words as,
"What kind of speech is meaningless and false?"
A bodhisattva does not speak thus:
"By what kind of discourse can the light of wisdom be prevented from arising?
A bodhisattva does not speak thus:
"By what kind of speech can one cause the mind not to give rise to joy, nor to be fully satisfied, and such that upon hearing it with the ear, no delight is produced?
The Bodhisattva does not speak such words as:
"By what kind of speech can one cause the destruction of both places?"
"World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva does not speak such words as:
'By what kind of discourse can I cause others to be unable to understand emptiness?'"
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
Among all forms of speech, such speech as that is the most firm and stable.
"By what kind of discourse can one cause others to understand emptiness?
"World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva can understand the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena—that they are without mind and without self, that their characteristic is non-dual, and that they remain far removed from dualistic characteristics while not abandoning the work performed for the sake of all sentient beings—this is called the unobstructed great compassion of a bodhisattva."
If a bodhisattva practices unobstructed great compassion, that bodhisattva is able to study what all buddhas have studied;
if they study what all buddhas have studied, that bodhisattva is able to know that all phenomena are like space;
because they know that all phenomena are like space, that bodhisattva attains the Space Treasury (Gaganagañja).
This bodhisattva, desiring to relinquish, is able to relinquish all forms of relinquishing, yet gives rise to no dualistic mind regarding relinquishment and stinginess;

regarding breaking precepts and upholding precepts, patience and anger, diligence and laziness, distraction and meditative concentration, and delusion and wisdom, they give rise to no dualistic conceptions.
This bodhisattva no longer seeks the sublime dharmas of the Buddhas, nor does he abandon the unwholesome dharmas of ordinary worldlings.
World-Honored One!
It is like all waters that enter the great ocean, which all become of one single taste, namely, the salty taste.
World-Honored One!
It is the same for a bodhisattva: having entered the great ocean of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all dharmas that are perceived are of a single flavor, namely, the flavor of true liberation.
World-Honored One!
It is, for example, like the light of the sun, which shines equally upon all sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
The wisdom of a bodhisattva is likewise: it illuminates all phenomena equally.
World-Honored One, all phenomena do not contradict emptiness.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva can know in this way, that bodhisattva is able to perceive true bodhi within all dharmas.
If a bodhisattva perceives true bodhi within all dharmas, that bodhisattva knows that all spoken sounds and voices are the words of the Buddha.”
This bodhisattva teaches the Dharma without attachment; this bodhisattva is said to have attained the unhindered eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
World-Honored One!
This is called the "Collection of the Supreme and Sublime Dharma."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
People of the world grasp at things erroneously and with inversion; they might say:
"It is because of the pāramitās that a bodhisattva receives his name."
"This is not so. Why is that? World-Honored One!"
"Because it is by depending on the bodhisattva that the various pāramitās receive their names.

World-Honored One, if it were by depending on the pāramitās that the bodhisattva receives his name, then one should also depend on all sentient beings to be called a 'bodhisattva'; however, this is not the case."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva gives birth to the various pāramitās and knows the various pāramitās; because the bodhisattva gives birth to the various pāramitās, they preach them for the sake of all sentient beings.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has always said:
"A bodhisattva can give rise to dharmas that have never been born, can accomplish dharmas that have never been accomplished, and can expound dharmas that have never been expounded."
"World-Honored One!

It is not that the various pāramitās can protect the bodhisattva; rather, it is the bodhisattva who can protect the various pāramitās. For this reason, it is said that the bodhisattva can protect all dharmas."
“World-Honored One!

The various pāramitās cannot sustain a bodhisattva; rather, it is the bodhisattva who can sustain the various pāramitās. For this reason, it is said that a bodhisattva is able to receive and uphold the Dharma.”
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are free from illness, because their own nature is stainless.
World-Honored One!”
All phenomena are non-dual, because they are far removed from sentient beings and the self;
all phenomena are mindless, because they are far removed from that which is to be grasped or abandoned;
all phenomena are devoid of consciousness, because they have no initial origination.
All dharmas have no characteristic of coming, because they are without interval;
all dharmas have no going, because they are immovable;
all dharmas have no death, because they have no life.
All dharmas are not animated, because they have never from the beginning consumed anything;
all dharmas are without substance, because they do not enter into combination;
all dharmas do not diminish, because the dharma-realm is without differentiation.
"All dharmas cannot be cut or severed, because they are formless;
all dharmas are like adamant, because the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is equal.
"World-Honored One!"
To know all phenomena in this way is for a bodhisattva to be able to know the true essence of all phenomena;
if one knows the true essence of all phenomena, that bodhisattva is able to know emptiness;
if one can know emptiness, that bodhisattva does not engage in dispute or contention with others.
If one does not contend with others, this bodhisattva is able to abide in the dharma of a śramaṇa;
if one can abide in the dharma of a śramaṇa, this bodhisattva is then able to abide nowhere;
if one can abide nowhere, this bodhisattva does not give rise to outflows within the realms of the outflows.
If one does not give rise to outflows regarding any objects of perception, this bodhisattva is able to be free from all illnesses;
if there are no illnesses, this bodhisattva is named a Tathāgata;
if a bodhisattva receives the name Tathāgata, this bodhisattva does not speak with duality.

If one does not speak these two words, this bodhisattva neither abandons the world nor grasps at nirvana; rather, they speak solely for the sake of all sentient beings, teaching the distancing from all conceptualization, delusion, and affliction.

“World-Honored One! This is called the collection of the supreme and wondrous Dharma; the collection that is non-perverted; it is called the collection of emptiness; the collection of signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, and non-ceasing; the collection of the patience toward the non-arising of dharmas; the collection of the Great Vehicle; the collection of the turning of the great wheel of Dharma; the collection of the great perfections; the collection of all the stages (bhūmis); and the collection of all dharmas that are non-perverted.”
“World-Honored One!

All bodhisattvas rely on the great assembly of the Dharma for their practice, cultivation, and observance. Some become universal monarchs (cakravartin) within various lands, upholding the ten paths of wholesome action and enabling sentient beings to dwell securely in those ten paths;
others become preeminent leaders, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they may attain supramundane excellence.”
Sometimes he becomes a great elder, able to cause sentient beings to weary of the evils of the world;
sometimes he becomes Śakra, Lord of the Devas, able to cause the gods to refrain from negligence;
sometimes he becomes Brahmā, able to cause sentient beings to abide in dhyāna-concentration, the four immeasurables, and so forth.
Sometimes he manifests as one of the Four Heavenly Kings, able to cause sentient beings not to defile their minds amidst all phenomena;
sometimes he manifests as a śramaṇa, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they do not hear evil dharmas;

sometimes he manifests as a brāhmaṇa, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they know the place of tranquility—himself tranquil and causing his retinue to also abide in tranquility, himself supple and causing his retinue to also attain suppleness, fully abiding in all places because he has attained great mastery.
They are able to act as great Dharma masters because they can sever all doubts of sentient beings;
they do not give rise to cowardice in any situation because all afflictions have been exhausted.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Collection of the Supreme and Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī:

“Mañjuśrī! If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this sublime and wondrous collection of Dharma spoken by Mañjuśrī, as well as the sublime and wondrous collections of Dharma of the bodhisattvas and the sublime and wondrous collections of Dharma of the śrāvakas, are able to understand and believe them, those sentient beings have deeply planted roots of goodness; they have not merely made offerings to a single Buddha, nor have they planted roots of goodness under one or two Buddhas alone.”
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
The profound bodhi of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, is the deep and wondrous realm of those who possess wisdom and are able to know the Dharma.
“Mañjuśrī! This sublime Dharma-gate cannot be heard by sentient beings with meager roots of goodness; even if they were to hear it, they would be unable to believe it.”

If a bodhisattva can personally realize it, that bodhisattva is able to have faith; furthermore, because they are protected by various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), such a person is able to believe, receive, and uphold [the teaching], and is able to attain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).
“Mañjuśrī! Apart from this practice of the Dharma, there is not a single person who attains Buddhahood. Mañjuśrī!”

In the past, as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges attained the bodhi of a Buddha; those Buddhas practiced such dharmic conduct and thereby attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Mañjuśrī! If a person, being far removed from this Dharma, desires to attain bodhi, that person is like one who attempts to bind space; they will be unable to attain the Dharma.”

If one departs from this practice of the Dharma, even the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti) cannot be attained; how much less can one attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and thereby achieve unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

“Mañjuśrī! My śrāvakas who have attained both-fold liberation, who have attained the eight liberations and the four analytical knowledges—even those śrāvakas do not attain liberation apart from this practice of the Dharma.”

“Mañjuśrī! It would be better to hear this profound and wondrous Dharma-gate and give rise to slander, thereby being reborn in the evil realms, than to give rise to faith in other shallow Dharma-gates and thereby be reborn in the good realms.”

Why is this? Those who slander this Dharma-gate will be born in hell; however, by hearing this Dharma-gate, they attain liberation in the present moment, whereas hearing other shallow Dharma-gates does not lead to birth in the good realms.
“Mañjuśrī! There are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this dharma-gate, can give rise to faith. What are these four?

It is said that such a person, in past lives, has heard this Dharma-gate; having heard it, they have rejoiced in it and possess great roots of goodness; adorned with great roots of goodness, they have well protected, perfected, and maintained the practice of hearing-wisdom.
“Mañjuśrī! These are called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva, upon hearing this dharma-gate, can give rise to faith. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!”
Furthermore, there are four qualities by which a bodhisattva, upon hearing this dharma-gate, can give rise to faith.
What are these four? They are:

constantly contemplating with right mindfulness; always fearing all unwholesome karma; always making the vow for great enlightenment; and possessing a nature that is upright, supple, peaceful, and delights in cultivating sublime practices.
“Mañjuśrī! These are called the four dharmas that a bodhisattva must accomplish in order to be able to give rise to faith upon hearing this Dharma-gate. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!”
If bodhisattvas accomplish four dharmas, they will not give rise to slander upon hearing this dharma-gate.
What are these four? They are:

being ultimately accomplished in the vow for enlightenment; attaining the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); accomplishing right view; and attaining the non-retrogressive mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mañjuśrī! These are called the four dharmas that, when fully accomplished, prevent one from giving rise to slander upon hearing this dharma-gate. Mañjuśrī!
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva, upon hearing this dharma-gate, can give rise to faith.
What are these four? They are:
achieving the wisdom of hearing, achieving prajñā, achieving emptiness, and attaining great dhāraṇī through meditative concentration.
Mañjuśrī! These are called the four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva, upon hearing this dharma-gate, can give rise to faith. Mañjuśrī!
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva, upon hearing this dharma-gate, is able to understand it fully.
What are these four? They are:

the accomplishment of the adornment of merit; the accomplishment of the adornment of the wisdom derived from hearing; the accomplishment of the adornment of knowledge; and the accomplishment of the adornment of a supple mind through various meditative concentrations.
Mañjuśrī! These are called the four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva, upon hearing this dharma-gate, is able to understand it. Mañjuśrī!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What are these four? They are:

that a bodhisattva perceives all forms as the form of a Buddha; hears all dharmas as the Dharma of a Buddha; remains far removed from all seeking, even to the point of not seeking the enlightenment of a Buddha; and does not retreat from great compassion.
Mañjuśrī! These are called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, Mañjuśrī!
All bodhisattvas should constantly seek to hear, read, and recite this sutra. Mañjuśrī!
Bodhisattvas who aspire to swiftly attain bodhi should always diligently seek to hear this Dharma-gate.
If a bodhisattva wishes to quickly receive the prediction of enlightenment, they should always diligently seek to hear this Dharma-gate;

if a bodhisattva wishes to sever the obstruction of karma, wishes to sever the obstruction of afflictions, and wishes to sever the obstruction to knowledge, that bodhisattva should always seek to hear this sutra;
if a bodhisattva wishes to obtain unsurpassed offerings for all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, that bodhisattva should always seek to hear this sutra.
"May I always protect the sublime Dharma; for this reason, a bodhisattva should constantly hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra.
Mañjuśrī! If there are people who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, are able to believe and accept it with patience, and do not give rise to slander—Mañjuśrī!"
"I bestow upon this person the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpāda removed from his neck eight million *asaṃkhyeya* jewel necklaces and scattered them over the Tathāgata, saying these words:
"World-Honored One!
"By virtue of this merit, may all sentient beings achieve the state of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

At that time, those necklaces remained in the air above the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, forming a great jeweled canopy of various supreme and wondrous adornments. Its four corners were of a magnitude exceeding those of devas and humans, adorned with exquisite features. Those śrāvakas, as well as all the bodhisattvas, Śakra-devendra, Brahmā-rāja, and the Four Heavenly Kings, had never before seen or heard of such a thing. This great jeweled canopy followed the Tathāgata wherever he went and remained stationary wherever the Tathāgata stayed.

When these wondrous events were manifested, immeasurable devas and humans were all struck with a sense of rare wonder and marvel; they stood with their palms joined above their heads, praising the Tathāgata and gazing up at him without blinking for even a moment.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Aśaṅkita gave rise to a heart of joy and wonder. He bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“O Tathāgata, vessel of all masses of merit; Among devas, humans, and living beings, only the Buddha can save.
In the world, there is no one superior to the Buddha; No one is more supreme, tranquil, or equal.”
With an impartial mind and conduct free from guile, they bind their hearts with compassion for the world;
like space, their minds are equanimous and untainted as they teach the Dharma for the peace and happiness of many.
The World-Honored One has no kin and no enemies; he is without sorrow and without joy.
Able to save the world like a skilled physician, he practices compassion toward the world without discrimination.
Asuras, devas, humans, nāgas, and yakṣas—by taking refuge in the Buddha, they attain tranquility.
The Buddha is supreme within the three realms; therefore, I now take refuge in him.
The Sugata has no further conditioned phenomena, yet he possesses no merit in the state of quiescence;
having abandoned the two paths and being free from discrimination, he dwells in the world having attained cessation.
The realm of quiescent extinction is unfathomable; only the Tathāgata, possessed of the ten powers, knows it.
Like the earth and space, it cannot be measured; therefore, I join my palms and bear it upon my head.
Neither sinking nor floating amidst the great waves, neither drifting nor dwelling—this Unsurpassed One;
the Buddha alone has reached the further shore of the ocean of existence. To the incomparable Ocean of Wisdom, I take refuge.
Just as a lotus in water cannot be defiled, The Buddha walks through the world unstained by worldly dharmas.
There is none who can equal the Buddha; Because he is peerless, I take refuge in him.
The Tathāgata knows no phenomena that he does not know; possessing the ten powers, he transcends all, and his prowess among the multitudes is peerless.
For this reason, the Buddha is named the Sole Hero Who Walks Alone.
Able to receive the nectar-like Dharma of all Buddhas, Therefore, one is far removed from all fears;
To the unsurpassed physician, the supreme Arhat, The one of great compassion, I take refuge.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anutpāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One alone knows my mind; I do not make this offering to the Tathāgata for my own sake.”
“World-Honored One!

Having offered this necklace as an offering to the Tathāgata and praised the Tathāgata, by virtue of these roots of goodness and merit, I pray that all sentient beings may attain the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas.”
“World-Honored One!
This is my intention.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance—when the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, smile with a serene countenance, it is never in vain.

At that time, the Tathāgata emitted from his face various kinds of immeasurable light rays—colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, crystal, gold, and silver—in infinite varieties. These lights universally illuminated the immeasurable and boundless worlds of the ten directions, extinguishing the immeasurable sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings in all evil realms and generating immeasurable joy and happiness for gods and humans. Having done so, they withdrew and circled the Tathāgata hundreds of thousands of millions of times before vanishing into the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.

At that time, the great assembly, seeing this radiance, felt joy in their hearts; leaping for joy and dwelling in peace and happiness, they joined their palms toward the Buddha and stood to one side, thinking:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata smile with such a serene countenance?"
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and asked about the cause and condition of the smile in verse:
"O Unsurpassed and Foremost Honored One!
The world, including gods and humans, gazes upon the Tathāgata’s abiding and doubts the cause of his smile.

Great Teacher, you who are free from afflictions and who know both the Dharma and those to be converted—this joyful countenance of yours is surely not without purpose; we pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
From the gateway of his face he radiates light, pure and bringing forth joy;
for devas, humans, and those in the evil realms, the light touches their bodies with peace and bliss.
The Great Being emits this radiance from the gateway of his face.
What is the meaning of this light?
I pray only that you, in your great compassion, will explain it.
From his teeth issues a most wondrous light, brilliant and exceedingly pure white.
Manifesting as most supreme, obscuring all other lights,
and causing other luminosity and darkness to not appear— by this, the world rejoices. For what purpose, then,
does the Buddha’s compassion act?
From what merit has this arisen?
We pray that you will explain the purpose of your compassion and sever our doubts.
For one who has distanced himself from afflictions, a smile does not occur without cause or condition.
The Light of Sublime Radiance emerges from the face-gate, Universally illuminating the ten directions;
Having performed its task, it returns and withdraws, Entering the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
This light arises from the Buddha’s intention, Manifesting the emergence of the Sage’s mind.
"Like lightning in the sky during the day, it shines everywhere without ceasing.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda: "Ānanda!"

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Aproduita (Unarisen) shall, after twelve kalpas in the future, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. His Buddha-name shall be Mahāprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The kalpa shall be named Praśastadeva, and the world shall be named Mahānanda.
Ānanda! That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāprabha shall have a lifespan of one great kalpa, and the lifespan of the sentient beings in that land shall be twelve small kalpas.

Ānanda! Just as the exquisite pleasures experienced by the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, so too are the exquisite pleasures experienced by the sentient beings in that Buddha-land.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to the Bodhisattva Anutpādita: “O Mahāsattva!
You have gained a most excellent benefit; today the Tathāgata has bestowed upon you a prophecy that you shall certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Bodhisattva Asaṃprasthita said:
"Venerable Subhūti! What dharma do you perceive that is called 'attaining Buddhahood'?"
Subhūti said: "Good son! I do not perceive any dharma that achieves anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

He asked: "Venerable Subhūti, if you do not perceive any dharma by which one attains Buddhahood, why did you deceive me, a Great Being, by bestowing upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Subhūti said: "Noble son!
Since the Tathāgata has bestowed upon you the prophecy that you shall certainly attain Buddhahood, it is for this reason that I have made this statement."
The Bodhisattva Asaṃprasthita said: "Venerable Subhūti!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, know phenomena as they truly are; therefore, the Buddha has said:
"You shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How does the Tathāgata know dharmas as they truly are? Subhūti!
If there is a bodhisattva who seeks awakening, the Buddhas do not bestow upon that person a prediction of enlightenment;
if there is a bodhisattva who does not seek awakening, the Tathāgatas then bestow a prediction upon them.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, know the dharmas as they truly are to be without the characteristic of receiving a prediction; yet, for the sake of planting various roots of goodness in sentient beings, they make this prediction: "You shall become a Buddha."
Subhūti! What dharma do you perceive that you speak these words:
"A Mahāsattva will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi"?
Subhūti said: "O son of good family!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, bestow predictions based upon conventional words and letters; we śrāvakas speak thus because we follow the World-Honored Buddha."
The Bodhisattva Aprodukta said: "Venerable Subhūti!
As for 'letters,' if they are based on worldly convention, they are called letters; however, from the perspective of the noble ones, they are not letters."
Why is this? Because that which is spoken by the Noble Ones is entirely true, whereas worldly speech is entirely false.
Therefore, Venerable Subhūti!
This worldly, false speech should not be spoken within the Noble Dharma. Venerable Subhūti!

Because bodhisattvas seek to protect sentient beings, if they were to hear the profound ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and become terrified or lose faith, for this reason the Noble Ones, out of great compassion, set aside the true Dharma and speak worldly, illusory words. This is done to guide and protect ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana); they would never speak in such a way for the sake of the Noble Ones.
If one acts as a noble one, then one speaks the true Dharma; this true Dharma is what the noble ones cherish and delight in.
What, Venerable Subhūti, is called the true Dharma of the noble ones?
Regarding the "sacred true dharma": the nature of the dharma of bodhi is eternally quiescent, and thus it is called "true reality.
